papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: Decoder Decomposition for the Analysis of the Latent Space of Nonlinear Autoencoders With Wind-Tunnel Experimental Data
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the latent space of nonlinear autoencoders, specifically in the context of fluid dynamics data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the decoder decomposition, a post-processing method to connect latent variables to coherent structures (POD modes) in autoencoders, enabling ranking and selection of latent variables for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The decoder decomposition is a simple and robust method for ranking and selecting latent variables based on flow physics, which aids in the design and interpretation of nonlinear autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
The dimension of the latent space significantly impacts the interpretability of autoencoders.
The decoder decomposition can identify physical and spurious latent variables.
Reconstruction error is a function of both latent space dimension and decoder size.
The method can rank and select latent variables based on the coherent structures they represent.
The method is successfully applied to both synthetic and experimental fluid dynamics data.
papers.abstract: Turbulent flows are chaotic and multi-scale dynamical systems, which have large numbers of degrees of freedom. Turbulent flows, however, can be modelled with a smaller number of degrees of freedom when using the appropriate coordinate system, which is the goal of dimensionality reduction via nonlinear autoencoders. Autoencoders are expressive tools, but they are difficult to interpret. The goal of this paper is to propose a method to aid the interpretability of autoencoders. This is the decoder decomposition. First, we propose the decoder decomposition, which is a post-processing method to connect the latent variables to the coherent structures of flows. Second, we apply the decoder decomposition to analyse the latent space of synthetic data of a two-dimensional unsteady wake past a cylinder. We find that the dimension of latent space has a significant impact on the interpretability of autoencoders. We identify the physical and spurious latent variables. Third, we apply the decoder decomposition to the latent space of wind-tunnel experimental data of a three-dimensional turbulent wake past a bluff body. We show that the reconstruction error is a function of both the latent space dimension and the decoder size, which are correlated. Finally, we apply the decoder decomposition to rank and select latent variables based on the coherent structures that they represent. This is useful to filter unwanted or spurious latent variables, or to pinpoint specific coherent structures of interest. The ability to rank and select latent variables will help users design and interpret nonlinear autoencoders.

papers.title: FIGNN: Feature-Specific Interpretability for Graph Neural Network Surrogate Models
papers.research_question: How can we design a Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture that provides feature-specific interpretability for multivariate prediction tasks on unstructured grids in scientific applications?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a feature-specific interpretable Graph Neural Network (FIGNN) architecture with independent Top-K pooling masks per output variable and an error-budget regularization term to align interpretability with predictive error, enabling localized, feature-wise attribution in scientific surrogate modeling.
papers.conclusion: FIGNN provides a balance between interpretability and predictive performance, offering domain experts detailed insights into feature-specific contributions to prediction accuracy in scientific surrogate modeling.
papers.key_findings:
FIGNN provides feature-specific interpretability masks that highlight physically meaningful spatial regions for each predicted variable, such as frontal boundaries in climate data and recirculation zones in fluid flow.
The error budget regularization effectively localizes prediction errors within the masked regions, with stronger regularization increasing error concentration at the cost of slightly reduced predictive accuracy.
FIGNN maintains competitive predictive performance compared to baseline GNN models on both atmospheric (SPEEDY) and fluid dynamics (BFS) datasets.
The method generalizes across distinct physical domains (climate and fluid dynamics) with different mesh types and governing equations.
There is a trade-off between interpretability (mask coherence and error localization) and predictive accuracy, controllable via the regularization parameter λ.
papers.limitation:
Error accumulation in multi-step rollouts leads to deteriorating prediction quality over long time horizons.
There is a trade-off between interpretability (mask coherence) and predictive accuracy, where higher regularization improves error localization but increases final loss.
future_direction: Extending the framework to spatially three-dimensional settings.
Real-time adaptive interpretability.
Uncertainty quantification strategies.
Using FIGNN for inverse problems like super-resolution, control, and optimization.
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel graph neural network (GNN) architecture, the Feature-specific Interpretable Graph Neural Network (FIGNN), designed to enhance the interpretability of deep learning surrogate models defined on unstructured grids in scientific applications. Traditional GNNs often obscure the distinct spatial influences of different features in multivariate prediction tasks. FIGNN addresses this limitation by introducing a feature-specific pooling strategy, which enables independent attribution of spatial importance for each predicted variable. Additionally, a mask-based regularization term is incorporated into the training objective to explicitly encourage alignment between interpretability and predictive error, promoting localized attribution of model performance. The method is evaluated for surrogate modeling of two physically distinct systems: the SPEEDY atmospheric circulation model and the backward-facing step (BFS) fluid dynamics benchmark. Results demonstrate that FIGNN achieves competitive predictive performance while revealing physically meaningful spatial patterns unique to each feature. Analysis of rollout stability, feature-wise error budgets, and spatial mask overlays confirm the utility of FIGNN as a general-purpose framework for interpretable surrogate modeling in complex physical domains.

papers.title: Unboxing the Black Box: Mechanistic Interpretability for Algorithmic Understanding of Neural Networks
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a unified taxonomy of mechanistic interpretability approaches, situates MI within the broader XAI landscape, and surveys key techniques and literature in the field.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems and invites new researchers into the field.
papers.key_findings:
The field of mechanistic interpretability has grown rapidly since 2020.
MI faces challenges such as superposition, spurious correlations, scalability, and evaluation problems.
MI offers opportunities for debugging, data privacy, robustness, control, human-in-the-loop, and trustworthiness.
future_direction: The need for standardized evaluation techniques.
Scaling up MI techniques to larger models.
Applying MI in real-world domains like finance and medicine.
papers.abstract: The black box nature of deep neural networks poses a significant challenge for the deployment of transparent and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) systems. With the growing presence of AI in society, it becomes increasingly important to develop methods that can explain and interpret the decisions made by these systems. To address this, mechanistic interpretability (MI) emerged as a promising and distinctive research program within the broader field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). MI is the process of studying the inner computations of neural networks and translating them into human-understandable algorithms. It encompasses reverse engineering techniques aimed at uncovering the computational algorithms implemented by neural networks. In this article, we propose a unified taxonomy of MI approaches and provide a detailed analysis of key techniques, illustrated with concrete examples and pseudo-code. We contextualize MI within the broader interpretability landscape, comparing its goals, methods, and insights to other strands of XAI. Additionally, we trace the development of MI as a research area, highlighting its conceptual roots and the accelerating pace of recent work. We argue that MI holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems -- treating models not only as tools for solving tasks, but also as systems to be studied and understood. We hope to invite new researchers into the field of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Randomness and signal propagation in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs): A neural PDE perspective
papers.research_question: What are the implications of the random-like weight matrices in trained Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for signal propagation and stability, and how can they be understood through the lens of neural PDEs and random matrix theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that trained PINN weights reside in a high-entropy regime consistent with random matrix theory, and that signal propagation in such networks can be interpreted through neural PDEs, with stability governed by the numerical properties of the underlying discretization schemes.
papers.conclusion: The neural PDE framework provides a useful perspective for interpreting signal propagation in deep networks, and the stability properties of the underlying numerical schemes are reflected in the structure of the learned weight matrices.
papers.key_findings:
Trained PINN weight matrices exhibit statistical and spectral properties consistent with predictions from random matrix theory, preferring a high-entropy regime.
Random and structured weight matrices can be associated with specific discretizations of neural PDEs.
The numerical stability of these discretizations governs the stability of signal propagation through the network.
Explicit numerical schemes (like the standard sequential PINN architecture) can lead to unstable signal evolution, whereas implicit and higher-order schemes yield stable dynamics for the same underlying neural PDE.
The failure of a PINN to learn the inviscid Burgers' equation is linked to deviations from random matrix statistics and unstable signal propagation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to the one-dimensional Burgers' equation and a specific PINN architecture (8 hidden layers, 100 neurons).
The connection between PINNs and (generalized) path integral solutions of PDEs is speculative and requires future exploration.
future_direction: Explore precise technical details of the connection between PINNs and path integral solutions of PDEs.
Extend the analysis to more complex PDEs and network architectures.
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often exhibit weight matrices that appear statistically random after training, yet their implications for signal propagation and stability remain unsatisfactorily understood, let alone the interpretability. In this work, we analyze the spectral and statistical properties of trained PINN weights using viscous and inviscid variants of the one-dimensional Burgers' equation, and show that the learned weights reside in a high-entropy regime consistent with predictions from random matrix theory. To investigate the dynamical consequences of such weight structures, we study the evolution of signal features inside a network through the lens of neural partial differential equations (neural PDEs). We show that random and structured weight matrices can be associated with specific discretizations of neural PDEs, and that the numerical stability of these discretizations governs the stability of signal propagation through the network. In particular, explicit unstable schemes lead to degraded signal evolution, whereas stable implicit and higher-order schemes yield well-behaved dynamics for the same underlying neural PDE. Our results offer an explicit example of how numerical stability and network architecture shape signal propagation in deep networks, in relation to random matrix and neural PDE descriptions in PINNs.

papers.title: Loss Jump During Loss Switch in Solving PDEs with Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do different loss functions impact the training of neural networks for solving partial differential equations (PDEs)?
papers.core_contribution: Discovers and analyzes a loss-jump phenomenon during loss switching in PDE-solving neural networks, attributing it to different frequency preferences under different loss functions.
papers.conclusion: The loss-jump phenomenon provides a valuable perspective for examining the underlying mechanisms of neural networks in solving PDEs.
papers.key_findings:
When switching the loss function from data loss to model loss, the neural network solution significantly deviates from the exact solution immediately, a phenomenon termed loss jump.
The loss-jump phenomenon arises from the different frequency preferences of neural networks under different loss functions.
Theoretical analysis explains the frequency preference of neural networks under model loss.
papers.abstract: Using neural networks to solve partial differential equations (PDEs) is gaining popularity as an alternative approach in the scientific computing community. Neural networks can integrate different types of information into the loss function. These include observation data, governing equations, and variational forms, etc. These loss functions can be broadly categorized into two types: observation data loss directly constrains and measures the model output, while other loss functions indirectly model the performance of the network, which can be classified as model loss. However, this alternative approach lacks a thorough understanding of its underlying mechanisms, including theoretical foundations and rigorous characterization of various phenomena. This work focuses on investigating how different loss functions impact the training of neural networks for solving PDEs. We discover a stable loss-jump phenomenon: when switching the loss function from the data loss to the model loss, which includes different orders of derivative information, the neural network solution significantly deviates from the exact solution immediately. Further experiments reveal that this phenomenon arises from the different frequency preferences of neural networks under different loss functions. We theoretically analyze the frequency preference of neural networks under model loss. This loss-jump phenomenon provides a valuable perspective for examining the underlying mechanisms of neural networks in solving PDEs.

papers.title: Neural Networks Discover Physical Principles from Observation with an Intuitive World Model
papers.research_question: Can neural networks discover and explain physical principles (such as Newton's laws and Coulomb's law) from raw visual observations, similar to how humans learn intuitive physics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Intuitive World Model (IWM), a neural network that learns physical principles (e.g., Newton's laws, Coulomb's law) from raw video data without built-in physics engines, and can provide explicit explanations and perform counterfactual reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the Intuitive World Model (IWM) can learn physical principles from visual observation, providing explicit explanations and counterfactual reasoning, mirroring a core aspect of human intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
IWM achieves state-of-the-art performance on causal reasoning tasks (factual, predictive, counterfactual) on the ComPhy dataset.
IWM learns interpretable physical principles, as shown by its ability to generate force diagrams and explain physical events.
The hierarchical learning paradigm enables IWM to progressively learn appearance, velocity, mass, and charge representations.
IWM can perform counterfactual imagination by manipulating inferred physical properties (mass, charge) and generating plausible alternative scenarios.
The learned causal modules capture relationships analogous to Newton's laws and Coulomb's law, as demonstrated by sensitivity analysis.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Humans readily grasp physical principles via visual observation, underpinning our ability to model the world and reason about events. In contrast, AI systems often fail to extract consistent physical rules from video, relying on black-box mechanisms that produce implausible outcomes. We introduce the Intuitive World Model (IWM), designed to learn physical principles directly from vision, mimicking human intuition. Drawing inspiration from developmental psychology, IWM utilizes a modular architecture to decompose interactions into force-based dynamics. Through observing objects collide and interact via charges, it identifies intrinsic properties like mass and charge and learns representations analogous to Newton's and Coulomb's laws. This paradigm uniquely allows neural networks to provide explicit explanations for physical phenomena and conduct counterfactual reasoning consistent with learned physical laws. Our work demonstrates that a developmentally-inspired approach empowers AI to acquire explicit, interpretable physical knowledge from observation, mirroring a core aspect of human intelligence.

papers.title: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for Echo State Networks applied to Earth System Variability
papers.research_question: How can Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) be applied to Echo State Networks (ESNs) to make them interpretable, and how does this apply to the detection of El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) from sea surface temperature anomalies?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) can be applied to Echo State Networks (ESNs) to interpret their decisions, and shows that the leak rate in the reservoir is a crucial parameter controlling memory and performance.
papers.conclusion: LRP can be applied to ESNs to open the black-box, and ESNs are effective for image classification tasks like ENSO detection, with advantages in training speed and parameter efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
LRP can be successfully applied to ESNs, providing relevance maps that highlight important input regions for classification.
The leak rate in the reservoir determines the memory time scale; too high leak rate causes the model to forget early inputs and performance drops.
ESNs achieve competitive accuracy with fewer trainable parameters compared to MLP, reducing overfitting risks.
The model focuses on the Niño 3.4 region for ENSO detection, which is physically reasonable.
The model is robust to random permutation of input columns, indicating it does not rely on the zonal structure of the data.
future_direction: Apply further xAI techniques (backward optimization, sensitivity analysis, salience maps) to ESN models.
Use ESN models for time series prediction with LRP as an alternative to attention mechanisms.
Apply ESNs with LRP to unsolved problems in climate and ocean science.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are known to be powerful methods for many hard problems (e.g. image classification, speech recognition or time series prediction). However, these models tend to produce black-box results and are often difficult to interpret. Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) is a widely used technique to understand how ANN models come to their conclusion and to understand what a model has learned. Here, we focus on Echo State Networks (ESNs) as a certain type of recurrent neural networks, also known as reservoir computing. ESNs are easy to train and only require a small number of trainable parameters, but are still black-box models. We show how LRP can be applied to ESNs in order to open the black-box. We also show how ESNs can be used not only for time series prediction but also for image classification: Our ESN model serves as a detector for El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) from sea surface temperature anomalies. ENSO is actually a well-known problem and has been extensively discussed before. But here we use this simple problem to demonstrate how LRP can significantly enhance the explainablility of ESNs.

papers.title: Loss Landscape Geometry and the Learning of Symmetries: Or, What Influence Functions Reveal About Robust Generalization
papers.research_question: Do neural emulators of PDE solution operators internalize physical symmetries, and how can we diagnose this through learning dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an influence-based diagnostic that measures gradient coherence across symmetry orbits to determine whether neural PDE emulators have internalized physical symmetries, linking it to generalization.
papers.conclusion: The proposed influence-based diagnostic reveals that gradient coherence across symmetry orbits is essential for robust generalization, providing a tool to assess whether models truly learn physics or just fit data.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient coherence across symmetry orbits is necessary for models to generalize over symmetry transformations.
Models can achieve low test error without learning symmetries, indicated by weak gradient coherence.
UNets and ViTs exhibit different patterns of gradient coherence: UNets show more uniform coupling, while ViTs concentrate influence on a subset of symmetry transformations.
Symmetry breaking in forward passes corresponds to suppressed cross-influence in the loss landscape.
The diagnostic can be used to evaluate symmetry learning and guide data augmentation.
papers.limitation:
Certain physically relevant symmetries (Galilean boosts, scaling) are not studied.
Empirical analysis is limited to UNet and ViT architectures.
Diagnostics characterize symmetry learning relative to the training distribution; when symmetry transformations are poorly represented in data, influence-based measures reflect this bias.
future_direction: Extending the influence-based analysis to probe the response under small Galilean boosts.
Development of approximate or relaxed symmetry mechanisms that retain structure to guide generalization while preserving optimization flexibility.
papers.abstract: We study how neural emulators of partial differential equation solution operators internalize physical symmetries by introducing an influence-based diagnostic that measures the propagation of parameter updates between symmetry-related states, defined as the metric-weighted overlap of loss gradients evaluated along group orbits. This quantity probes the local geometry of the learned loss landscape and goes beyond forward-pass equivariance tests by directly assessing whether learning dynamics couple physically equivalent configurations. Applying our diagnostic to autoregressive fluid flow emulators, we show that orbit-wise gradient coherence provides the mechanism for learning to generalize over symmetry transformations and indicates when training selects a symmetry compatible basin. The result is a novel technique for evaluating if surrogate models have internalized symmetry properties of the known solution operator.

papers.title: Using data assimilation tools to dissect GraphDOP
papers.research_question: How can Data Assimilation (DA) diagnostic tools, such as Forecast Sensitivity-based Observation Impact (FSOI), be applied to Machine Learning models to enhance their interpretability and explainability?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that Data Assimilation diagnostic tools (FSOI and sensitivity analysis) can be successfully transferred to ML models like GraphDOP, enhancing interpretability and explainability by showing the model captures physically meaningful processes.
papers.conclusion: Data Assimilation diagnostic tools, particularly FSOI, are effective for interpreting and explaining the GraphDOP model, confirming it captures real physical processes and constructs a coherent internal representation from heterogeneous observational data.
papers.key_findings:
GraphDOP's sliding attention window learns meteorological features and spatial relationships from observation data.
GraphDOP uses information from satellite radiances (e.g., ATMS channels) to predict surface variables like 2-meter temperature.
GraphDOP tracks the movement of storm systems (e.g., extratropical storms) by shifting its attention with forecast lead time, similar to physical dynamics.
FSOI analysis reveals GraphDOP builds a coherent internal representation of the Earth system by blending information from conventional and satellite observations.
Some satellite channels (e.g., ATMS channel 22) have a larger impact on reducing forecast error, while others (e.g., channels 4 and 17) can increase error.
papers.limitation: The results are based on a version of GraphDOP trained on a limited selection of observation types to reduce computational cost, not the full state-of-the-art model.
future_direction: Replicate the study with the current state-of-the-art GraphDOP model to evaluate the importance of different observation types.
Use the presented tools to benchmark the quality of different AI-DOP models, ensuring they provide correct forecasts for the right reasons.
Implement an online observation Quality Control (QC) mechanism based on the impact measured by the FSOI diagnostic.
papers.abstract: The Data Assimilation (DA) community has been developing various diagnostics to understand the importance of the observing system in accurately forecasting the weather. They usually rely on the ability to compute the derivatives of the physical model output with respect to its initial condition. For example, the Forecast Sensitivity-based Observation Impact (FSOI) estimates the impact on the forecast error of each observation processed in the DA system. This paper presents how these DA diagnostic tools are transferred to Machine Learning (ML) models, as their derivatives are readily available through automatic differentiation. We specifically explore the interpretability and explainability of the observation-driven GraphDOP model developed at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). The interpretability study demonstrates the effectiveness of GraphDOP's sliding attention window to learn the meteorological features present in the observation datasets and to learn the spatial relationships between different regions. Making these relationships more transparent confirms that GraphDOP captures real, physically meaningful processes, such as the movement of storm systems. The explainability of GraphDOP is explored by applying the FSOI tool to study the impact of the different observations on the forecast error. This inspection reveals that GraphDOP creates an internal representation of the Earth system by combining the information from conventional and satellite observations.

papers.title: Mapping Knowledge Representations to Concepts: A Review and New Perspectives
papers.research_question: How do current methods extract internal knowledge representations in a neural network and map them to human-understandable concepts? Can Deductive-Nomological (D-N) explanation taxonomy and causal types of explanations be useful in order to analyse what can be expected, and not expected, from knowledge representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a targeted review of research that aims to associate internal neural network representations with human understandable concepts, and proposes using Deductive-Nomological explanations and theories of causality as a taxonomy to understand the capabilities and limitations of such explanations.
papers.conclusion: The review raises important questions about the goal of explanations and the type of knowledge extractable from neural networks, emphasizing the need to differentiate between understanding the trained model and providing actionable decisions. It argues for involving users to emphasize contextual dependence and refocus research on the limitations of ML systems.
papers.key_findings:
Methods for extracting knowledge representations are dominated by two approaches: Feature Based Attribution (FBA) for local understanding and Internal Knowledge Representation (IKR) extraction for global understanding.
There is an ambiguity in the goal of model explainability: understanding the ML model versus providing actionable explanations in the deployment domain.
The reviewed research lacks user studies, despite heavy reliance on human abilities to compare images and infer concepts.
Explanations that aim for intervention or counterfactual reasoning rely on causal relations, but these are only valid for the ML model in isolation and not necessarily for the real-world domain.
The Deductive-Nomological explanation taxonomy is found useful for analyzing what can be expected from neural network explanations, highlighting that current methods typically aim for kind-data or model-data relations, not theory-data or entity-data relations.
papers.limitation:
The choice to use the D-N model and Overton's schematic overview delimits the type of explanations aimed for and excludes pragmatic, inductive statistical, teleological, and historical explanations.
The understanding of the concept 'concept' is not well-grounded from an ontological and epistemological perspective.
future_direction: Conducting user studies that actively involve users to emphasize contextual dependence.
Combining IKR and FBA methods in studies aiming for a global meta-perspective of model understanding.

Using scientific explanations and theories to formulate falsifiable hypotheses and evaluate how well a trained ML model models the usage domain, moving beyond the idea that more data solves the problem of induction.
papers.abstract: The success of neural networks builds to a large extent on their ability to create internal knowledge representations from real-world high-dimensional data, such as images, sound, or text. Approaches to extract and present these representations, in order to explain the neural network's decisions, is an active and multifaceted research field. To gain a deeper understanding of a central aspect of this field, we have performed a targeted review focusing on research that aims to associate internal representations with human understandable concepts. In doing this, we added a perspective on the existing research by using primarily deductive nomological explanations as a proposed taxonomy. We find this taxonomy and theories of causality, useful for understanding what can be expected, and not expected, from neural network explanations. The analysis additionally uncovers an ambiguity in the reviewed literature related to the goal of model explainability; is it understanding the ML model or, is it actionable explanations useful in the deployment domain?

papers.title: Interpreting CFD Surrogates through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to interpret the latent representations of graph-based CFD surrogate models to enhance explainability and trustworthiness?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a post-hoc interpretability framework for graph-based CFD surrogate models using sparse autoencoders to extract interpretable latent features that correspond to physical flow structures.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoding is a practical and effective tool for explaining graph surrogates in fluid dynamics, offering a model-agnostic pathway to enhance explainability and trustworthiness in CFD applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAE yields interpretable and physically meaningful representations aligned with phenomena like vorticity or flow structures.
Global and time-local salient coordinates show temporal consistency, with variance and mean-absolute metrics capturing coherent features.
Mesh-space visualization reveals that aggregated latent activity hierarchically expands from cylinder surface to wake, mirroring physical importance.
Individual latent dimensions specialize in distinct flow structures, confirming disentanglement of physical phenomena.
SAE-based saliency consistently outperforms baselines like embedding-norm and PCA in aligning with high-vorticity regions.
papers.abstract: Learning-based surrogate models have become a practical alternative to high-fidelity CFD solvers, but their latent representations remain opaque and hinder adoption in safety-critical or regulation-bound settings. This work introduces a posthoc interpretability framework for graph-based surrogate models used in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) by leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs). By obtaining an overcomplete basis in the node embedding space of a pretrained surrogate, the method extracts a dictionary of interpretable latent features. The approach enables the identification of monosemantic concepts aligned with physical phenomena such as vorticity or flow structures, offering a model-agnostic pathway to enhance explainability and trustworthiness in CFD applications.

papers.title: Symmetry and Generalisation in Neural Approximations of Renormalisation Transformations
papers.research_question: What role do parameter symmetry and network expressivity play in the generalisation behaviour of neural networks when learning a real-space renormalisation group transformation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a competition between symmetry constraints and expressivity in neural networks learning renormalization transformations, with overly complex or overconstrained models generalizing poorly. It extends a cumulant propagation framework from MLPs to GNNs to elucidate internal information processing.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that balancing symmetry and expressivity is crucial for generalization in neural networks learning physical transformations, and the cumulant propagation framework offers insight into their internal information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Symmetrically constrained weights in MLPs combined with nonlinear activations (e.g., quadratic) lead to poor generalization, as shown analytically.
Linear networks with symmetric weights generalize well, but adding nonlinearities (ReLU, quadratic) under symmetry constraints degrades generalization.
The independent node approximation for cumulant propagation in GNNs is limited, especially for higher-order cumulants, due to neglected correlations from message passing.
GNNs perform comparably to MLPs on simple two-node graphs but their inductive biases are not beneficial for tasks lacking structural complexity.
Networks with learnable spline activations and fixed weights generalize poorly, while training both weights and splines yields linear solutions that generalize well.
papers.limitation:
The independent node approximation for GNN cumulant propagation is crude and neglects important interactions induced by message passing and weight sharing.
The study is limited to simple network architectures (shallow MLPs and GNNs) and synthetic tasks.
future_direction: Extending the cumulant propagation framework to more complex architectures and tasks.
Investigating the role of symmetry breaking in hierarchical learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have proven enormously successful at using multiple layers of representation to learn relevant features of structured data. Encoding physical symmetries into these models can improve performance on difficult tasks, and recent work has motivated the principle of parameter symmetry breaking and restoration as a unifying mechanism underlying their hierarchical learning dynamics. We evaluate the role of parameter symmetry and network expressivity in the generalisation behaviour of neural networks when learning a real-space renormalisation group (RG) transformation, using the central limit theorem (CLT) as a test case map. We consider simple multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and graph neural networks (GNNs), and vary weight symmetries and activation functions across architectures. Our results reveal a competition between symmetry constraints and expressivity, with overly complex or overconstrained models generalising poorly. We analytically demonstrate this poor generalisation behaviour for certain constrained MLP architectures by recasting the CLT as a cumulant recursion relation and making use of an established framework to propagate cumulants through MLPs. We also empirically validate an extension of this framework from MLPs to GNNs, elucidating the internal information processing performed by these more complex models. These findings offer new insight into the learning dynamics of symmetric networks and their limitations in modelling structured physical transformations.

papers.title: Position: Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in SAEs
papers.research_question: How can feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be achieved and measured to improve the reliability of mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and proposes the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to measure consistency. It shows that high consistency is achievable with appropriate architectural choices (e.g., TopK SAEs) and that high PW-MCC correlates with semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.conclusion: The paper calls for a community-wide shift towards valuing and systematically measuring feature consistency in SAEs for cumulative progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
High feature consistency (PW-MCC ≈ 0.80) is achievable with TopK SAEs on real-world LLM activations.
PW-MCC reliably tracks ground-truth feature recovery (GT-MCC) in synthetic experiments.
Feature consistency is frequency-dependent: more frequent features are learned more consistently.
Different SAE architectures yield different levels of consistency, with TopK SAEs performing best.
High PW-MCC scores correlate strongly with the semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.limitation:
The focus is on SAEs, and other interpretability methods may have different consistency challenges.
The study uses a specific metric (PW-MCC) for a specific notion of consistency (strong feature consistency).
The real-world experiments are limited to two base models and one dataset.
The automated interpretation pipeline has its own limitations.
future_direction: Extending consistency analysis to other interpretability methods beyond SAEs.
Developing more nuanced metrics for consistency that go beyond strong feature consistency.
Investigating the relationship between consistency and downstream task performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a prominent tool in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for decomposing neural network activations into interpretable features. However, the aspiration to identify a canonical set of features is challenged by the observed inconsistency of learned SAE features across different training runs, undermining the reliability and efficiency of MI research. This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in SAEs -- the reliable convergence to equivalent feature sets across independent runs. We propose using the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to operationalize consistency and demonstrate that high levels are achievable (0.80 for TopK SAEs on LLM activations) with appropriate architectural choices. Our contributions include detailing the benefits of prioritizing consistency; providing theoretical grounding and synthetic validation using a model organism, which verifies PW-MCC as a reliable proxy for ground-truth recovery; and extending these findings to real-world LLM data, where high feature consistency strongly correlates with the semantic similarity of learned feature explanations. We call for a community-wide shift towards systematically measuring feature consistency to foster robust cumulative progress in MI.

papers.title: A reproducing kernel framework for interpretable parameter estimation and learning in dynamical systems
papers.research_question: How can explainable machine learning models be used for accurate, interpretable, and computationally efficient parameter estimation in dynamical systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework combining explainable machine learning models with SHAP-based interpretability for parameter estimation in dynamical systems, demonstrating accurate, interpretable, and efficient estimation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed feature-based learning framework for parameter estimation in differential equation systems combines predictive modeling with post-hoc explainability, with kernel-based methods (KRR and GPR) achieving higher predictive accuracy and robustness compared to neural network baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Kernel-based methods (KRR and GPR) consistently outperformed neural network models (MLP and CNN) in parameter estimation accuracy.
Statistical features extracted from trajectories were more informative for parameter estimation than frequency-domain or spectrogram features.
SHAP-based feature attribution revealed consistent feature importance rankings across different model types, indicating robust feature-to-parameter relationships.
The proposed framework achieves accurate parameter estimation while providing transparency into the inference process through explainability techniques.
The integration of simulation-based dataset generation, feature extraction, and interpretable modeling offers a new perspective for combining machine learning with domain-specific modeling.
papers.limitation:
Further theoretical analysis is needed to formalize the connection between system dynamics and feature relevance.
Validation has been limited to synthetic datasets; extending to real-world data is important for broader practical applicability.
Current kernel-based methods do not scale efficiently, and neural architectures require larger datasets to fully leverage their capacity, indicating scalability and data volume limitations.
future_direction: Extend the methodology to stable multi-parameter estimation.
Develop data-driven techniques for identifying informative parameter ranges.
Design adaptive dataset generation strategies to improve training efficiency and interpretability.
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate a suite of explainable machine learning models -- including Kernel Ridge Regression, Gaussian Process Regression, Convolutional Neural Networks, and Multi-Layer Perceptrons -- for parameter inference in systems of differential equations. By combining these models with explainability techniques such as SHapley Additive exPlanations, we extract explicit feature-to-parameter mappings, offering deeper insight into the inference process. Building on these insights, we propose lightweight, hand-engineered estimators that approximate parameter estimation tasks without requiring complex optimization. Additionally, we introduce a systematic methodology for dataset generation, incorporating time-series simulation and diverse feature extraction. Our results demonstrate that explainability-driven modeling can achieve accurate, interpretable, and computationally efficient parameter estimation, offering a new perspective on the integration of machine learning with domain-specific modeling.

papers.title: Scalable Mechanistic Neural Networks for Differential Equations and Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we reformulate the Mechanistic Neural Network to achieve linear time and space complexity with respect to sequence length while maintaining accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces S-MNN, a reformulation of the Mechanistic Neural Network that reduces computational time and space complexities from cubic/quadratic to linear in sequence length while maintaining accuracy.
papers.conclusion: S-MNN addresses the scalability limitations of MNN by reducing complexities to linear in sequence length, retaining precision and enabling efficient modeling of long-term dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
S-MNN matches the precision of the original MNN across various benchmarks.
S-MNN reduces computational time and memory usage significantly, enabling handling of long sequences.
The reformulation eliminates slack variables and uses a banded matrix structure for efficient solving.
S-MNN demonstrates practical applicability on long-term climate data forecasting.
The solver is numerically stable and GPU-friendly, achieving linear scaling in time and memory.
papers.abstract: We propose Scalable Mechanistic Neural Network (S-MNN), an enhanced neural network framework designed for scientific machine learning applications involving long temporal sequences. By reformulating the original Mechanistic Neural Network (MNN) (Pervez et al., 2024), we reduce the computational time and space complexities from cubic and quadratic with respect to the sequence length, respectively, to linear. This significant improvement enables efficient modeling of long-term dynamics without sacrificing accuracy or interpretability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that S-MNN matches the original MNN in precision while substantially reducing computational resources. Consequently, S-MNN can drop-in replace the original MNN in applications, providing a practical and efficient tool for integrating mechanistic bottlenecks into neural network models of complex dynamical systems. Source code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/ScalableMNN.

papers.title: Neural Earthquake Forecasting with Minimal Information: Limits, Interpretability, and the Role of Markov Structure
papers.research_question: Can neural and hybrid models for earthquake forecasting generalize temporally when trained on early data and tested on future unseen events?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a hybrid neural-Markov model for earthquake forecasting and a temporal cross-validation framework, showing that model performance degrades on future data due to non-stationarity, highlighting the importance of temporal evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Neural and hybrid models for earthquake forecasting fail to generalize to future data due to temporal non-stationarity, highlighting the need for temporally realistic evaluation and caution in applying machine learning to sparse forecasting settings.
papers.key_findings:
The hybrid model outperforms the Markov baseline on validation data but fails to generalize to the most recent quintile of the catalog.
The final quintile of seismicity exhibits more Markov-consistent behavior than earlier data, indicating temporal non-stationarity.
Integrated Gradients attribution shows a shift in feature importance between validation and test sets, with magnitude features becoming more relevant in the test set.
Temporal cross-validation reveals that model performance is highly dependent on the temporal location of the test data, with the last quintile consistently underperforming.
The study underscores the risk of overfitting to early patterns and the need for temporally realistic benchmarks in earthquake forecasting.
papers.limitation:
Small sample size affects all statistical models based on this data.
Sparse input features limited to simple descriptors of past events restrict the models' ability to capture complex physical dynamics.
The Markov prior is static and unable to account for possible changes in seismic regimes.
Results are based on a single regional earthquake catalog without additional geophysical or contextual data.
Only feedforward architectures were considered; models with more explicit temporal reasoning were not explored.
future_direction: Refine the use of prior knowledge with dynamic extensions of the Markov model or hierarchical priors that adapt across segments of the catalog.
Incorporate additional physical variables such as fault-specific information, geodetic signals, or stress evolution proxies.
Explore dynamically updated models or time-aware architectures to track evolving patterns more effectively.
papers.abstract: Abstract Forecasting earthquake sequences remains a central challenge in seismology, particularly under non-stationary conditions. While deep learning models have shown promise, their ability to generalize across time remains poorly understood. We evaluate neural and hybrid (NN + Markov) models for short-term earthquake forecasting on a regional catalog using temporally stratified cross-validation. Models are trained on earlier portions of the catalog and evaluated on future unseen events, enabling realistic assessment of temporal generalization. We find that while these models outperform a purely Markovian model on validation data, their test performance degrades substantially in the most recent quintile. A detailed attribution analysis reveals a shift in feature relevance over time, with later data exhibiting simpler, more Markov-consistent behavior. To support interpretability, we apply Integrated Gradients, a type of explainable AI (XAI) to analyze how models rely on different input features. These results highlight the risks of overfitting to early patterns in seismicity and underscore the importance of temporally realistic benchmarks. We conclude that forecasting skill is inherently time-dependent and benefits from combining physical priors with data-driven methods.

papers.title: Noether: The More Things Change, the More Stay the Same
papers.research_question: How do symmetries in neural networks interact with learning algorithms, and what conserved quantities arise from these symmetries during optimization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that symmetries in neural networks lead to conserved quantities during optimization, which constrain the optimization path and help understand dynamics like balance conditions and boundedness.
papers.conclusion: Symmetry is an important tool for understanding the performance of neural networks under gradient descent.
papers.key_findings:
For ReLU networks, gradient descent leads to balance equations between consecutive layers.
For linear networks, symmetries lead to balancedness conditions on weight matrices.
Data augmentation introduces symmetries that constrain the optimization path.
Conserved quantities are derived for various activation functions (ReLU, linear, Swish) and optimization algorithms (gradient flow, Newtonian dynamics, Nesterov).
future_direction: Determine if conservation laws for Swish can explain its empirical advantage over ReLU.
Derive bounds for Nesterov's accelerated gradient flow similar to Newtonian dynamics.
papers.abstract: Symmetries have proven to be important ingredients in the analysis of neural networks. So far their use has mostly been implicit or seemingly coincidental. We undertake a systematic study of the role that symmetry plays. In particular, we clarify how symmetry interacts with the learning algorithm. The key ingredient in our study is played by Noether's celebrated theorem which, informally speaking, states that symmetry leads to conserved quantities (e.g., conservation of energy or conservation of momentum). In the realm of neural networks under gradient descent, model symmetries imply restrictions on the gradient path. E.g., we show that symmetry of activation functions leads to boundedness of weight matrices, for the specific case of linear activations it leads to balance equations of consecutive layers, data augmentation leads to gradient paths that have "momentum"-type restrictions, and time symmetry leads to a version of the Neural Tangent Kernel. Symmetry alone does not specify the optimization path, but the more symmetries are contained in the model the more restrictions are imposed on the path. Since symmetry also implies over-parametrization, this in effect implies that some part of this over-parametrization is cancelled out by the existence of the conserved quantities. Symmetry can therefore be thought of as one further important tool in understanding the performance of neural networks under gradient descent.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Advancing AI-Scientist Understanding: Multi-Agent LLMs with Interpretable Physics Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the reliability, transparency, and interpretability of LLM outputs in physics problem-solving?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a multi-agent LLM framework with an interpretation module that transforms opaque LLM outputs into structured, executable, and physically grounded science models to improve interpretability and verifiability in physics reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The multi-agent LLM framework with an interpretation module marks a significant step toward more reliable, interpretable, and verifiable AI-augmented scientific reasoning by transforming LLM outputs into transparent, executable science models.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully structures complex LLM reasoning into explicit science models, enabling validation through code execution and interactive tools.
Case studies demonstrate the framework's ability to detect flaws in LLM-generated solutions and enhance human-AI collaboration.
The interpretation module, consisting of specialized agents (summarizer, model builder, tester, etc.), bridges the gap between AI-generated reasoning and human scientific intuition.
The approach improves both numerical and theoretical consistency of LLM outputs in physics problem-solving.
The system fosters collaborative reasoning by keeping human experts central to the validation and refinement process.
future_direction: Extend the framework to a broader range of physics domains and other scientific fields.
Refine each agent's capabilities and enhance the interactive elements of the user interface.
Investigate scalability, handling of increasingly complex models, and integration of advanced techniques like real-time interactive debugging and deeper reasoning transparency.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are playing an increasingly important role in physics research by assisting with symbolic manipulation, numerical computation, and scientific reasoning. However, ensuring the reliability, transparency, and interpretability of their outputs remains a major challenge. In this work, we introduce a novel multi-agent LLM physicist framework that fosters collaboration between AI and human scientists through three key modules: a reasoning module, an interpretation module, and an AI-scientist interaction module. Recognizing that effective physics reasoning demands logical rigor, quantitative accuracy, and alignment with established theoretical models, we propose an interpretation module that employs a team of specialized LLM agents-including summarizers, model builders, visualization tools, and testers-to systematically structure LLM outputs into transparent, physically grounded science models. A case study demonstrates that our approach significantly improves interpretability, enables systematic validation, and enhances human-AI collaboration in physics problem-solving and discovery. Our work bridges free-form LLM reasoning with interpretable, executable models for scientific analysis, enabling more transparent and verifiable AI-augmented research.

papers.title: Investigation of Internal Functioning of the Radial-Basis-Function Neural Network River Flow Forecasting Models
papers.research_question: Can hydrological knowledge be extracted from Radial Basis Function Neural Networks (RBFNNs) by interpreting their internal functioning, specifically by examining the responses of hidden layer neurons to understand how they represent flow components in river flow forecasting?
papers.core_contribution: The hidden neurons in an RBFNN for river flow forecasting are not arbitrary but represent specific flow components (baseflow, interflow, surface runoff), demonstrating that hydrological knowledge can be extracted from the model's internal functioning.
papers.conclusion: The RBFNN can be used as an effective flow forecasting tool, and its hidden neurons activate in a way that corresponds to hydrological flow components, suggesting that the network's internal functioning is interpretable and can extract meaningful hydrological knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The RBFNN is an effective tool for daily flow forecasting.
The activation of hidden nodes is not arbitrary; each node dominates in one of the flow domains (low, medium, high) and represents flow components resembling baseflow, interflow, and surface runoff.
The proportional contribution from each hidden neuron varies over time, reflecting dominance in specific flow ranges.
The RBFNN parameters (centers, spreads, weights) function to decompose the flow hydrograph into meaningful components.
The method provides insight into the internal functioning of RBFNNs, showing they can mimic local models corresponding to hydrological processes.
papers.limitation: The study uses a limited number of catchments, so the findings may not generalize to all catchments.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to a large number of catchments with different characteristics.
Investigate the sensitivity of the number of RBFs and network structure to represent physical processes.
papers.abstract: This paper deals with the challenging problem of hydrological interpretation of the internal functioning of artificial neural networks (ANNs) by extracting knowledge from their solutions. The neural network used in this study is based on the structure of the radial-basis-function neural network (RBFNN), which is considered as an alternative to the multilayer perceptron for solving complex modeling problems. This network consists of input, hidden, and output layers. The network is trained using the daily data of two catchments having different characteristics and from two different regions in the world. The present day and antecedent observed discharges are used as inputs to the network to forecast the flow one day ahead. A range of quantitative and qualitative techniques are used for hydrological interpretation of the internal functioning by examining the responses of the hidden layer nodes. The results of the study show that a single hidden layered RBFNN is an effective tool to forecast the daily flows and that the activation of the hidden layer nodes are far from arbitrary, but appear to represent flow components of the predicted hydrograph. The results of the study confirm that the three nodes in the hidden layer of this model effectively divide the input data space in such a way that the contribution from each node dominates in one of the flow domains—low, medium, or high—and form, in a crude manner, the base flow, interflow and surface runoff components of the hydrograph.

papers.title: Additive-feature-attribution methods: a review on explainable artificial intelligence for fluid dynamics and heat transfer
papers.core_contribution: This review paper summarizes the application of additive-feature-attribution methods (SHAP) in fluid dynamics and heat transfer, highlighting their importance for interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models.
papers.conclusion: This review shows that explainability techniques, and in particular additive-feature-attribution methods, are crucial for implementing interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models in the fluid-mechanics field.
papers.key_findings:
Additive-feature-attribution methods are crucial for implementing interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models in fluid mechanics.
SHAP values provide a unique solution for understanding the model by linking input features with the model prediction.
The review categorizes applications into turbulence modeling, fluid-mechanics fundamentals, and applied problems in fluid dynamics and heat transfer.
papers.abstract: The use of data-driven methods in fluid mechanics has surged dramatically in recent years due to their capacity to adapt to the complex and multi-scale nature of turbulent flows, as well as to detect patterns in large-scale simulations or experimental tests. In order to interpret the relationships generated in the models during the training process, numerical attributions need to be assigned to the input features. One important example are the additive-feature-attribution methods. These explainability methods link the input features with the model prediction, providing an interpretation based on a linear formulation of the models. The SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP values) are formulated as the only possible interpretation that offers a unique solution for understanding the model. In this manuscript, the additive-feature-attribution methods are presented, showing four common implementations in the literature: kernel SHAP, tree SHAP, gradient SHAP, and deep SHAP. Then, the main applications of the additive-feature-attribution methods are introduced, dividing them into three main groups: turbulence modeling, fluid-mechanics fundamentals, and applied problems in fluid dynamics and heat transfer. This review shows thatexplainability techniques, and in particular additive-feature-attribution methods, are crucial for implementing interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models in the fluid-mechanics field.

papers.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we automate the discovery of circuits in neural networks for mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability workflow and introduces the ACDC algorithm to automate circuit discovery by using activation patching to find important connections in the computational graph.
papers.conclusion: ACDC is a step towards automating circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability, showing promise on several tasks but with limitations that need to be addressed in future work.
papers.key_findings:
ACDC successfully rediscovers known circuits, such as the Greater-Than circuit in GPT-2 Small and the IOI circuit.
ACDC selects a sparse set of edges (e.g., 68 out of 32,000 in GPT-2 Small for IOI) that match manually found circuits.
ACDC performs competitively with gradient-based methods like Subnetwork Probing and Head Importance Score for Pruning.
ACDC is not robust in all settings, e.g., it fails on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC can miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
papers.limitation:
ACDC can fail in some settings, such as on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC may miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
The ground-truth circuits from previous work are not 100% reliable, limiting the evaluation.
future_direction: Automating the functional interpretation of model components.
Improving circuit discovery methods to handle more complex behaviors and models.
papers.abstract: Through considerable effort and intuition, several recent works have reverse-engineered nontrivial behaviors of transformer models. This paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability process they followed. First, researchers choose a metric and dataset that elicit the desired model behavior. Then, they apply activation patching to find which abstract neural network units are involved in the behavior. By varying the dataset, metric, and units under investigation, researchers can understand the functionality of each component. We automate one of the process' steps: to identify the circuit that implements the specified behavior in the model's computational graph. We propose several algorithms and reproduce previous interpretability results to validate them. For example, the ACDC algorithm rediscovered 5/5 of the component types in a circuit in GPT-2 Small that computes the Greater-Than operation. ACDC selected 68 of the 32,000 edges in GPT-2 Small, all of which were manually found by previous work. Our code is available at https://github.com/ArthurConmy/Automatic-Circuit-Discovery.

papers.title: Noether's Learning Dynamics: Role of Symmetry Breaking in Neural\n Networks
papers.research_question: What is the role of symmetry breaking in the learning dynamics of neural networks? Specifically, how does kinetic symmetry breaking affect efficiency and stability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a theoretical framework based on Lagrangian mechanics to study learning dynamics, revealing that kinetic symmetry breaking induces an implicit adaptive optimization mechanism akin to RMSProp in networks with normalization layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, through the lens of Lagrangian mechanics, we have established a theoretical foundation to discover geometric design principles for the learning dynamics of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Kinetic symmetry breaking (KSB) is a key mechanism in learning dynamics where the kinetic energy (learning rule) breaks the symmetry of the potential (loss function).
Noether’s Learning Dynamics (NLD) generalizes Noether’s theorem to account for KSB and describes the motion of the Noether charge.
In networks with normalization layers, KSB induces an implicit adaptive optimization mechanism that scales gradients similarly to RMSProp.
The implicit adaptive optimization requires finite learning rates and is amplified by momentum and weight decay.
Empirical validation shows that unconstrained filter norm (allowing implicit adaptation) leads to better performance with large learning rates and momentum.
future_direction: Directly simulate gradient flow with implicit acceleration to keep the benefits of finite learning rates.
Explore the role of symmetry breaking in other components of deep learning, such as attention mechanisms or recurrent networks.
papers.abstract:
In nature, symmetry governs regularities, while symmetry breaking brings
texture. In artificial neural networks, symmetry has been a central design
principle to efficiently capture regularities in the world, but the role of
symmetry breaking is not well understood. Here, we develop a theoretical
framework to study the "geometry of learning dynamics" in neural networks, and
reveal a key mechanism of explicit symmetry breaking behind the efficiency and
stability of modern neural networks. To build this understanding, we model the
discrete learning dynamics of gradient descent using a continuous-time
Lagrangian formulation, in which the learning rule corresponds to the kinetic
energy and the loss function corresponds to the potential energy. Then, we
identify "kinetic symmetry breaking" (KSB), the condition when the kinetic
energy explicitly breaks the symmetry of the potential function. We generalize
Noether's theorem known in physics to take into account KSB and derive the
resulting motion of the Noether charge: "Noether's Learning Dynamics" (NLD).
Finally, we apply NLD to neural networks with normalization layers and reveal
how KSB introduces a mechanism of "implicit adaptive optimization",
establishing an analogy between learning dynamics induced by normalization
layers and RMSProp. Overall, through the lens of Lagrangian mechanics, we have
established a theoretical foundation to discover geometric design principles
for the learning dynamics of neural networks.

papers.title: Interpretability for Time Series Transformers using A Concept Bottleneck Framework
papers.research_question: How can we make time series transformers interpretable by steering them to learn predefined, interpretable concepts while maintaining forecasting performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models and Centered Kernel Alignment to steer time series transformers to learn predefined interpretable concepts (e.g., a linear surrogate model and time features) in a designated bottleneck layer, improving interpretability without significantly harming forecasting performance.
papers.conclusion: The concept bottleneck framework successfully improves the interpretability of time series transformers by encouraging specific components to align with human-understandable concepts, with minimal impact on forecasting accuracy, and enables faithful local interventions.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework maintains model performance (MSE, MAE) on benchmark datasets while making the bottleneck layer's representations highly similar to the predefined concepts, as measured by CKA.
Component visualizations and activation patching interventions confirm that the bottleneck components learn and causally influence the model's predictions based on the intended concepts.
The framework is successfully applied to three different transformer architectures (Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer, FEDformer) on synthetic and real-world time series data.
Including a 'free' component in the bottleneck (not constrained by concepts) can help maintain performance and capture additional, non-predefined patterns in the data.
The intervention experiment demonstrates that the model's performance on time-shifted data can be restored by patching the activations of the time-concept component, confirming the causal role of the bottleneck.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes that relevant, interpretable concepts are known a priori and provided to the model.
The framework introduces additional computational cost during training due to the CKA loss calculation.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other types of sequential data beyond time series.
Exploring more complex or domain-specific interpretable concepts.
Investigating the use of the framework for model debugging and out-of-distribution robustness.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability focuses on reverse engineering the internal mechanisms learned by neural networks. We extend our focus and propose to mechanistically forward engineer using our framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models. In the context of long-term time series forecasting, we modify the training objective to encourage a model to develop representations which are similar to predefined, interpretable concepts using Centered Kernel Alignment. This steers the bottleneck components to learn the predefined concepts, while allowing other components to learn other, undefined concepts. We apply the framework to the Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer and FEDformer, and present an in-depth analysis on synthetic data and on a variety of benchmark datasets. We find that the model performance remains mostly unaffected, while the model shows much improved interpretability. Additionally, we verify the interpretation of the bottleneck components with an intervention experiment using activation patching.

papers.title: Unification of Symmetries Inside Neural Networks: Transformer, Feedforward and Neural ODE
papers.research_question: How can gauge symmetries from physics be applied to understand parametric redundancies in neural networks, and can the inner workings of neural networks be interpreted through spacetime diffeomorphisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper unifies symmetries in neural networks by interpreting parametric redundancies as gauge symmetries, showing that gauge symmetries in neural ODEs are spacetime diffeomorphisms, and that rescaling symmetries in feedforward networks and transformers correspond to these diffeomorphisms.
