Our proposed method for accelerating automated circuit discovery, Per Attention Head Quantization (PAHQ), takes a fundamentally different approach by optimizing the efficiency of each individual patching operation. PAHQ leverages a fundamental alignment between activation patching and mixed-precision quantization (MPQ): interpretability analysis through patching essentially performs targeted ablation studies. Therefore, we can maintain high precision exclusively for investigated components while safely reducing precision elsewhere in the network. PAHQ-accelerated ACDC reduces runtime by up to 80\% and memory consumption by up to 30\% compared to unaccelerated ACDC while maintaining faithfulness. Importantly, our method readily integrates with existing edge-based circuit discovery techniques by modifying the attention computation mechanism. This training-free approach provides a practical and novel pathway for accelerating mechanistic interpretability methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/626619403/PAHQ.

papers.title: Using explainability to design physics-aware CNNs for solving subsurface inverse problems
papers.research_question: How can explainability techniques be used to design physics-aware convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for solving subsurface inverse problems?
papers.core_contribution: A framework for using explainability techniques (Score-CAM and Deep SHAP) to iteratively select CNN hyperparameters (e.g., kernel size, network depth) to develop physics-aware models for subsurface imaging that maintain high predictive accuracy while improving descriptive accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that explainability methods (Score-CAM and Deep SHAP) can be used to iteratively tune CNN hyperparameters, leading to physics-aware models with high descriptive accuracy without compromising predictive accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Initial deep CNNs (Transpose Convolution and Dense networks) had good predictive accuracy but low descriptive accuracy, as they focused on non-physical, low-power regions in the input dispersion images.
Changing the kernel size from 3x3 to 3x1 in deep networks did not significantly change predictive accuracy but showed slightly better descriptive accuracy.
Reducing network depth (shallow networks) improved descriptive accuracy, with the shallow 3x1 kernel network focusing primarily on the physically meaningful high-power modal trend in the dispersion images.
The shallow 3x1 kernel CNN is recommended as it achieves high descriptive accuracy (making logical, physics-aware predictions) without a considerable loss in predictive accuracy.
papers.limitation: The shallow network recommended is sensitive to noisy inputs and may require additional denoising layers for field applications.
future_direction: Adding denoising layers to the shallow network for robustness to noisy field data.
Extending the framework to tune more hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: We present a novel method of using explainability techniques to design physics-aware neural networks. We demonstrate our approach by developing a convolutional neural network (CNN) for solving an inverse problem for shallow subsurface imaging. Although CNNs have gained popularity in recent years across many fields, the development of CNNs remains an art, as there are no clear guidelines regarding the selection of hyperparameters that will yield the best network. While optimization algorithms may be used to select hyperparameters automatically, these methods focus on developing networks with high predictive accuracy while disregarding model explainability (descriptive accuracy). However, the field of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) addresses the absence of model explainability by providing tools that allow developers to evaluate the internal logic of neural networks. In this study, we use the explainability methods Score-CAM and Deep SHAP to select hyperparameters, such as kernel sizes and network depth, to develop a physics-aware CNN for shallow subsurface imaging. We begin with a relatively deep Encoder-Decoder network, which uses surface wave dispersion images as inputs and generates 2D shear wave velocity subsurface images as outputs. Through model explanations, we ultimately find that a shallow CNN using two convolutional layers with an atypical kernel size of 3x1 yields comparable predictive accuracy but with increased descriptive accuracy. We also show that explainability methods can be used to evaluate the network's complexity and decision-making. We believe this method can be used to develop neural networks with high predictive accuracy while also providing inherent explainability.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety -- A Review
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes mechanistic interpretability research, establishing foundational concepts, surveying methodologies, and examining its relevance to AI safety, while advocating for future directions.
papers.limitation:
Scalability challenges and risks of human reliance.
Cherry-picking and streetlight interpretability.
future_direction: Clarifying concepts and integrating with existing literature.
Setting standards through metrics, benchmarks, and algorithmic testbeds.
Scaling up techniques to handle complex models and behaviors.
Expanding scope to vision, multimodal, and reinforcement learning models.
papers.abstract: Understanding AI systems' inner workings is critical for ensuring value alignment and safety. This review explores mechanistic interpretability: reverse engineering the computational mechanisms and representations learned by neural networks into human-understandable algorithms and concepts to provide a granular, causal understanding. We establish foundational concepts such as features encoding knowledge within neural activations and hypotheses about their representation and computation. We survey methodologies for causally dissecting model behaviors and assess the relevance of mechanistic interpretability to AI safety. We examine benefits in understanding, control, alignment, and risks such as capability gains and dual-use concerns. We investigate challenges surrounding scalability, automation, and comprehensive interpretation. We advocate for clarifying concepts, setting standards, and scaling techniques to handle complex models and behaviors and expand to domains such as vision and reinforcement learning. Mechanistic interpretability could help prevent catastrophic outcomes as AI systems become more powerful and inscrutable.

papers.title: LLMs learn governing principles of dynamical systems, revealing an in-context neural scaling law
papers.research_question: Can LLMs learn the governing principles of dynamical systems from in-context data, and does the accuracy of learned rules scale with context length?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can learn the probabilistic transition rules of various dynamical systems from in-context data without fine-tuning, and the accuracy of the learned rules follows a power-law scaling with context length, revealing an in-context neural scaling law.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained LLMs can accurately recover the probabilistic transition rules underlying deterministic, chaotic, and stochastic time series when provided with sufficient context, and this learning follows an in-context scaling law.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs (LLaMA-13b, LLaMA-70b) can accurately predict the next state in time series from stochastic, chaotic, continuous, and discrete dynamical systems without any fine-tuning or prompt engineering.
The discrepancy between the learned transition rules and ground truth decreases as a power law with the length of the observed time series, indicating an in-context neural scaling law.
The introduced Hierarchy-PDF algorithm efficiently extracts probability density functions for multi-digit numbers from LLM predictions.
For deterministic systems, the squared deviations from the mean (SDM) loss is more stable than the Bhattacharyya distance for capturing learning dynamics.
LLMs can learn both the mean and variance of next-state distributions for stochastic systems, as demonstrated on the noisy logistic map and geometric Brownian motion.
papers.limitation:
Although unlikely, the possibility of data leakage (memorization) cannot be completely ruled out and requires rigorous testing in future work.
The study does not evaluate newer models like LLaMA-3 due to time and computational constraints, limiting the comprehensiveness of the findings.
future_direction: Investigating how LLMs encode spatio-temporal features in stochastic dynamical time series and how they represent the learned transition rules.
Examining how LLMs perform subtasks necessary for learning stochastic dynamical systems, such as collecting Markovian transition statistics from discrete data and performing density estimation.
Assessing to what extent training on natural language enhances a transformer's mathematical ability to in-context learn dynamical systems, and vice-versa.
papers.abstract: Pretrained large language models (LLMs) are surprisingly effective at performing zero-shot tasks, including time-series forecasting. However, understanding the mechanisms behind such capabilities remains highly challenging due to the complexity of the models. We study LLMs' ability to extrapolate the behavior of dynamical systems whose evolution is governed by principles of physical interest. Our results show that LLaMA 2, a language model trained primarily on texts, achieves accurate predictions of dynamical system time series without fine-tuning or prompt engineering. Moreover, the accuracy of the learned physical rules increases with the length of the input context window, revealing an in-context version of neural scaling law. Along the way, we present a flexible and efficient algorithm for extracting probability density functions of multi-digit numbers directly from LLMs.

papers.title: Differentiable Autoencoding Neural Operator for Interpretable and Integrable Latent Space Modeling
papers.research_question: How to achieve interpretable latent space modeling in scientific machine learning by integrating differentiable PDE solvers for physics-consistent dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DIANO, a deterministic autoencoding neural operator framework that constructs interpretable latent spaces for dimensionality and geometric reduction, with integrated differentiable PDE solvers for physics-consistent temporal evolution.
papers.conclusion: DIANO demonstrates capability for interpretable and integrable latent space modeling, enabling dimensional and geometrical reduction with physics-based dynamics for complex spatio-temporal flows.
papers.key_findings:
DIANO produces interpretable latent vorticity structures with fewer Fourier modes, balancing reconstruction accuracy and interpretability.
DIANO enables temporal evolution of latent states using integrated PDE solvers, accurately predicting future flow fields.
The framework supports geometrical reduction from 2D to 1D, solving reduced PDEs in latent space and reconstructing to original geometry.
DIANO outperforms baseline models like CNO, CNN-AE, and NN-AE in terms of latent space interpretability and reconstruction error.
Solving lower-fidelity PDEs in latent space allows trade-offs between solver complexity, efficiency, and accuracy.
papers.abstract: Scientific machine learning has enabled the extraction of physical insights from high-dimensional spatiotemporal flow data using linear and nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques. Despite these advances, achieving interpretability within the latent space remains a challenge. To address this, we propose the DIfferentiable Autoencoding Neural Operator (DIANO), a deterministic autoencoding neural operator framework that constructs physically interpretable latent spaces for both dimensional and geometric reduction, with the provision to enforce differential governing equations directly within the latent space. Built upon neural operators, DIANO compresses high-dimensional input functions into a low-dimensional latent space via spatial coarsening through an encoding neural operator and subsequently reconstructs the original inputs using a decoding neural operator through spatial refinement. We assess DIANO's latent space interpretability and performance in dimensionality reduction against baseline models, including the Convolutional Neural Operator and standard autoencoders. Furthermore, a fully differentiable partial differential equation (PDE) solver is developed and integrated within the latent space, enabling the temporal advancement of both high- and low-fidelity PDEs, thereby embedding physical priors into the latent dynamics. We further investigate various PDE formulations, including the 2D unsteady advection-diffusion and the 3D Pressure-Poisson equation, to examine their influence on shaping the latent flow representations. Benchmark problems considered include flow past a 2D cylinder, flow through a 2D symmetric stenosed artery, and a 3D patient-specific coronary artery. These case studies demonstrate DIANO's capability to solve PDEs within a latent space that facilitates both dimensional and geometrical reduction while allowing latent interpretability.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: Exploration and adaptation of large language models for specialized domains
papers.research_question: Can large language models overcome challenges in specialized domains, and how can they be effectively adapted to domain-specific requirements?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation provides insights into the inner workings of LLMs and proposes adaptation methods that demonstrate LLMs can be effectively used in specialized domains, particularly clinical NLP.
papers.conclusion: The work provides new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models and multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.
papers.key_findings:
Layers of Transformer-based LLMs encode different dimensions of input text, with contextual representations and general language knowledge being beneficial for complex tasks.
Pre-trained language models outperform traditional approaches on clinical tasks.
Integration of domain-specific resources (like ICD hierarchy) improves model generalization.
Behavioral testing framework can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts.
Prototypical networks can provide interpretable diagnosis predictions.
papers.limitation: There is no ground truth in clinical data
future_direction: Integration of multimodal and multilingual data
Efficient methods for large language models
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed the field of natural language processing (NLP). Their improved performance on various NLP benchmarks makes them a promising tool—also for the application in specialized domains. Such domains are characterized by highly trained professionals with particular domain expertise. Since these experts are rare, improving the efficiency of their work with automated systems is especially desirable. However, domain-specific text resources hold various challenges for NLP systems. These challenges include distinct language, noisy and scarce data, and a high level of variation. Further, specialized domains present an increased need for transparent systems since they are often applied in high stakes settings. In this dissertation, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can overcome some of these challenges and propose methods to effectively adapt them to domain-specific requirements. We first investigate the inner workings and abilities of LLMs and show how they can fill the gaps that are present in previous NLP algorithms for specialized domains. To this end, we explore the sources of errors produced by earlier systems to identify which of them can be addressed by using LLMs. Following this, we take a closer look at how information is processed within Transformer-based LLMs to better understand their capabilities. We find that their layers encode different dimensions of the input text. Here, the contextual vector representation, and the general language knowledge learned during pre-training are especially beneficial for solving complex and multi-step tasks common in specialized domains. Following this exploration, we propose solutions for further adapting LLMs to the requirements of domain-specific tasks. We focus on the clinical domain, which incorporates many typical challenges found in specialized domains. We show how to improve generalization by integrating different domain-specific resources into our models. We further analyze the behavior of the produced models and propose a behavioral testing framework that can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts. Finally, we present an approach for incorporating the benefits of LLMs while fulfilling requirements such as interpretability and modularity. The presented solutions show improvements in performance on benchmark datasets and in manually conducted analyses with medical professionals. Our work provides both new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models as well as multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: Translation Equivariant Transformer Neural Processes
papers.research_question: How to incorporate translation equivariance into transformer neural processes to improve their performance on spatio-temporal data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces translation equivariant transformer neural processes (TE-TNPs) by developing translation equivariant attention mechanisms, improving performance on spatio-temporal tasks.
papers.conclusion: TE-TNPs and TE-PT-TNPs are effective and versatile models that incorporate translation equivariance, performing on par or better than state-of-the-art NPs, though with increased computational cost.
papers.key_findings:
TE-TNPs outperform non-translation-equivariant TNPs and other NP baselines on synthetic 1-D regression, especially when test data is shifted.
TE-PT-TNPs achieve state-of-the-art performance on image completion tasks with MNIST and CIFAR10.
TE-PT-TNPs significantly outperform other models on Kolmogorov flow and environmental data modelling.
Translation equivariance helps models generalize to inputs outside the training range.
Dynamically updating input locations improves performance for complex input distributions.
papers.limitation:
Increased computational cost due to passing input locations through attention mechanisms at each layer.
Initialization of pseudo-locations in TE-PT-TNPs can lead to poor performance in pathological cases.
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of neural processes (NPs) in modelling posterior prediction maps -- the mapping from data to posterior predictive distributions -- has significantly improved since their inception. This improvement can be attributed to two principal factors: (1) advancements in the architecture of permutation invariant set functions, which are intrinsic to all NPs; and (2) leveraging symmetries present in the true posterior predictive map, which are problem dependent. Transformers are a notable development in permutation invariant set functions, and their utility within NPs has been demonstrated through the family of models we refer to as TNPs. Despite significant interest in TNPs, little attention has been given to incorporating symmetries. Notably, the posterior prediction maps for data that are stationary -- a common assumption in spatio-temporal modelling -- exhibit translation equivariance. In this paper, we introduce of a new family of translation equivariant TNPs that incorporate translation equivariance. Through an extensive range of experiments on synthetic and real-world spatio-temporal data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of TE-TNPs relative to their non-translation-equivariant counterparts and other NP baselines.

papers.title: Representation Mechanics: Invariant-Governed Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can neural networks with set-valued operations and learned selection achieve generalization by learning and preserving invariants, as evidenced by early phase transitions (the Platonic Spike)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Representation Mechanics, showing that neural networks with set-valued operations and learned selection can achieve generalization by learning invariants, as evidenced by the Platonic Spike (early phase transition where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that invariant-preserving inductive bias is sufficient for rule learning and that constructing reliable AI requires respecting the mechanics of representation (treating embeddings as physical objects with inertia, boundaries, and elasticity).
papers.key_findings:
Set-valued weights with learned selection lead to early phase transitions (Platonic Spike) where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy.
Classical activations (e.g., GELU, ELU, ReLU) interfere with basin preservation and cause overfitting or boundary erosion.
Basin preservation via path freezing can prevent catastrophic forgetting by maintaining separatrix integrity.
The Surgical Clutch mechanism allows for invariant maintenance under continual learning by dynamically routing gradients.
The architecture achieves high accuracy on synthetic logic and language tasks without relying on n-gram statistics.
papers.limitation: The current work uses explicit rule contexts, which may not be available in all domains, and the architecture has not yet been tested at scale.
future_direction: Testing the architecture at scale
Exploring amplification strategies (more branches, hierarchical scoring, contrastive loss)
Extending to domains without explicit rule contexts
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> We present Representation Mechanics, a theoretical and empirical framework characterizing learning in invariant-governed domains. We demonstrate that neural networks with set-valued operations (discrete potentials {-W, 0, +W}) and learned selection exhibit sharp phase transitions to generalization without pretraining. The Platonic Spike (Early Phase Transition)—where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy in early epochs—signals the discovery of structural invariants before instance memorization. We validate these findings on controlled synthetic tasks (spiral classification, closed-world logic, declarative language) to isolate geometric mechanics from natural language statistical confounds. We contrast this Form-First paradigm with diffusion-dominated learning and define the conditions (Basin Preservation and Friction Set tracking) required to maintain these invariants under continual learning pressure. Our results suggest that restricting representational freedom via discrete potentials is not a limitation but a necessary inductive bias for rule-consistent generalization.

papers.title: A Differential Manifold Perspective and Universality Analysis of Continuous Attractors in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we establish a unified mathematical framework to analyze continuous attractors in artificial neural networks from a differential manifold perspective?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a unified framework based on differential manifolds and Jacobian matrix analysis to study continuous attractors, demonstrating universal singular value stratification in classification networks and linking attractor dimensionality to eigenvalue/singular value structure.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a novel, unified approach to investigating continuous attractors via eigenvalue/singular value analysis of the Jacobian, validates the prevalence of stratification in classification networks, and lays a foundation for a general theory of attractors in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed differential manifold framework is compatible with prior conclusions about continuous attractors.
Continuous attractor phenomena are linked to eigenvalues of the local Jacobian matrix, with stratification indicating approximate attractor behavior.
Singular value stratification is universal across common classification models (MLP, CNN, ResNet) and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, Fruit).
The framework can determine the dimensionality of continuous attractors via the rank of the Jacobian.
Approximate continuous attractor behavior, indicated by eigenvalue/singular value stratification, emerges during neural network training and correlates with generalization.
papers.limitation:
Lacks a rigorous mathematical derivation extending eigenvalue stratification to singular value stratification.
The existence of continuous attractors in tasks beyond classification remains an open question.
future_direction: Develop a general theory of continuous attractors in neural networks.
Apply the methodology to deep neural networks to study optimization landscapes, generalization mechanisms, and training stability.
papers.abstract: Continuous attractors are critical for information processing in both biological and artificial neural systems, with implications for spatial navigation, memory, and deep learning optimization. However, existing research lacks a unified framework to analyze their properties across diverse dynamical systems, limiting cross-architectural generalizability. This study establishes a novel framework from the perspective of differential manifolds to investigate continuous attractors in artificial neural networks. It verifies compatibility with prior conclusions, elucidates links between continuous attractor phenomena and eigenvalues of the local Jacobian matrix, and demonstrates the universality of singular value stratification in common classification models and datasets. These findings suggest continuous attractors may be ubiquitous in general neural networks, highlighting the need for a general theory, with the proposed framework offering a promising foundation given the close mathematical connection between eigenvalues and singular values.

papers.title: Statistical Physics of Deep Neural Networks: Generalization Capability, Beyond the Infinite Width, and Feature Learning
papers.research_question: This thesis investigates three interconnected questions: (1) Can we derive an improved asymptotic bound on the generalization performance of DNNs? (2) How do DNNs behave in a thermodynamic limit where the number of training examples scales with the number of neurons per layer? (3) Do DNNs truly learn dataset features or merely memorize them?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis contributes three main results: (1) an improved asymptotic bound on generalization error that depends only on the last layer size, (2) a statistical mechanics framework for DNNs in a proportional regime beyond the infinite width limit, linking them to Student's t-processes, and (3) a task-explicit analysis showing conditions under which DNNs learn dataset features rather than memorizing.
papers.conclusion: The thesis demonstrates that statistical physics methods can provide significant insights into the generalization, behavior in proportional regimes, and feature learning of DNNs, contributing to more interpretable AI.
papers.key_findings:
An asymptotic generalization bound that depends only on the last layer size, improving classical statistical learning theory bounds.
A closed formula for the generalization error of a finite-width one-hidden layer network in the proportional regime.
An approximate expression for the partition function of deep neural networks in the proportional regime.
A link between deep neural networks in the proportional regime and Student's t-processes.
Evidence that DNNs can learn dataset features rather than memorizing, as shown by analyzing the volume of the solution space and Gaussianity breaking.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at many tasks, often rivaling or surpassing human performance. Yet their internal processes remain elusive, frequently described as "black boxes." While performance can be refined experimentally, achieving a fundamental grasp of their inner workings is still a challenge. Statistical Mechanics has long tackled computational problems, and this thesis applies physics-based insights to understand DNNs via three complementary approaches. First, by averaging over data, we derive an asymptotic bound on generalization that depends solely on the size of the last layer, rather than on the total number of parameters -- revealing how deep architectures process information differently across layers. Second, adopting a data-dependent viewpoint, we explore a finite-width thermodynamic limit beyond the infinite-width regime. This leads to: (i) a closed-form expression for the generalization error in a finite-width one-hidden-layer network (regression task); (ii) an approximate partition function for deeper architectures; and (iii) a link between deep networks in this thermodynamic limit and Student's t-processes. Finally, from a task-explicit perspective, we present a preliminary analysis of how DNNs interact with a controlled dataset, investigating whether they truly internalize its structure -- collapsing to the teacher -- or merely memorize it. By understanding when a network must learn data structure rather than just memorize, it sheds light on fostering meaningful internal representations. In essence, this thesis leverages the synergy between Statistical Physics and Machine Learning to illuminate the inner behavior of DNNs.

papers.title: Gradient Routing: Masking Gradients to Localize Computation in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can gradient routing, a training method that applies data-dependent masks to gradients, be used to localize capabilities to specific subregions of neural networks for interpretability, unlearning, and oversight?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces gradient routing, a training method that uses data-dependent gradient masks to localize capabilities to specific subregions of neural networks, enabling interpretable representations, robust unlearning, and scalable oversight.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that gradient routing is a promising localization technique for real-world applications with scarce quality data, and may address limitations of black-box training in high-stakes machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient routing can partition learned representations in an interpretable way, as demonstrated by splitting MNIST digit encodings into non-overlapping halves.
Gradient routing enables robust unlearning via ablation of a pre-specified network subregion, outperforming data filtering when labels are limited.
Gradient routing allows scalable oversight in reinforcement learning by localizing modules responsible for different behaviors, even with limited labeled data.
Gradient routing exhibits an absorption effect, where localization applied to narrow data (e.g., specific tokens) generalizes to broader capabilities (e.g., semantic concepts).
Gradient routing can localize concepts to individual dimensions of the residual stream, enabling model steering with a single scalar value.
papers.limitation:
Clean separation of representations in the MNIST autoencoder depends on specific problem setup and heavy L1 regularization.
The learning dynamics of gradient routing, including potential 'internal tug of war' effects, remain an open question.
The reinforcement learning environment used is simple and may not reflect the complexity of real-world problems.
future_direction: Further investigation into the learning dynamics of gradient routing.
Application of gradient routing to more complex environments and larger models.
Empirical and conceptual work needed for scalable oversight in real-world settings.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are trained primarily based on their inputs and outputs, without regard for their internal mechanisms. These neglected mechanisms determine properties that are critical for safety, like (i) transparency; (ii) the absence of sensitive information or harmful capabilities; and (iii) reliable generalization of goals beyond the training distribution. To address this shortcoming, we introduce gradient routing, a training method that isolates capabilities to specific subregions of a neural network. Gradient routing applies data-dependent, weighted masks to gradients during backpropagation. These masks are supplied by the user in order to configure which parameters are updated by which data points. We show that gradient routing can be used to (1) learn representations which are partitioned in an interpretable way; (2) enable robust unlearning via ablation of a pre-specified network subregion; and (3) achieve scalable oversight of a reinforcement learner by localizing modules responsible for different behaviors. Throughout, we find that gradient routing localizes capabilities even when applied to a limited, ad-hoc subset of the data. We conclude that the approach holds promise for challenging, real-world applications where quality data are scarce.

papers.title: Encoding and Understanding Astrophysical Information in Large Language Model-Generated Summaries
papers.research_question: To what extent does prompt engineering affect the correlation between text embeddings and physical quantities, and how is physics information encoded in text summaries?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can encode physical information from astrophysical text, with structured prompting improving alignment between embeddings and physical quantities, and sparse autoencoders reveal the semantic concepts driving this encoding.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can capture, learn, and represent physics concepts in textual data, and prompt engineering enhances the correlation between text embeddings and physical quantities. Sparse autoencoders provide insight into the semantic concepts underlying this encoding.
papers.key_findings:
Structured prompts significantly improve the clustering purity of LLM embeddings with respect to physical quantities, with improvements up to 57.5% for variability index.
Sparse autoencoders extract interpretable features from text embeddings that correlate with specific astrophysical properties, such as non-thermal characteristics linked to power-law gamma values.
LLMs infer physical parameters from text descriptions even when numerical values are not explicitly stated, demonstrating an understanding of astrophysical concepts.
Concepts like 'eclipsing binaries' and 'galaxy cluster thermal dynamics' are encoded in the embeddings and associated with physical measurements.
The method allows for visual and quantitative analysis of how physics is encoded in language through t-SNE clustering and SAE feature activation.
future_direction: Expanding the dataset to include more sources
Optimizing prompting with different models
Creating an interface for astronomer validation of possibly anomalous objects
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated the ability to generalize well at many levels across domains, modalities, and even shown in-context learning capabilities. This enables research questions regarding how they can be used to encode physical information that is usually only available from scientific measurements, and loosely encoded in textual descriptions. Using astrophysics as a test bed, we investigate if LLM embeddings can codify physical summary statistics that are obtained from scientific measurements through two main questions: 1) Does prompting play a role on how those quantities are codified by the LLM? and 2) What aspects of language are most important in encoding the physics represented by the measurement? We investigate this using sparse autoencoders that extract interpretable features from the text.

papers.title: Getting a CLUE: A Method for Explaining Uncertainty Estimates
papers.research_question: How can we interpret uncertainty estimates from probabilistic models by finding counterfactual explanations that indicate how to change an input to make the model more confident?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Counterfactual Latent Uncertainty Explanations (CLUE), a method to generate counterfactual explanations for uncertainty estimates by searching in the latent space of a deep generative model, and proposes a framework for evaluating such explanations.
papers.conclusion: CLUE is an effective method for generating counterfactual explanations of uncertainty, outperforming baselines and helping practitioners understand sources of uncertainty.
papers.key_findings:
CLUE outperforms baseline methods in explaining uncertainty across multiple datasets.
CLUE generates counterfactuals that are on the data manifold and plausible.
The proposed computational evaluation framework allows for quantitative assessment of counterfactual explanations.
User studies demonstrate that CLUE helps practitioners predict on which new inputs a BNN will be uncertain.
papers.limitation:
CLUE relies on the quality of the auxiliary deep generative model; if the DGM fails to capture the data manifold, CLUE may generate unrealistic counterfactuals.
CLUE is designed for differentiable probabilistic models, which may limit its applicability.
future_direction: Extending CLUE to other types of uncertainty estimates.
Exploring the use of CLUE in active learning and Bayesian optimization.
Investigating other distance metrics for the counterfactual search.
papers.abstract: Both uncertainty estimation and interpretability are important factors for trustworthy machine learning systems. However, there is little work at the intersection of these two areas. We address this gap by proposing a novel method for interpreting uncertainty estimates from differentiable probabilistic models, like Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). Our method, Counterfactual Latent Uncertainty Explanations (CLUE), indicates how to change an input, while keeping it on the data manifold, such that a BNN becomes more confident about the input's prediction. We validate CLUE through 1) a novel framework for evaluating counterfactual explanations of uncertainty, 2) a series of ablation experiments, and 3) a user study. Our experiments show that CLUE outperforms baselines and enables practitioners to better understand which input patterns are responsible for predictive uncertainty.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: Explaining the Machine Learning Solution of the Ising Model
papers.research_question: How can we explain the results from machine learning models applied to the Ising model? Specifically, how do PCA and a simple neural network identify phases and the critical temperature?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that PCA identifies the order parameter and temperature as the control variable, and that a single-layer neural network informed by symmetry can accurately predict the critical temperature, with the explanation revealing that the network learns to use the magnetization direction.
papers.conclusion: The explanation of the strategies used by simpler ML models indicates the directions that can be taken to fully explain more sophisticated ones, opening the ML black-boxes and paving the way to extract physical laws from model parameters.
papers.key_findings:
PCA not only identifies the magnetization as the order parameter but also shows that the greatest variance is in the direction of the temperature gradient.
A single-layer neural network (SLNN) with no hidden layers, informed by spin inversion symmetry, can accurately estimate the critical temperature of the Ising model.
The SLNN works by aligning its weight vector with the magnetization direction and scaling the argument to separate phases.
A one-hidden-layer NN with two units can solve the general case without sign restriction, and the output layer combines the hidden units' outputs to correct labeling.
The explanation allows predicting the minimal NN architecture needed for more complex phase transitions.
papers.limitation:
The method may require more hidden units or non-linear techniques for more complex phase diagrams.
It has not yet been possible to extract physical laws from the inferred parameters.
future_direction: Applying the method to other physics systems with more general phase transitions, both classical and quantum.
Extracting physical laws from the parameters of the models.
papers.abstract: As powerful as machine learning (ML) techniques are in solving problems involving data with large dimensionality, explaining the results from the fitted parameters remains a challenging task of utmost importance, especially in physics applications. This work shows how this can be accomplished for the ferromagnetic Ising model, the main target of several ML studies in statistical physics. Here it is demonstrated that the successful unsupervised identification of the phases and order parameter by principal component analysis, a common method in those studies, detects that the magnetization per spin has its greatest variation with the temperature, the actual control parameter of the phase transition. Then, by using a neural network (NN) without hidden layers (the simplest possible) and informed by the symmetry of the Hamiltonian, an explanation is provided for the strategy used in finding the supervised learning solution for the critical temperature of the model's continuous phase transition. This allows the prediction of the minimal extension of the NN to solve the problem when the symmetry is not known, which becomes also explainable. These results pave the way to a physics-informed explainable generalized framework, enabling the extraction of physical laws and principles from the parameters of the models.

papers.title: Efficient Representations are Controllable Representations
papers.research_question: What is the most brute-force way to install interpretable, controllable features into a model’s activations? Can a model's efficiency pressure be exploited to induce interpretable, controllable representations?
papers.core_contribution: By finetuning an LLM with a simple auxiliary loss to write binary feature classifications into a small set of residual stream dimensions, the model reorganizes to depend on these flags, making them genuine internal features that can be used to steer generation at inference time. This works due to the model's efficiency pressure under capacity constraints.
papers.conclusion: The residual stream is writable, and a model's own efficiency pressure can be exploited to induce interpretable and controllable representations. This inverts the usual controllability problem by providing signals that the model will naturally consolidate around.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns to write correct feature flags to the designated 'fenced' dimensions after training.
The model learns to depend on these flags during generation, as shown by overwriting experiments that causally steer generation.
The model erodes its own alternative representations of the fenced features, consolidating feature information into the fenced dimensions.
The efficiency pressure (representational cost) leads the model to consolidate around the reliably supplied feature signals.
The method incurs a negligible perplexity cost when fencing a small number of dimensions, but the cost grows as more dimensions are fenced.
papers.limitation:
Early layers (k < 5) struggle to produce clean flags, consistent with the view that early layers have not yet derived the relevant features.
At the current level of training, the model has begun to erode previous representations but some residual information persists in the remaining dimensions.
papers.abstract: What is the most brute-force way to install interpretable, controllable features into a model's activations? Controlling how LLMs internally represent concepts typically requires sophisticated methods to first identify, then intervene on the model's existing feature geometry. We bypass all of this. We finetune an LLM with a simple auxiliary loss, training 16 of its 3072 residual stream dimensions to be inert interpretability flags that simply indicate what concepts are required for generation. The model reorganizes around them anyway, learning to rely on these flags during actual generation tasks. As a result, these inert flags become genuine internal features: interpretable control switches that allow us to steer generation at inference time. Why does this work? When a feature is reliably supplied at a fixed location, gradient descent gradually eliminates redundant encodings elsewhere, and the model erodes its own alternative representations. A model's efficiency pressure is a lever - exploitable to induce interpretable, controllable representations.

papers.title: Does TabPFN Understand Causal Structures?
papers.research_question: Does TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model, encode causal knowledge in its internal representations beyond statistical correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and introduces an adapter framework that can extract this information for causal discovery, outperforming traditional statistical methods.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and the proposed adapter framework can extract this information for causal discovery, establishing a new direction for interpretable and adaptable tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Causal information is concentrated in the middle layers (4-6) of TabPFN's encoder.
The proposed framework extracts causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and outperforms statistical baselines (GIES, IGSP, DCDI) on ROC AUC, performing closely to the specialized neural causal discovery model A VICI.
The decoder architecture is crucial for performance; using a learnable decoder significantly improves results compared to using no decoder.
Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, particularly for dense graph structures like Erdős-Rényi and Stochastic Block Model graphs.
Using embeddings from the pre-trained TabPFN encoder (optimal weights) yields better causal discovery performance than using randomly initialized or degraded encoder weights.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, and the approach is sensitive to the type of graph structure.
future_direction: Leveraging pre-trained tabular models for extracting causal structures and improving their interpretability.
Understanding how tabular foundation models reason about different datasets.
Repurposing tabular foundation models for different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Causal discovery is fundamental for multiple scientific domains, yet extracting causal information from real world data remains a significant challenge. Given the recent success on real data, we investigate whether TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model pre-trained on synthetic datasets generated from structural causal models, encodes causal information in its internal representations. We develop an adapter framework using a learnable decoder and causal tokens that extract causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and decode them into adjacency matrices for causal discovery. Our evaluations demonstrate that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, outperforming several traditional causal discovery algorithms, with such causal information being concentrated in mid-range layers. These findings establish a new direction for interpretable and adaptable foundation models and demonstrate the potential for leveraging pre-trained tabular models for causal discovery.

papers.title: Neural Networks as Physics-Consistent Surrogates: An \textit{Explainable AI} Validation Framework for Learning Constitutive Relations
papers.research_question: How can neural networks for constitutive modeling of solid materials be validated and interpreted to confirm they learn physically meaningful principles rather than merely curve-fitting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops and applies a Physics-Explainable AI (XAI) framework to validate that neural network surrogates for constitutive modeling learn underlying physical mechanisms (stiffness, history-dependence, temporal damping) rather than just curve-fitting.
papers.conclusion: The Physics-XAI framework successfully validates that neural constitutive models learn physically interpretable representations of stiffness, path dependence, and fractional-order memory, transforming them from black boxes into transparent, mechanically grounded glass boxes.
papers.key_findings:
For hyperelasticity, gradient-based attributions (Grad Input and Integrated Gradients) match the analytical tangent modulus, proving the network learned material stiffness.
For elastoplasticity, SHAP and PCA show the RNN internalizes path-dependent memory, with plastic strain identified as the dominant feature governing stress prediction.
For viscoelasticity, latent-space and wavelet analyses of GRU layers reveal a temporal hierarchy encoding instantaneous elastic response, intermediate relaxation, and long-term fractional memory.
The Physics-Aware Distillation (PAD) procedure extracts interpretable material constants (e.g., Mooney-Rivlin coefficients) from the trained neural networks.
Quantitative metrics (MSE, MAE, R2, attribution correlations) confirm high fidelity and physical consistency across all three material models.
papers.limitation: The work focuses on uniaxial settings and noise-free synthetic data.
future_direction: Extend to multiaxial loading, anisotropic materials, and experimental datasets.
Integrate XAI with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs).
Incorporate uncertainty quantification and robustness analysis for verification and validation.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a Physics-\textit{Explainable AI} (XAI) framework to validate and interpret neural networks for the constitutive modeling of solid materials. The study bridges the gap between data-driven models and continuum mechanics by applying a suite of explainability methods to neural networks trained on three distinct material behaviors: hyperelasticity (\textit{Mooney-Rivlin}), elastoplasticity (\textit{Chaboche}), and viscoelasticity (\textit{Fractional Zener}). First, high-fidelity surrogate models, including dense feed-forward networks, LSTMs, and GRUs, are trained on synthetically generated data to accurately capture complex material responses. The core of the work then employs XAI techniques to "open the black box" and confirm that the networks learn physically meaningful principles. For hyperelasticity, gradient-based attributions (\textit{Grad Input} (GI)) successfully match the analytical tangent modulus, proving the network learned material stiffness. For elastoplasticity, \textit{SHapley Additive exPlanations} (SHAP) and \textit{Principal Component Analysis} (PCA) demonstrate the \textit{Recurrent Neural Network} (RNN) internalizes path-dependent memory, with SHAP identifying \textit{plastic strain} as the dominant feature governing the stress prediction. For viscoelasticity, latent-space and wavelet analyses of the \textit{Gated Recurrent Unit. } GRU layers reveal a clear temporal hierarchy, with different layers encoding instantaneous elastic response, intermediate relaxation, and long-term fractional memory. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that the XAI framework can verify that the neural networks are not merely curve-fitting but are, in fact, learning the underlying physical mechanisms of stiffness, history-dependence, and temporal damping.

papers.title: Do Llamas understand the periodic table?
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) represent the periodic table of elements, and what is the geometric structure of their hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally develop structured geometric representations (a 3D spiral) of the periodic table in their hidden states, with knowledge encoded as continuous manifolds in middle layers that sharpen into categorical distinctions in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs represent symbolic scientific knowledge as coherent, geometry-aware manifolds that reflect the natural order of the physical world, which can inform interpretability and trust in LLMs for scientific applications.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure in LLM hidden states aligns with the conceptual organization of the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous, overlapping attribute subspaces, while deeper layers sharpen decision boundaries and integrate linguistic context.
Linguistic structure increasingly shapes factual representations in later layers.
Strong linear associations between related attributes in middle layers enable indirect recall.
Regression probing shows continuous numerical features are effectively represented in intermediate layers, while classification probing shows later layers are better for fine-grained categorical decisions.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to chemical elements in the periodic table; future studies could expand to other chemical structures and properties.
The hypothesis-driven validation of geometric structures may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Expand to other chemical structures and properties.
Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge.
papers.abstract: We observe a 3D spiral structure in the hidden states of LLMs that aligns with the conceptual structure of the periodic table.

papers.title: Data-Driven Insights into Jet Turbulence: Explainable AI Approaches
papers.research_question: Which regions of a turbulent jet flow field are most relevant for prediction by a neural network, and how do different XAI methods compare in identifying these regions?
papers.core_contribution: Applying XAI methods to a turbulent jet prediction model reveals that regions of moderate vorticity, rather than high vorticity, are most important for prediction, and these regions correspond to areas of high dissipation. Gradient-based methods (Grad-CAM and Gradient-SHAP) provide a less biased view compared to SHAP.
papers.conclusion: XAI methods applied to a jet turbulence prediction model show that regions of moderate vorticity are key for prediction and are linked to high dissipation. Gradient-based methods avoid segmentation bias and highlight uniformly distributed, nearly circular structures associated with vortex rings and turbulent mixing.
papers.key_findings:
The most relevant flow structures for prediction are not those with high vorticity but those with moderate vorticity (ω*_z between 0.25 and 0.5).
Structures with high normalized Shapley values coincide with those contributing most to turbulent kinetic energy dissipation.
Grad-CAM and Gradient-SHAP identify regions with uniform spatial distribution, suggesting correlation with momentum transport by smaller-scale vortices.
The identified structures by Grad-CAM and Gradient-SHAP are often nearly circular (shape factor close to 1), indicating vortex rings are dominant in energy transfer and mixing.
Compared to SHAP, Grad-CAM and Gradient-SHAP do not require pre-segmentation and thus avoid bias, providing a more direct identification of physically significant regions.
papers.limitation: SHAP requires pre-defined segmentation of the flow field into regions, which may introduce bias in identifying relevant features.
papers.abstract: In this study, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods are applied to analyze flow fields obtained through PIV measurements of an axisymmetric turbulent jet. A convolutional neural network (U-Net) was trained to predict velocity fields at subsequent time steps. Three XAI methods: SHapley Additive explanations (SHAP), Gradient-SHAP, and Grad-CAM were employed to identify the flow field regions relevant for prediction. SHAP requires predefined segmentation of the flow field into relevant regions, while Gradient-SHAP and Grad-CAM avoid this bias by generating gradient-based heatmaps. The results show that the most relevant structures do not necessarily coincide with regions of maximum vorticity but rather with those exhibiting moderate vorticity, highlighting the critical role of these regions in energy transfer and jet dynamics. Additionally, structures with high turbulent dissipation values are identified as the most significant. Gradient-SHAP and Grad-CAM methods reveal a uniform spatial distribution of relevant regions, emphasizing the contribution of nearly circular structures to turbulent mixing. This study advances the understanding of turbulent dynamics through XAI tools, providing an innovative approach to correlate machine learning models with physical phenomena.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: A simple probabilistic neural network for machine understanding
papers.research_question: What are the properties of learning machines with a fixed internal representation, derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, in unsupervised learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM), a probabilistic neural network with a fixed internal representation derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, and shows that it has desirable properties like continuity, controllable compression, and ability to support functions beyond generalization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that learning machines with a fixed internal representation, such as the HFM, operate in a qualitatively different regime from traditional models like RBMs, with data-specific information stored in weights and potential for higher cognitive functions.
papers.key_findings:
The HFM is uniquely identified by the principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance when hidden units are binary.
The HFM exhibits a phase transition at a critical coupling parameter g, with a divergence in specific heat.
Training the HFM with an EM algorithm allows features to be learned sequentially, with low-order features remaining stable as new features are added.
The internal representation of the HFM is robust to changes in the coupling parameter and dataset size, and low-order features capture most of the relevant information.
The learning modality of HFM is qualitatively different from RBMs: in HFM, data-specific information is stored in the weights, while in RBMs it is transferred to the internal representation.
future_direction: Investigating whether a universal data-independent internal representation emerges spontaneously in deep layers of learning architectures.
Relating the findings to thermodynamic costs of learning.
Exploring the hypothesis that internal representations evolve with depth in hierarchical learning systems.
papers.abstract: We discuss probabilistic neural networks with a fixed internal representation as models for machine understanding. Here understanding is intended as mapping data to an already existing representation which encodes an {\em a priori} organisation of the feature space. We derive the internal representation by requiring that it satisfies the principles of maximal relevance and of maximal ignorance about how different features are combined. We show that, when hidden units are binary variables, these two principles identify a unique model -- the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM) -- which is fully solvable and provides a natural interpretation in terms of features. We argue that learning machines with this architecture enjoy a number of interesting properties, like the continuity of the representation with respect to changes in parameters and data, the possibility to control the level of compression and the ability to support functions that go beyond generalisation. We explore the behaviour of the model with extensive numerical experiments and argue that models where the internal representation is fixed reproduce a learning modality which is qualitatively different from that of traditional models such as Restricted Boltzmann Machines.

papers.title: Validating Mechanistic Interpretations: An Axiomatic Approach
papers.research_question: How can we formally characterize and validate mechanistic interpretations of neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a set of axioms that formally characterize a mechanistic interpretation as a description that approximately captures the semantics of a neural network in a compositional manner, and demonstrates their applicability for validation.
papers.conclusion: The axiomatic approach provides a rigorous foundation for validating mechanistic interpretations of neural networks, and its utility is demonstrated through case studies on modular addition and 2-SAT models.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed axioms provide a formal framework for validating mechanistic interpretations, requiring both component-wise and compositional evaluation.
In the 2-SAT case study, the model's first block parses the input formula into clauses, while the second block evaluates satisfiability via enumeration of variable assignments.
The axioms can reveal errors in interpretations that component-wise evaluation alone might miss, highlighting the importance of compositional validation.
The approach is successfully applied to validate an existing interpretation of a modular addition model and a new interpretation of a 2-SAT model.
The axioms are inspired by abstract interpretation and require the definition of abstraction and concretization functions to map between concrete and abstract representations.
papers.limitation:
The axioms are necessary but may not be sufficient in all cases for characterizing a mechanistic interpretation.
The axioms require the model's output to be discrete and necessitate the design of abstraction and concretization functions, which can be challenging.
future_direction: Extending the approach to analyze models trained for other problems.
Exploring the more informal axioms (Axioms 5 and 6) related to the compilability of the mechanistic interpretation.
Applying the framework to circuit-style interpretations, such as the Indirect Object Identification circuit.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse engineer the computation performed by a neural network in terms of its internal components. Although there is a growing body of research on mechanistic interpretation of neural networks, the notion of a mechanistic interpretation itself is often ad-hoc. Inspired by the notion of abstract interpretation from the program analysis literature that aims to develop approximate semantics for programs, we give a set of axioms that formally characterize a mechanistic interpretation as a description that approximately captures the semantics of the neural network under analysis in a compositional manner. We demonstrate the applicability of these axioms for validating mechanistic interpretations on an existing, well-known interpretability study as well as on a new case study involving a Transformer-based model trained to solve the well-known 2-SAT problem.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior.
