We use here the concept of physically-constrained neural networks (PCNN) to predict the input-output relation in a physical system, while, at the same time fulfilling the physical constraints. With this goal, the internal hidden state variables of the system are associated with a set of internal neuron layers, whose values are constrained by known physical relations, as well as any additional knowledge on the system. Furthermore, when having enough data, it is possible to infer knowledge about the internal structure of the system and, if parameterized, to predict the state parameters for a particular input-output relation. We show that this approach, besides getting physically-based predictions, accelerates the training process, reduces the amount of data required to get similar accuracy, filters partly the intrinsic noise in the experimental data and provides improved extrapolation capacity.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Learning from nature: insights into GraphDOP's representations of the Earth System
papers.research_question: How does the GraphDOP model, trained solely on meteorological observations, develop internal representations of the Earth System state, structure, dynamics, and observing system characteristics?
papers.core_contribution: The GraphDOP model, trained exclusively on Earth System observations without prior physical knowledge, develops coherent internal representations (a 'world model') of the underlying physical state, viewing effects, and meteorological dynamics to successfully predict future observations.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks trained purely on observations of the Earth System can develop internal representations of the physical world, including state, dynamics, and observing system characteristics, providing a foundation for future data-driven weather prediction models.
papers.key_findings:
GraphDOP constructs a unified latent representation of the Earth System state that is common across diverse observation types, such as cloud structures being consistent in predictions for satellite radiances and in-situ cloud fraction measurements.
The model learns to emulate complex viewing effects, such as limb effects in microwave sounders and sunglint in visible imagery, mapping from its latent state to observed variables.
GraphDOP develops internal representations of meteorological structures and dynamics, enabling it to infer unobserved, non-local variables (e.g., jet streams, surface pressure) from limited input observations, such as from a single geostationary satellite.
In the absence of input observations, the model's predictions revert to a learned climatological prior, demonstrating the role of learned priors in its inference.
The model captures the complex dynamics of extra-tropical weather systems, including rapid cyclogenesis, with skill approaching physics-based systems.
papers.limitation:
The current GraphDOP configuration is restricted to using only 12 hours of observations as input, with no background state provided.
It remains an open question whether external bias correction schemes are necessary or if the model can learn to correct for systematic observation errors internally.
Questions remain over whether the observational coverage is sufficiently complete to provide enough constraint for observation-only approaches to reach their full potential.
future_direction: Introduce recurrence and cycle through several input windows, carrying information forward via the latent space to provide a prior estimate of the current state.
Investigate the model's handling of systematic observation errors to determine if external bias correction is necessary.
Explore whether longer input windows or cycling information from earlier windows can extend the area of skillful predictions beyond directly observed regions.
papers.abstract: Through a series of experiments, we provide evidence that the GraphDOP model - trained solely on meteorological observations, using no prior knowledge - develops internal representations of the Earth System state, structure and dynamics as well as the characteristics of different observing systems. Firstly, we demonstrate that the network constructs a unified latent representation of the Earth System state which is common across different observation types. For example, cloud structures maintain physical consistency whether viewed in predictions for satellite radiances from different sensors, or for direct in-situ measurements of the cloud fraction. Secondly, we show examples that suggest that the network learns to emulate viewing effects - learned observation operators that map from the unified state representation to observed properties. Microwave sounder limb effects and geometric viewing effects, such as sunglint in visible imagery, are both well captured. Finally, we demonstrate that the model develops rich internal representations of the structure of meteorological systems and their dynamics. For instance, when the network is only provided with observations from a single infrared instrument, it is able to infer unobserved, non-local structures such as jet streams, surface pressure patterns and warm and cold air masses associated with synoptic systems. This work provides insights into how neural networks trained solely on observations of the Earth System spontaneously develop coherent internal representations of the physical world in order to meet the training objective - enhancing our understanding and guiding future development of these models.

papers.title: Discovering Symbolic Models from Deep Learning with Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: How can we combine deep learning and symbolic regression to extract interpretable symbolic models from neural networks, specifically Graph Neural Networks, to discover physical laws and improve generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that combines deep learning (specifically Graph Neural Networks with strong inductive biases) and symbolic regression to distill interpretable symbolic models from neural networks, enabling the discovery of physical laws and improving generalization.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully distills symbolic, interpretable models from Graph Neural Networks, recovers known physical laws, discovers new formulas in cosmology, and improves generalization, offering a promising direction for interpreting deep learning models and advancing scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
The method can extract known physical equations (e.g., force laws and Hamiltonians) from the learned representations of Graph Neural Networks.
Applied to a cosmology dataset, the framework discovered a new analytic formula for predicting dark matter halo concentration from the mass distribution of nearby structures.
The extracted symbolic expressions generalized to out-of-distribution data better than the original Graph Neural Network model.
The framework demonstrates that neural networks can learn representations that are linear transformations of true physical quantities (e.g., forces) when appropriate inductive biases are applied.
The approach offers a pathway to interpret neural networks and discover novel physical principles from the representations they learn.
future_direction: Extending the framework to gridded PDE data using existing symbolic regression packages for PDEs.
Using other symbolic regression packages (e.g., PySR, grammar-based methods) as drop-in replacements for eureqa in the framework.
papers.abstract: We develop a general approach to distill symbolic representations of a learned deep model by introducing strong inductive biases. We focus on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The technique works as follows: we first encourage sparse latent representations when we train a GNN in a supervised setting, then we apply symbolic regression to components of the learned model to extract explicit physical relations. We find the correct known equations, including force laws and Hamiltonians, can be extracted from the neural network. We then apply our method to a non-trivial cosmology example-a detailed dark matter simulation-and discover a new analytic formula which can predict the concentration of dark matter from the mass distribution of nearby cosmic structures. The symbolic expressions extracted from the GNN using our technique also generalized to out-of-distribution data better than the GNN itself. Our approach offers alternative directions for interpreting neural networks and discovering novel physical principles from the representations they learn.

papers.title: GINN-KAN: Interpretability pipelining with applications in Physics Informed Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we create an interpretable neural network that combines the strengths of GINN and KAN to overcome their individual limitations and be effectively applied to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GINN-KAN, a novel interpretable neural network that combines the strengths of GINN and KAN, and demonstrates its application to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), creating interpretable PINNs that outperform black-box networks.
papers.conclusion: GINN-KAN represents a significant step forward in developing interpretable neural networks, offering a promising balance between interpretability and performance, and can be seamlessly integrated into existing machine learning frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
GINN-KAN outperforms both GINN and KAN on the Feynman symbolic regression benchmark datasets.
GINN-KAN augmented PINNs outperform traditional PINNs with black-box networks on 15 different partial differential equations.
GINN struggles to learn non-Laurent polynomial (non-LP) equations, while KAN struggles to learn equations containing multiplicative terms.
GINN-KAN combines the strengths of both GINN and KAN, performing well on both LP and non-LP equations and on equations with multiplications.
GINN-KAN can be trained using backpropagation and integrated into existing machine learning pipelines with minimal adjustments.
papers.limitation: GINN-KAN is restricted to inputs with positive values, a limitation inherited from GINN.
future_direction: Explore more robust architectures that maintain interpretability while overcoming the positive input limitation.
Develop better regularization techniques to enable GINN-KAN to accurately discover concise ground truth equations.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are powerful function approximators, yet their ``black-box" nature often renders them opaque and difficult to interpret. While many post-hoc explanation methods exist, they typically fail to capture the underlying reasoning processes of the networks. A truly interpretable neural network would be trained similarly to conventional models using techniques such as backpropagation, but additionally provide insights into the learned input-output relationships. In this work, we introduce the concept of interpretability pipelineing, to incorporate multiple interpretability techniques to outperform each individual technique. To this end, we first evaluate several architectures that promise such interpretability, with a particular focus on two recent models selected for their potential to incorporate interpretability into standard neural network architectures while still leveraging backpropagation: the Growing Interpretable Neural Network (GINN) and Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KAN). We analyze the limitations and strengths of each and introduce a novel interpretable neural network GINN-KAN that synthesizes the advantages of both models. When tested on the Feynman symbolic regression benchmark datasets, GINN-KAN outperforms both GINN and KAN. To highlight the capabilities and the generalizability of this approach, we position GINN-KAN as an alternative to conventional black-box networks in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). We expect this to have far-reaching implications in the application of deep learning pipelines in the natural sciences. Our experiments with this interpretable PINN on 15 different partial differential equations demonstrate that GINN-KAN augmented PINNs outperform PINNs with black-box networks in solving differential equations and surpass the capabilities of both GINN and KAN.

papers.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
papers.research_question: How can we unify existing methods for interpreting model predictions and assign feature importance values that satisfy desirable properties?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SHAP, a unified framework for interpreting model predictions that unifies six existing methods and provides a unique solution with desirable properties, leading to new methods with improved computational performance and consistency with human intuition.
papers.conclusion: The SHAP framework identifies the class of additive feature importance methods and shows there is a unique solution in this class that adheres to desirable properties, providing a unified approach to model interpretation with improved estimation methods.
papers.key_findings:
SHAP unifies six existing feature attribution methods: LIME, DeepLIFT, Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation, Shapley regression values, Shapley sampling values, and Quantitative Input Influence.
SHAP values are the unique solution in the class of additive feature attribution methods that satisfy local accuracy, missingness, and consistency.
Kernel SHAP provides more accurate estimates with fewer model evaluations than previous sampling-based methods like Shapley sampling values.
SHAP values are more consistent with human intuition than LIME and DeepLIFT in user studies on simple models.
Deep SHAP, a compositional approximation for deep networks, improves upon DeepLIFT by better approximating Shapley values.
papers.limitation: Exact computation of SHAP values is challenging and requires approximations, which may rely on assumptions like feature independence or model linearity.
future_direction: Developing faster model-type-specific estimation methods that make fewer assumptions.
Integrating work on estimating interaction effects from game theory.
Defining new explanation model classes.
papers.abstract: Understanding why a model makes a certain prediction can be as crucial as the prediction's accuracy in many applications. However, the highest accuracy for large modern datasets is often achieved by complex models that even experts struggle to interpret, such as ensemble or deep learning models, creating a tension between accuracy and interpretability. In response, various methods have recently been proposed to help users interpret the predictions of complex models, but it is often unclear how these methods are related and when one method is preferable over another. To address this problem, we present a unified framework for interpreting predictions, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). SHAP assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. Its novel components include: (1) the identification of a new class of additive feature importance measures, and (2) theoretical results showing there is a unique solution in this class with a set of desirable properties. The new class unifies six existing methods, notable because several recent methods in the class lack the proposed desirable properties. Based on insights from this unification, we present new methods that show improved computational performance and/or better consistency with human intuition than previous approaches.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability, and how can we define and demarcate mechanistic interpretability as a scientific practice?
papers.core_contribution: The paper defines mechanistic interpretability as the practice of producing model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable explanations of neural networks, and argues that the Principle of Explanatory Optimism is a necessary precondition for its success.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability is a valuable scientific practice for understanding neural networks, grounded in the Explanatory View and dependent on the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, and provides a framework for defining and pursuing faithful explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal mechanisms (ur-explanations), not just its input-output behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability is formally defined as seeking explanations that are model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable.
Mechanistic interpretability has inherent limits due to the value-ladenness and theory-ladenness of explanations, and its focus on model-level explanations excludes system-level complexities.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism states that the algorithmic structure learned by generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, and without this assumption, mechanistic interpretability is intractable.
papers.limitation:
Explanations in mechanistic interpretability are value-laden, as the choice of precision and metrics depends on the interpreter's goals and values.
Explanations are theory-laden, as interpretability methods rely on theoretical commitments (e.g., sparse autoencoders assume sparsity and linearity).
Mechanistic interpretability focuses on model-level explanations, but AI systems involve additional components beyond the model, limiting the scope of MI for understanding system behavior.
future_direction: Increased focus on criteria that make explanations accessible to diverse humans, involving human-computer interaction and social sciences.
Development of a new field focusing on system-level explanations, building on mechanistic interpretability.
Collaboration between philosophy, computational complexity, and machine learning to investigate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural net- works through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability re- search is a principled approach to understanding models be- cause neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI’s inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: From Neurons to Neutrons: A Case Study in Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability extract scientific knowledge from neural networks trained on physics data, and can such insights align with human-derived domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can extract scientifically meaningful representations from neural networks trained on nuclear physics data, aligning with human-derived concepts like the semi-empirical mass formula and shell model.
papers.conclusion: These findings provide a proof-of-concept that neural networks, when trained on scientific data, can learn useful representations that align with human knowledge, opening exciting possibilities for future research on richer data and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings of proton and neutron numbers exhibit a helix structure that encodes nuclear physics concepts like the volume and asymmetry terms.
The orderedness of embeddings along the first principal component correlates with generalization performance.
Penultimate layer features correspond to terms in the semi-empirical mass formula and nuclear shell model.
Latent space topography reveals the algorithm used by the model for binding energy prediction, geometrically representing the SEMF.
Models trained on nuclear data learn representations similar to those trained on pseudo data from human-derived theory.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted knowledge is not guaranteed; representations may be complex and not easily distilled into interpretable theories.
Lack of quantitative metrics to assess interpretability.
Symbolic regression from neural features did not yield fully interpretable improvements over human-derived models.
Requires interdisciplinary collaborations and close partnerships between machine learning researchers and domain experts.
future_direction: Applying interpretability to richer data and more complex tasks.
Developing quantitative metrics for interpretability.
Exploring other scientific domains for knowledge extraction.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) promises a path toward fully understanding how neural networks make their predictions. Prior work demonstrates that even when trained to perform simple arithmetic, models can implement a variety of algorithms (sometimes concurrently) depending on initialization and hyperparameters. Does this mean neuron-level interpretability techniques have limited applicability? We argue that high-dimensional neural networks can learn low-dimensional representations of their training data that are useful beyond simply making good predictions. Such representations can be understood through the mechanistic interpretability lens and provide insights that are surprisingly faithful to human-derived domain knowledge. This indicates that such approaches to interpretability can be useful for deriving a new understanding of a problem from models trained to solve it. As a case study, we extract nuclear physics concepts by studying models trained to reproduce nuclear data.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability -- The Strange Science Part I.i
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability? How can we define mechanistic interpretability and what are its inherent limits?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a philosophical framework for mechanistic interpretability, including the Explanatory View Hypothesis, a definition of mechanistic interpretability as producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations, and the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that if the Principle of Explanatory Optimism holds, interpretability could enable humans to understand machine knowledge, making it a crucial scientific endeavor for the future of human understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory Faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal ur-explanations, and is well-defined under the Explanatory View.
Mechanistic Interpretability is defined as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks.
Mechanistic Interpretability has inherent limits, such as theory-ladenness and the potential for high explanatory complexity that may make models incomprehensible to humans.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism, which states that the algorithmic structure of generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability may be limited by the theory-ladenness of observations, where the interpreter's prior theories influence what they can discover.
There is a risk that the explanatory complexity of models might be too high for humans to understand, which would make mechanistic interpretability intractable.
future_direction: Formalize the conjectures of Strong and Weak Explanatory Optimism, including defining explanatory complexity classes and explanatory universality.
Prove the formalized conjectures to assess the truth value of the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural networks through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability research is a principled approach to understanding models because neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI's inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: On the Internal Semantics of Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How do time-series foundation models internally represent fundamental time-series concepts? Specifically, which layers encode which concepts, are concept parameters linearly recoverable, how do representations evolve in terms of disentanglement and abstraction across depth, and how do models process compositions of concepts?
papers.core_contribution: A systematic probe-based analysis of time-series foundation models reveals that early layers capture local, time-domain patterns while deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals, and that while atomic concepts are linearly recoverable, representing compositions of concepts remains a challenge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a structured account of TSFM semantics, showing a layered hierarchy of concept learning and highlighting composition as a key limitation for representing interacting temporal phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers mainly capture local, time-domain patterns such as AR(1) coefficient, trend slope, and level shifts.
Deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals (e.g., variance shifts), with representations becoming more disentangled and abstract with depth.
Spectral and time-warping concepts are the least linearly recoverable from model embeddings.
TSFMs exhibit strong linear compositional properties for most concept pairs, but probe performance degrades for composite concepts, revealing interference.
Representations become more organized and linearly recoverable with increased context length in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
While atomic concepts are reliably localized, composition remains a challenge, underscoring a key limitation in current TSFMs’ ability to represent interacting temporal phenomena.
Spectral and time-warping factors are the least linearly accessible.
future_direction: Explore additional TSFMs, multivariate and irregular datasets.
Adopt controlled-capacity non-linear or causal probes.
Investigate architectures and objectives that better linearize phase and time-warping, and non-linear conditional steering.
papers.abstract: Time-series Foundation Models (TSFMs) have recently emerged as a universal paradigm for learning across diverse temporal domains. However, despite their empirical success, the internal mechanisms by which these models represent fundamental time-series concepts remain poorly understood. In this work, we undertake a systematic investigation of concept interpretability in TSFMs. Specifically, we examine: (i) which layers encode which concepts, (ii) whether concept parameters are linearly recoverable, (iii) how representations evolve in terms of concept disentanglement and abstraction across model depth, and (iv) how models process compositions of concepts. We systematically probe these questions using layer-wise analyses, linear recoverability tests, and representation similarity measures, providing a structured account of TSFM semantics. The resulting insights show that early layers mainly capture local, time-domain patterns (e.g., AR(1), level shifts, trends), while deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals, with spectral and warping factors remaining the hardest to recover linearly. In compositional settings, however, probe performance degrades, revealing interference between concepts. This highlights that while atomic concepts are reliably localized, composition remains a challenge, underscoring a key limitation in current TSFMs' ability to represent interacting temporal phenomena.

papers.title: Cellular automata as convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules, specifically in the context of cellular automata?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that convolutional neural networks can represent and learn arbitrary cellular automata rules, and that the internal representations of trained networks reflect the complexity (entropy) of the CA rules.
papers.conclusion: Convolutional neural networks can learn cellular automata rules, and the complexity of the rules affects the depth and specialization of the learned representations, suggesting that the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Any cellular automaton can be represented by a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture.
A general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture can learn arbitrary CA rules when given videos of the CA as training data.
In the limit of large network widths, training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates.
Cellular automata with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations.
The entropy of the CA rule table influences the specificity of the internal representations in the trained network.
future_direction: Determine whether neural networks can more broadly inform efforts to understand the dynamical space of CA, including relating a CA's a priori rules to its apparent dynamical complexity during simulation.
Relate observations to more general patterns in deep networks, such as the information bottleneck.
papers.abstract: Deep-learning techniques have recently demonstrated broad success in predicting complex dynamical systems ranging from turbulence to human speech, motivating broader questions about how neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules. We explore this problem in the context of cellular automata (CA), simple dynamical systems that are intrinsically discrete and thus difficult to analyze using standard tools from dynamical systems theory. We show that any CA may readily be represented using a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture. This motivates the development of a general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture, which we find can learn the dynamical rules for arbitrary CA when given videos of the CA as training data. In the limit of large network widths, we find that training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates, and that common patterns emerge in the structure of networks trained on different CA rulesets. We train ensembles of networks on randomly sampled CA, and we probe how the trained networks internally represent the CA rules using an information-theoretic technique based on distributions of layer activation patterns. We find that CA with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations-illustrating how the underlying complexity of the CA's rules influences the specificity of these internal representations. Our results suggest how the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: Decoder Decomposition for the Analysis of the Latent Space of Nonlinear Autoencoders With Wind-Tunnel Experimental Data
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the latent space of nonlinear autoencoders, specifically in the context of fluid dynamics data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the decoder decomposition, a post-processing method to connect latent variables to coherent structures (POD modes) in autoencoders, enabling ranking and selection of latent variables for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The decoder decomposition is a simple and robust method for ranking and selecting latent variables based on flow physics, which aids in the design and interpretation of nonlinear autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
The dimension of the latent space significantly impacts the interpretability of autoencoders.
The decoder decomposition can identify physical and spurious latent variables.
Reconstruction error is a function of both latent space dimension and decoder size.
The method can rank and select latent variables based on the coherent structures they represent.
The method is successfully applied to both synthetic and experimental fluid dynamics data.
papers.abstract: Turbulent flows are chaotic and multi-scale dynamical systems, which have large numbers of degrees of freedom. Turbulent flows, however, can be modelled with a smaller number of degrees of freedom when using the appropriate coordinate system, which is the goal of dimensionality reduction via nonlinear autoencoders. Autoencoders are expressive tools, but they are difficult to interpret. The goal of this paper is to propose a method to aid the interpretability of autoencoders. This is the decoder decomposition. First, we propose the decoder decomposition, which is a post-processing method to connect the latent variables to the coherent structures of flows. Second, we apply the decoder decomposition to analyse the latent space of synthetic data of a two-dimensional unsteady wake past a cylinder. We find that the dimension of latent space has a significant impact on the interpretability of autoencoders. We identify the physical and spurious latent variables. Third, we apply the decoder decomposition to the latent space of wind-tunnel experimental data of a three-dimensional turbulent wake past a bluff body. We show that the reconstruction error is a function of both the latent space dimension and the decoder size, which are correlated. Finally, we apply the decoder decomposition to rank and select latent variables based on the coherent structures that they represent. This is useful to filter unwanted or spurious latent variables, or to pinpoint specific coherent structures of interest. The ability to rank and select latent variables will help users design and interpret nonlinear autoencoders.

papers.title: FIGNN: Feature-Specific Interpretability for Graph Neural Network Surrogate Models
papers.research_question: How can we design a Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture that provides feature-specific interpretability for multivariate prediction tasks on unstructured grids in scientific applications?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a feature-specific interpretable Graph Neural Network (FIGNN) architecture with independent Top-K pooling masks per output variable and an error-budget regularization term to align interpretability with predictive error, enabling localized, feature-wise attribution in scientific surrogate modeling.
papers.conclusion: FIGNN provides a balance between interpretability and predictive performance, offering domain experts detailed insights into feature-specific contributions to prediction accuracy in scientific surrogate modeling.
papers.key_findings:
FIGNN provides feature-specific interpretability masks that highlight physically meaningful spatial regions for each predicted variable, such as frontal boundaries in climate data and recirculation zones in fluid flow.
The error budget regularization effectively localizes prediction errors within the masked regions, with stronger regularization increasing error concentration at the cost of slightly reduced predictive accuracy.
FIGNN maintains competitive predictive performance compared to baseline GNN models on both atmospheric (SPEEDY) and fluid dynamics (BFS) datasets.
The method generalizes across distinct physical domains (climate and fluid dynamics) with different mesh types and governing equations.
There is a trade-off between interpretability (mask coherence and error localization) and predictive accuracy, controllable via the regularization parameter λ.
papers.limitation:
Error accumulation in multi-step rollouts leads to deteriorating prediction quality over long time horizons.
There is a trade-off between interpretability (mask coherence) and predictive accuracy, where higher regularization improves error localization but increases final loss.
future_direction: Extending the framework to spatially three-dimensional settings.
Real-time adaptive interpretability.
Uncertainty quantification strategies.
Using FIGNN for inverse problems like super-resolution, control, and optimization.
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel graph neural network (GNN) architecture, the Feature-specific Interpretable Graph Neural Network (FIGNN), designed to enhance the interpretability of deep learning surrogate models defined on unstructured grids in scientific applications. Traditional GNNs often obscure the distinct spatial influences of different features in multivariate prediction tasks. FIGNN addresses this limitation by introducing a feature-specific pooling strategy, which enables independent attribution of spatial importance for each predicted variable. Additionally, a mask-based regularization term is incorporated into the training objective to explicitly encourage alignment between interpretability and predictive error, promoting localized attribution of model performance. The method is evaluated for surrogate modeling of two physically distinct systems: the SPEEDY atmospheric circulation model and the backward-facing step (BFS) fluid dynamics benchmark. Results demonstrate that FIGNN achieves competitive predictive performance while revealing physically meaningful spatial patterns unique to each feature. Analysis of rollout stability, feature-wise error budgets, and spatial mask overlays confirm the utility of FIGNN as a general-purpose framework for interpretable surrogate modeling in complex physical domains.

papers.title: Unboxing the Black Box: Mechanistic Interpretability for Algorithmic Understanding of Neural Networks
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a unified taxonomy of mechanistic interpretability approaches, situates MI within the broader XAI landscape, and surveys key techniques and literature in the field.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems and invites new researchers into the field.
papers.key_findings:
The field of mechanistic interpretability has grown rapidly since 2020.
MI faces challenges such as superposition, spurious correlations, scalability, and evaluation problems.
MI offers opportunities for debugging, data privacy, robustness, control, human-in-the-loop, and trustworthiness.
future_direction: The need for standardized evaluation techniques.
Scaling up MI techniques to larger models.
Applying MI in real-world domains like finance and medicine.
papers.abstract: The black box nature of deep neural networks poses a significant challenge for the deployment of transparent and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) systems. With the growing presence of AI in society, it becomes increasingly important to develop methods that can explain and interpret the decisions made by these systems. To address this, mechanistic interpretability (MI) emerged as a promising and distinctive research program within the broader field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). MI is the process of studying the inner computations of neural networks and translating them into human-understandable algorithms. It encompasses reverse engineering techniques aimed at uncovering the computational algorithms implemented by neural networks. In this article, we propose a unified taxonomy of MI approaches and provide a detailed analysis of key techniques, illustrated with concrete examples and pseudo-code. We contextualize MI within the broader interpretability landscape, comparing its goals, methods, and insights to other strands of XAI. Additionally, we trace the development of MI as a research area, highlighting its conceptual roots and the accelerating pace of recent work. We argue that MI holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems -- treating models not only as tools for solving tasks, but also as systems to be studied and understood. We hope to invite new researchers into the field of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Randomness and signal propagation in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs): A neural PDE perspective
papers.research_question: What are the implications of the random-like weight matrices in trained Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for signal propagation and stability, and how can they be understood through the lens of neural PDEs and random matrix theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that trained PINN weights reside in a high-entropy regime consistent with random matrix theory, and that signal propagation in such networks can be interpreted through neural PDEs, with stability governed by the numerical properties of the underlying discretization schemes.
papers.conclusion: The neural PDE framework provides a useful perspective for interpreting signal propagation in deep networks, and the stability properties of the underlying numerical schemes are reflected in the structure of the learned weight matrices.
papers.key_findings:
Trained PINN weight matrices exhibit statistical and spectral properties consistent with predictions from random matrix theory, preferring a high-entropy regime.
Random and structured weight matrices can be associated with specific discretizations of neural PDEs.
The numerical stability of these discretizations governs the stability of signal propagation through the network.
Explicit numerical schemes (like the standard sequential PINN architecture) can lead to unstable signal evolution, whereas implicit and higher-order schemes yield stable dynamics for the same underlying neural PDE.
The failure of a PINN to learn the inviscid Burgers' equation is linked to deviations from random matrix statistics and unstable signal propagation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to the one-dimensional Burgers' equation and a specific PINN architecture (8 hidden layers, 100 neurons).
The connection between PINNs and (generalized) path integral solutions of PDEs is speculative and requires future exploration.
future_direction: Explore precise technical details of the connection between PINNs and path integral solutions of PDEs.
Extend the analysis to more complex PDEs and network architectures.
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often exhibit weight matrices that appear statistically random after training, yet their implications for signal propagation and stability remain unsatisfactorily understood, let alone the interpretability. In this work, we analyze the spectral and statistical properties of trained PINN weights using viscous and inviscid variants of the one-dimensional Burgers' equation, and show that the learned weights reside in a high-entropy regime consistent with predictions from random matrix theory. To investigate the dynamical consequences of such weight structures, we study the evolution of signal features inside a network through the lens of neural partial differential equations (neural PDEs). We show that random and structured weight matrices can be associated with specific discretizations of neural PDEs, and that the numerical stability of these discretizations governs the stability of signal propagation through the network. In particular, explicit unstable schemes lead to degraded signal evolution, whereas stable implicit and higher-order schemes yield well-behaved dynamics for the same underlying neural PDE. Our results offer an explicit example of how numerical stability and network architecture shape signal propagation in deep networks, in relation to random matrix and neural PDE descriptions in PINNs.

papers.title: Loss Jump During Loss Switch in Solving PDEs with Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do different loss functions impact the training of neural networks for solving partial differential equations (PDEs)?
papers.core_contribution: Discovers and analyzes a loss-jump phenomenon during loss switching in PDE-solving neural networks, attributing it to different frequency preferences under different loss functions.
papers.conclusion: The loss-jump phenomenon provides a valuable perspective for examining the underlying mechanisms of neural networks in solving PDEs.
papers.key_findings:
When switching the loss function from data loss to model loss, the neural network solution significantly deviates from the exact solution immediately, a phenomenon termed loss jump.
The loss-jump phenomenon arises from the different frequency preferences of neural networks under different loss functions.
Theoretical analysis explains the frequency preference of neural networks under model loss.
papers.abstract: Using neural networks to solve partial differential equations (PDEs) is gaining popularity as an alternative approach in the scientific computing community. Neural networks can integrate different types of information into the loss function. These include observation data, governing equations, and variational forms, etc. These loss functions can be broadly categorized into two types: observation data loss directly constrains and measures the model output, while other loss functions indirectly model the performance of the network, which can be classified as model loss. However, this alternative approach lacks a thorough understanding of its underlying mechanisms, including theoretical foundations and rigorous characterization of various phenomena. This work focuses on investigating how different loss functions impact the training of neural networks for solving PDEs. We discover a stable loss-jump phenomenon: when switching the loss function from the data loss to the model loss, which includes different orders of derivative information, the neural network solution significantly deviates from the exact solution immediately. Further experiments reveal that this phenomenon arises from the different frequency preferences of neural networks under different loss functions. We theoretically analyze the frequency preference of neural networks under model loss. This loss-jump phenomenon provides a valuable perspective for examining the underlying mechanisms of neural networks in solving PDEs.

papers.title: Neural Networks Discover Physical Principles from Observation with an Intuitive World Model
papers.research_question: Can neural networks discover and explain physical principles (such as Newton's laws and Coulomb's law) from raw visual observations, similar to how humans learn intuitive physics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Intuitive World Model (IWM), a neural network that learns physical principles (e.g., Newton's laws, Coulomb's law) from raw video data without built-in physics engines, and can provide explicit explanations and perform counterfactual reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the Intuitive World Model (IWM) can learn physical principles from visual observation, providing explicit explanations and counterfactual reasoning, mirroring a core aspect of human intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
IWM achieves state-of-the-art performance on causal reasoning tasks (factual, predictive, counterfactual) on the ComPhy dataset.
IWM learns interpretable physical principles, as shown by its ability to generate force diagrams and explain physical events.
The hierarchical learning paradigm enables IWM to progressively learn appearance, velocity, mass, and charge representations.
IWM can perform counterfactual imagination by manipulating inferred physical properties (mass, charge) and generating plausible alternative scenarios.
The learned causal modules capture relationships analogous to Newton's laws and Coulomb's law, as demonstrated by sensitivity analysis.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Humans readily grasp physical principles via visual observation, underpinning our ability to model the world and reason about events. In contrast, AI systems often fail to extract consistent physical rules from video, relying on black-box mechanisms that produce implausible outcomes. We introduce the Intuitive World Model (IWM), designed to learn physical principles directly from vision, mimicking human intuition. Drawing inspiration from developmental psychology, IWM utilizes a modular architecture to decompose interactions into force-based dynamics. Through observing objects collide and interact via charges, it identifies intrinsic properties like mass and charge and learns representations analogous to Newton's and Coulomb's laws. This paradigm uniquely allows neural networks to provide explicit explanations for physical phenomena and conduct counterfactual reasoning consistent with learned physical laws. Our work demonstrates that a developmentally-inspired approach empowers AI to acquire explicit, interpretable physical knowledge from observation, mirroring a core aspect of human intelligence.

papers.title: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for Echo State Networks applied to Earth System Variability
papers.research_question: How can Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) be applied to Echo State Networks (ESNs) to make them interpretable, and how does this apply to the detection of El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) from sea surface temperature anomalies?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) can be applied to Echo State Networks (ESNs) to interpret their decisions, and shows that the leak rate in the reservoir is a crucial parameter controlling memory and performance.
papers.conclusion: LRP can be applied to ESNs to open the black-box, and ESNs are effective for image classification tasks like ENSO detection, with advantages in training speed and parameter efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
LRP can be successfully applied to ESNs, providing relevance maps that highlight important input regions for classification.
The leak rate in the reservoir determines the memory time scale; too high leak rate causes the model to forget early inputs and performance drops.
ESNs achieve competitive accuracy with fewer trainable parameters compared to MLP, reducing overfitting risks.
The model focuses on the Niño 3.4 region for ENSO detection, which is physically reasonable.
The model is robust to random permutation of input columns, indicating it does not rely on the zonal structure of the data.
future_direction: Apply further xAI techniques (backward optimization, sensitivity analysis, salience maps) to ESN models.
Use ESN models for time series prediction with LRP as an alternative to attention mechanisms.
Apply ESNs with LRP to unsolved problems in climate and ocean science.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are known to be powerful methods for many hard problems (e.g. image classification, speech recognition or time series prediction). However, these models tend to produce black-box results and are often difficult to interpret. Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) is a widely used technique to understand how ANN models come to their conclusion and to understand what a model has learned. Here, we focus on Echo State Networks (ESNs) as a certain type of recurrent neural networks, also known as reservoir computing. ESNs are easy to train and only require a small number of trainable parameters, but are still black-box models. We show how LRP can be applied to ESNs in order to open the black-box. We also show how ESNs can be used not only for time series prediction but also for image classification: Our ESN model serves as a detector for El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) from sea surface temperature anomalies. ENSO is actually a well-known problem and has been extensively discussed before. But here we use this simple problem to demonstrate how LRP can significantly enhance the explainablility of ESNs.

papers.title: Loss Landscape Geometry and the Learning of Symmetries: Or, What Influence Functions Reveal About Robust Generalization
papers.research_question: Do neural emulators of PDE solution operators internalize physical symmetries, and how can we diagnose this through learning dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an influence-based diagnostic that measures gradient coherence across symmetry orbits to determine whether neural PDE emulators have internalized physical symmetries, linking it to generalization.
papers.conclusion: The proposed influence-based diagnostic reveals that gradient coherence across symmetry orbits is essential for robust generalization, providing a tool to assess whether models truly learn physics or just fit data.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient coherence across symmetry orbits is necessary for models to generalize over symmetry transformations.
Models can achieve low test error without learning symmetries, indicated by weak gradient coherence.
UNets and ViTs exhibit different patterns of gradient coherence: UNets show more uniform coupling, while ViTs concentrate influence on a subset of symmetry transformations.
Symmetry breaking in forward passes corresponds to suppressed cross-influence in the loss landscape.
The diagnostic can be used to evaluate symmetry learning and guide data augmentation.
papers.limitation:
Certain physically relevant symmetries (Galilean boosts, scaling) are not studied.
Empirical analysis is limited to UNet and ViT architectures.
Diagnostics characterize symmetry learning relative to the training distribution; when symmetry transformations are poorly represented in data, influence-based measures reflect this bias.
future_direction: Extending the influence-based analysis to probe the response under small Galilean boosts.
Development of approximate or relaxed symmetry mechanisms that retain structure to guide generalization while preserving optimization flexibility.
papers.abstract: We study how neural emulators of partial differential equation solution operators internalize physical symmetries by introducing an influence-based diagnostic that measures the propagation of parameter updates between symmetry-related states, defined as the metric-weighted overlap of loss gradients evaluated along group orbits. This quantity probes the local geometry of the learned loss landscape and goes beyond forward-pass equivariance tests by directly assessing whether learning dynamics couple physically equivalent configurations. Applying our diagnostic to autoregressive fluid flow emulators, we show that orbit-wise gradient coherence provides the mechanism for learning to generalize over symmetry transformations and indicates when training selects a symmetry compatible basin. The result is a novel technique for evaluating if surrogate models have internalized symmetry properties of the known solution operator.

papers.title: Using data assimilation tools to dissect GraphDOP
papers.research_question: How can Data Assimilation (DA) diagnostic tools, such as Forecast Sensitivity-based Observation Impact (FSOI), be applied to Machine Learning models to enhance their interpretability and explainability?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that Data Assimilation diagnostic tools (FSOI and sensitivity analysis) can be successfully transferred to ML models like GraphDOP, enhancing interpretability and explainability by showing the model captures physically meaningful processes.
papers.conclusion: Data Assimilation diagnostic tools, particularly FSOI, are effective for interpreting and explaining the GraphDOP model, confirming it captures real physical processes and constructs a coherent internal representation from heterogeneous observational data.
papers.key_findings:
GraphDOP's sliding attention window learns meteorological features and spatial relationships from observation data.
GraphDOP uses information from satellite radiances (e.g., ATMS channels) to predict surface variables like 2-meter temperature.
GraphDOP tracks the movement of storm systems (e.g., extratropical storms) by shifting its attention with forecast lead time, similar to physical dynamics.
FSOI analysis reveals GraphDOP builds a coherent internal representation of the Earth system by blending information from conventional and satellite observations.
Some satellite channels (e.g., ATMS channel 22) have a larger impact on reducing forecast error, while others (e.g., channels 4 and 17) can increase error.
papers.limitation: The results are based on a version of GraphDOP trained on a limited selection of observation types to reduce computational cost, not the full state-of-the-art model.
future_direction: Replicate the study with the current state-of-the-art GraphDOP model to evaluate the importance of different observation types.
Use the presented tools to benchmark the quality of different AI-DOP models, ensuring they provide correct forecasts for the right reasons.
Implement an online observation Quality Control (QC) mechanism based on the impact measured by the FSOI diagnostic.
papers.abstract: The Data Assimilation (DA) community has been developing various diagnostics to understand the importance of the observing system in accurately forecasting the weather. They usually rely on the ability to compute the derivatives of the physical model output with respect to its initial condition. For example, the Forecast Sensitivity-based Observation Impact (FSOI) estimates the impact on the forecast error of each observation processed in the DA system. This paper presents how these DA diagnostic tools are transferred to Machine Learning (ML) models, as their derivatives are readily available through automatic differentiation. We specifically explore the interpretability and explainability of the observation-driven GraphDOP model developed at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). The interpretability study demonstrates the effectiveness of GraphDOP's sliding attention window to learn the meteorological features present in the observation datasets and to learn the spatial relationships between different regions. Making these relationships more transparent confirms that GraphDOP captures real, physically meaningful processes, such as the movement of storm systems. The explainability of GraphDOP is explored by applying the FSOI tool to study the impact of the different observations on the forecast error. This inspection reveals that GraphDOP creates an internal representation of the Earth system by combining the information from conventional and satellite observations.

papers.title: Mapping Knowledge Representations to Concepts: A Review and New Perspectives
papers.research_question: How do current methods extract internal knowledge representations in a neural network and map them to human-understandable concepts? Can Deductive-Nomological (D-N) explanation taxonomy and causal types of explanations be useful in order to analyse what can be expected, and not expected, from knowledge representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a targeted review of research that aims to associate internal neural network representations with human understandable concepts, and proposes using Deductive-Nomological explanations and theories of causality as a taxonomy to understand the capabilities and limitations of such explanations.
papers.conclusion: The review raises important questions about the goal of explanations and the type of knowledge extractable from neural networks, emphasizing the need to differentiate between understanding the trained model and providing actionable decisions. It argues for involving users to emphasize contextual dependence and refocus research on the limitations of ML systems.
papers.key_findings:
Methods for extracting knowledge representations are dominated by two approaches: Feature Based Attribution (FBA) for local understanding and Internal Knowledge Representation (IKR) extraction for global understanding.
There is an ambiguity in the goal of model explainability: understanding the ML model versus providing actionable explanations in the deployment domain.
The reviewed research lacks user studies, despite heavy reliance on human abilities to compare images and infer concepts.
Explanations that aim for intervention or counterfactual reasoning rely on causal relations, but these are only valid for the ML model in isolation and not necessarily for the real-world domain.
The Deductive-Nomological explanation taxonomy is found useful for analyzing what can be expected from neural network explanations, highlighting that current methods typically aim for kind-data or model-data relations, not theory-data or entity-data relations.
papers.limitation:
The choice to use the D-N model and Overton's schematic overview delimits the type of explanations aimed for and excludes pragmatic, inductive statistical, teleological, and historical explanations.
The understanding of the concept 'concept' is not well-grounded from an ontological and epistemological perspective.
future_direction: Conducting user studies that actively involve users to emphasize contextual dependence.
Combining IKR and FBA methods in studies aiming for a global meta-perspective of model understanding.

Using scientific explanations and theories to formulate falsifiable hypotheses and evaluate how well a trained ML model models the usage domain, moving beyond the idea that more data solves the problem of induction.
papers.abstract: The success of neural networks builds to a large extent on their ability to create internal knowledge representations from real-world high-dimensional data, such as images, sound, or text. Approaches to extract and present these representations, in order to explain the neural network's decisions, is an active and multifaceted research field. To gain a deeper understanding of a central aspect of this field, we have performed a targeted review focusing on research that aims to associate internal representations with human understandable concepts. In doing this, we added a perspective on the existing research by using primarily deductive nomological explanations as a proposed taxonomy. We find this taxonomy and theories of causality, useful for understanding what can be expected, and not expected, from neural network explanations. The analysis additionally uncovers an ambiguity in the reviewed literature related to the goal of model explainability; is it understanding the ML model or, is it actionable explanations useful in the deployment domain?

papers.title: Interpreting CFD Surrogates through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to interpret the latent representations of graph-based CFD surrogate models to enhance explainability and trustworthiness?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a post-hoc interpretability framework for graph-based CFD surrogate models using sparse autoencoders to extract interpretable latent features that correspond to physical flow structures.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoding is a practical and effective tool for explaining graph surrogates in fluid dynamics, offering a model-agnostic pathway to enhance explainability and trustworthiness in CFD applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAE yields interpretable and physically meaningful representations aligned with phenomena like vorticity or flow structures.
Global and time-local salient coordinates show temporal consistency, with variance and mean-absolute metrics capturing coherent features.
Mesh-space visualization reveals that aggregated latent activity hierarchically expands from cylinder surface to wake, mirroring physical importance.
Individual latent dimensions specialize in distinct flow structures, confirming disentanglement of physical phenomena.
SAE-based saliency consistently outperforms baselines like embedding-norm and PCA in aligning with high-vorticity regions.
papers.abstract: Learning-based surrogate models have become a practical alternative to high-fidelity CFD solvers, but their latent representations remain opaque and hinder adoption in safety-critical or regulation-bound settings. This work introduces a posthoc interpretability framework for graph-based surrogate models used in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) by leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs). By obtaining an overcomplete basis in the node embedding space of a pretrained surrogate, the method extracts a dictionary of interpretable latent features. The approach enables the identification of monosemantic concepts aligned with physical phenomena such as vorticity or flow structures, offering a model-agnostic pathway to enhance explainability and trustworthiness in CFD applications.

papers.title: Symmetry and Generalisation in Neural Approximations of Renormalisation Transformations
papers.research_question: What role do parameter symmetry and network expressivity play in the generalisation behaviour of neural networks when learning a real-space renormalisation group transformation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a competition between symmetry constraints and expressivity in neural networks learning renormalization transformations, with overly complex or overconstrained models generalizing poorly. It extends a cumulant propagation framework from MLPs to GNNs to elucidate internal information processing.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that balancing symmetry and expressivity is crucial for generalization in neural networks learning physical transformations, and the cumulant propagation framework offers insight into their internal information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Symmetrically constrained weights in MLPs combined with nonlinear activations (e.g., quadratic) lead to poor generalization, as shown analytically.
Linear networks with symmetric weights generalize well, but adding nonlinearities (ReLU, quadratic) under symmetry constraints degrades generalization.
The independent node approximation for cumulant propagation in GNNs is limited, especially for higher-order cumulants, due to neglected correlations from message passing.
GNNs perform comparably to MLPs on simple two-node graphs but their inductive biases are not beneficial for tasks lacking structural complexity.
Networks with learnable spline activations and fixed weights generalize poorly, while training both weights and splines yields linear solutions that generalize well.
papers.limitation:
The independent node approximation for GNN cumulant propagation is crude and neglects important interactions induced by message passing and weight sharing.
The study is limited to simple network architectures (shallow MLPs and GNNs) and synthetic tasks.
future_direction: Extending the cumulant propagation framework to more complex architectures and tasks.
Investigating the role of symmetry breaking in hierarchical learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have proven enormously successful at using multiple layers of representation to learn relevant features of structured data. Encoding physical symmetries into these models can improve performance on difficult tasks, and recent work has motivated the principle of parameter symmetry breaking and restoration as a unifying mechanism underlying their hierarchical learning dynamics. We evaluate the role of parameter symmetry and network expressivity in the generalisation behaviour of neural networks when learning a real-space renormalisation group (RG) transformation, using the central limit theorem (CLT) as a test case map. We consider simple multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and graph neural networks (GNNs), and vary weight symmetries and activation functions across architectures. Our results reveal a competition between symmetry constraints and expressivity, with overly complex or overconstrained models generalising poorly.
