We analytically demonstrate this poor generalisation behaviour for certain constrained MLP architectures by recasting the CLT as a cumulant recursion relation and making use of an established framework to propagate cumulants through MLPs. We also empirically validate an extension of this framework from MLPs to GNNs, elucidating the internal information processing performed by these more complex models. These findings offer new insight into the learning dynamics of symmetric networks and their limitations in modelling structured physical transformations.

papers.title: Position: Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in SAEs
papers.research_question: How can feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be achieved and measured to improve the reliability of mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and proposes the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to measure consistency. It shows that high consistency is achievable with appropriate architectural choices (e.g., TopK SAEs) and that high PW-MCC correlates with semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.conclusion: The paper calls for a community-wide shift towards valuing and systematically measuring feature consistency in SAEs for cumulative progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
High feature consistency (PW-MCC ≈ 0.80) is achievable with TopK SAEs on real-world LLM activations.
PW-MCC reliably tracks ground-truth feature recovery (GT-MCC) in synthetic experiments.
Feature consistency is frequency-dependent: more frequent features are learned more consistently.
Different SAE architectures yield different levels of consistency, with TopK SAEs performing best.
High PW-MCC scores correlate strongly with the semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.limitation:
The focus is on SAEs, and other interpretability methods may have different consistency challenges.
The study uses a specific metric (PW-MCC) for a specific notion of consistency (strong feature consistency).
The real-world experiments are limited to two base models and one dataset.
The automated interpretation pipeline has its own limitations.
future_direction: Extending consistency analysis to other interpretability methods beyond SAEs.
Developing more nuanced metrics for consistency that go beyond strong feature consistency.
Investigating the relationship between consistency and downstream task performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a prominent tool in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for decomposing neural network activations into interpretable features. However, the aspiration to identify a canonical set of features is challenged by the observed inconsistency of learned SAE features across different training runs, undermining the reliability and efficiency of MI research. This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in SAEs -- the reliable convergence to equivalent feature sets across independent runs. We propose using the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to operationalize consistency and demonstrate that high levels are achievable (0.80 for TopK SAEs on LLM activations) with appropriate architectural choices. Our contributions include detailing the benefits of prioritizing consistency; providing theoretical grounding and synthetic validation using a model organism, which verifies PW-MCC as a reliable proxy for ground-truth recovery; and extending these findings to real-world LLM data, where high feature consistency strongly correlates with the semantic similarity of learned feature explanations. We call for a community-wide shift towards systematically measuring feature consistency to foster robust cumulative progress in MI.

papers.title: A reproducing kernel framework for interpretable parameter estimation and learning in dynamical systems
papers.research_question: How can explainable machine learning models be used for accurate, interpretable, and computationally efficient parameter estimation in dynamical systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework combining explainable machine learning models with SHAP-based interpretability for parameter estimation in dynamical systems, demonstrating accurate, interpretable, and efficient estimation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed feature-based learning framework for parameter estimation in differential equation systems combines predictive modeling with post-hoc explainability, with kernel-based methods (KRR and GPR) achieving higher predictive accuracy and robustness compared to neural network baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Kernel-based methods (KRR and GPR) consistently outperformed neural network models (MLP and CNN) in parameter estimation accuracy.
Statistical features extracted from trajectories were more informative for parameter estimation than frequency-domain or spectrogram features.
SHAP-based feature attribution revealed consistent feature importance rankings across different model types, indicating robust feature-to-parameter relationships.
The proposed framework achieves accurate parameter estimation while providing transparency into the inference process through explainability techniques.
The integration of simulation-based dataset generation, feature extraction, and interpretable modeling offers a new perspective for combining machine learning with domain-specific modeling.
papers.limitation:
Further theoretical analysis is needed to formalize the connection between system dynamics and feature relevance.
Validation has been limited to synthetic datasets; extending to real-world data is important for broader practical applicability.
Current kernel-based methods do not scale efficiently, and neural architectures require larger datasets to fully leverage their capacity, indicating scalability and data volume limitations.
future_direction: Extend the methodology to stable multi-parameter estimation.
Develop data-driven techniques for identifying informative parameter ranges.
Design adaptive dataset generation strategies to improve training efficiency and interpretability.
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate a suite of explainable machine learning models -- including Kernel Ridge Regression, Gaussian Process Regression, Convolutional Neural Networks, and Multi-Layer Perceptrons -- for parameter inference in systems of differential equations. By combining these models with explainability techniques such as SHapley Additive exPlanations, we extract explicit feature-to-parameter mappings, offering deeper insight into the inference process. Building on these insights, we propose lightweight, hand-engineered estimators that approximate parameter estimation tasks without requiring complex optimization. Additionally, we introduce a systematic methodology for dataset generation, incorporating time-series simulation and diverse feature extraction. Our results demonstrate that explainability-driven modeling can achieve accurate, interpretable, and computationally efficient parameter estimation, offering a new perspective on the integration of machine learning with domain-specific modeling.

papers.title: Scalable Mechanistic Neural Networks for Differential Equations and Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we reformulate the Mechanistic Neural Network to achieve linear time and space complexity with respect to sequence length while maintaining accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces S-MNN, a reformulation of the Mechanistic Neural Network that reduces computational time and space complexities from cubic/quadratic to linear in sequence length while maintaining accuracy.
papers.conclusion: S-MNN addresses the scalability limitations of MNN by reducing complexities to linear in sequence length, retaining precision and enabling efficient modeling of long-term dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
S-MNN matches the precision of the original MNN across various benchmarks.
S-MNN reduces computational time and memory usage significantly, enabling handling of long sequences.
The reformulation eliminates slack variables and uses a banded matrix structure for efficient solving.
S-MNN demonstrates practical applicability on long-term climate data forecasting.
The solver is numerically stable and GPU-friendly, achieving linear scaling in time and memory.
papers.abstract: We propose Scalable Mechanistic Neural Network (S-MNN), an enhanced neural network framework designed for scientific machine learning applications involving long temporal sequences. By reformulating the original Mechanistic Neural Network (MNN) (Pervez et al., 2024), we reduce the computational time and space complexities from cubic and quadratic with respect to the sequence length, respectively, to linear. This significant improvement enables efficient modeling of long-term dynamics without sacrificing accuracy or interpretability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that S-MNN matches the original MNN in precision while substantially reducing computational resources. Consequently, S-MNN can drop-in replace the original MNN in applications, providing a practical and efficient tool for integrating mechanistic bottlenecks into neural network models of complex dynamical systems. Source code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/ScalableMNN.

papers.title: Neural Earthquake Forecasting with Minimal Information: Limits, Interpretability, and the Role of Markov Structure
papers.research_question: Can neural and hybrid models for earthquake forecasting generalize temporally when trained on early data and tested on future unseen events?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a hybrid neural-Markov model for earthquake forecasting and a temporal cross-validation framework, showing that model performance degrades on future data due to non-stationarity, highlighting the importance of temporal evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Neural and hybrid models for earthquake forecasting fail to generalize to future data due to temporal non-stationarity, highlighting the need for temporally realistic evaluation and caution in applying machine learning to sparse forecasting settings.
papers.key_findings:
The hybrid model outperforms the Markov baseline on validation data but fails to generalize to the most recent quintile of the catalog.
The final quintile of seismicity exhibits more Markov-consistent behavior than earlier data, indicating temporal non-stationarity.
Integrated Gradients attribution shows a shift in feature importance between validation and test sets, with magnitude features becoming more relevant in the test set.
Temporal cross-validation reveals that model performance is highly dependent on the temporal location of the test data, with the last quintile consistently underperforming.
The study underscores the risk of overfitting to early patterns and the need for temporally realistic benchmarks in earthquake forecasting.
papers.limitation:
Small sample size affects all statistical models based on this data.
Sparse input features limited to simple descriptors of past events restrict the models' ability to capture complex physical dynamics.
The Markov prior is static and unable to account for possible changes in seismic regimes.
Results are based on a single regional earthquake catalog without additional geophysical or contextual data.
Only feedforward architectures were considered; models with more explicit temporal reasoning were not explored.
future_direction: Refine the use of prior knowledge with dynamic extensions of the Markov model or hierarchical priors that adapt across segments of the catalog.
Incorporate additional physical variables such as fault-specific information, geodetic signals, or stress evolution proxies.
Explore dynamically updated models or time-aware architectures to track evolving patterns more effectively.
papers.abstract: Abstract Forecasting earthquake sequences remains a central challenge in seismology, particularly under non-stationary conditions. While deep learning models have shown promise, their ability to generalize across time remains poorly understood. We evaluate neural and hybrid (NN + Markov) models for short-term earthquake forecasting on a regional catalog using temporally stratified cross-validation. Models are trained on earlier portions of the catalog and evaluated on future unseen events, enabling realistic assessment of temporal generalization. We find that while these models outperform a purely Markovian model on validation data, their test performance degrades substantially in the most recent quintile. A detailed attribution analysis reveals a shift in feature relevance over time, with later data exhibiting simpler, more Markov-consistent behavior. To support interpretability, we apply Integrated Gradients, a type of explainable AI (XAI) to analyze how models rely on different input features. These results highlight the risks of overfitting to early patterns in seismicity and underscore the importance of temporally realistic benchmarks. We conclude that forecasting skill is inherently time-dependent and benefits from combining physical priors with data-driven methods.

papers.title: Noether: The More Things Change, the More Stay the Same
papers.research_question: How do symmetries in neural networks interact with learning algorithms, and what conserved quantities arise from these symmetries during optimization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that symmetries in neural networks lead to conserved quantities during optimization, which constrain the optimization path and help understand dynamics like balance conditions and boundedness.
papers.conclusion: Symmetry is an important tool for understanding the performance of neural networks under gradient descent.
papers.key_findings:
For ReLU networks, gradient descent leads to balance equations between consecutive layers.
For linear networks, symmetries lead to balancedness conditions on weight matrices.
Data augmentation introduces symmetries that constrain the optimization path.
Conserved quantities are derived for various activation functions (ReLU, linear, Swish) and optimization algorithms (gradient flow, Newtonian dynamics, Nesterov).
future_direction: Determine if conservation laws for Swish can explain its empirical advantage over ReLU.
Derive bounds for Nesterov's accelerated gradient flow similar to Newtonian dynamics.
papers.abstract: Symmetries have proven to be important ingredients in the analysis of neural networks. So far their use has mostly been implicit or seemingly coincidental. We undertake a systematic study of the role that symmetry plays. In particular, we clarify how symmetry interacts with the learning algorithm. The key ingredient in our study is played by Noether's celebrated theorem which, informally speaking, states that symmetry leads to conserved quantities (e.g., conservation of energy or conservation of momentum). In the realm of neural networks under gradient descent, model symmetries imply restrictions on the gradient path. E.g., we show that symmetry of activation functions leads to boundedness of weight matrices, for the specific case of linear activations it leads to balance equations of consecutive layers, data augmentation leads to gradient paths that have "momentum"-type restrictions, and time symmetry leads to a version of the Neural Tangent Kernel. Symmetry alone does not specify the optimization path, but the more symmetries are contained in the model the more restrictions are imposed on the path. Since symmetry also implies over-parametrization, this in effect implies that some part of this over-parametrization is cancelled out by the existence of the conserved quantities. Symmetry can therefore be thought of as one further important tool in understanding the performance of neural networks under gradient descent.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Advancing AI-Scientist Understanding: Multi-Agent LLMs with Interpretable Physics Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the reliability, transparency, and interpretability of LLM outputs in physics problem-solving?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a multi-agent LLM framework with an interpretation module that transforms opaque LLM outputs into structured, executable, and physically grounded science models to improve interpretability and verifiability in physics reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The multi-agent LLM framework with an interpretation module marks a significant step toward more reliable, interpretable, and verifiable AI-augmented scientific reasoning by transforming LLM outputs into transparent, executable science models.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully structures complex LLM reasoning into explicit science models, enabling validation through code execution and interactive tools.
Case studies demonstrate the framework's ability to detect flaws in LLM-generated solutions and enhance human-AI collaboration.
The interpretation module, consisting of specialized agents (summarizer, model builder, tester, etc.), bridges the gap between AI-generated reasoning and human scientific intuition.
The approach improves both numerical and theoretical consistency of LLM outputs in physics problem-solving.
The system fosters collaborative reasoning by keeping human experts central to the validation and refinement process.
future_direction: Extend the framework to a broader range of physics domains and other scientific fields.
Refine each agent's capabilities and enhance the interactive elements of the user interface.
Investigate scalability, handling of increasingly complex models, and integration of advanced techniques like real-time interactive debugging and deeper reasoning transparency.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are playing an increasingly important role in physics research by assisting with symbolic manipulation, numerical computation, and scientific reasoning. However, ensuring the reliability, transparency, and interpretability of their outputs remains a major challenge. In this work, we introduce a novel multi-agent LLM physicist framework that fosters collaboration between AI and human scientists through three key modules: a reasoning module, an interpretation module, and an AI-scientist interaction module. Recognizing that effective physics reasoning demands logical rigor, quantitative accuracy, and alignment with established theoretical models, we propose an interpretation module that employs a team of specialized LLM agents-including summarizers, model builders, visualization tools, and testers-to systematically structure LLM outputs into transparent, physically grounded science models. A case study demonstrates that our approach significantly improves interpretability, enables systematic validation, and enhances human-AI collaboration in physics problem-solving and discovery. Our work bridges free-form LLM reasoning with interpretable, executable models for scientific analysis, enabling more transparent and verifiable AI-augmented research.

papers.title: Investigation of Internal Functioning of the Radial-Basis-Function Neural Network River Flow Forecasting Models
papers.research_question: Can hydrological knowledge be extracted from Radial Basis Function Neural Networks (RBFNNs) by interpreting their internal functioning, specifically by examining the responses of hidden layer neurons to understand how they represent flow components in river flow forecasting?
papers.core_contribution: The hidden neurons in an RBFNN for river flow forecasting are not arbitrary but represent specific flow components (baseflow, interflow, surface runoff), demonstrating that hydrological knowledge can be extracted from the model's internal functioning.
papers.conclusion: The RBFNN can be used as an effective flow forecasting tool, and its hidden neurons activate in a way that corresponds to hydrological flow components, suggesting that the network's internal functioning is interpretable and can extract meaningful hydrological knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The RBFNN is an effective tool for daily flow forecasting.
The activation of hidden nodes is not arbitrary; each node dominates in one of the flow domains (low, medium, high) and represents flow components resembling baseflow, interflow, and surface runoff.
The proportional contribution from each hidden neuron varies over time, reflecting dominance in specific flow ranges.
The RBFNN parameters (centers, spreads, weights) function to decompose the flow hydrograph into meaningful components.
The method provides insight into the internal functioning of RBFNNs, showing they can mimic local models corresponding to hydrological processes.
papers.limitation: The study uses a limited number of catchments, so the findings may not generalize to all catchments.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to a large number of catchments with different characteristics.
Investigate the sensitivity of the number of RBFs and network structure to represent physical processes.
papers.abstract: This paper deals with the challenging problem of hydrological interpretation of the internal functioning of artificial neural networks (ANNs) by extracting knowledge from their solutions. The neural network used in this study is based on the structure of the radial-basis-function neural network (RBFNN), which is considered as an alternative to the multilayer perceptron for solving complex modeling problems. This network consists of input, hidden, and output layers. The network is trained using the daily data of two catchments having different characteristics and from two different regions in the world. The present day and antecedent observed discharges are used as inputs to the network to forecast the flow one day ahead. A range of quantitative and qualitative techniques are used for hydrological interpretation of the internal functioning by examining the responses of the hidden layer nodes. The results of the study show that a single hidden layered RBFNN is an effective tool to forecast the daily flows and that the activation of the hidden layer nodes are far from arbitrary, but appear to represent flow components of the predicted hydrograph. The results of the study confirm that the three nodes in the hidden layer of this model effectively divide the input data space in such a way that the contribution from each node dominates in one of the flow domains—low, medium, or high—and form, in a crude manner, the base flow, interflow and surface runoff components of the hydrograph.

papers.title: Additive-feature-attribution methods: a review on explainable artificial intelligence for fluid dynamics and heat transfer
papers.core_contribution: This review paper summarizes the application of additive-feature-attribution methods (SHAP) in fluid dynamics and heat transfer, highlighting their importance for interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models.
papers.conclusion: This review shows that explainability techniques, and in particular additive-feature-attribution methods, are crucial for implementing interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models in the fluid-mechanics field.
papers.key_findings:
Additive-feature-attribution methods are crucial for implementing interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models in fluid mechanics.
SHAP values provide a unique solution for understanding the model by linking input features with the model prediction.
The review categorizes applications into turbulence modeling, fluid-mechanics fundamentals, and applied problems in fluid dynamics and heat transfer.
papers.abstract: The use of data-driven methods in fluid mechanics has surged dramatically in recent years due to their capacity to adapt to the complex and multi-scale nature of turbulent flows, as well as to detect patterns in large-scale simulations or experimental tests. In order to interpret the relationships generated in the models during the training process, numerical attributions need to be assigned to the input features. One important example are the additive-feature-attribution methods. These explainability methods link the input features with the model prediction, providing an interpretation based on a linear formulation of the models. The SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP values) are formulated as the only possible interpretation that offers a unique solution for understanding the model. In this manuscript, the additive-feature-attribution methods are presented, showing four common implementations in the literature: kernel SHAP, tree SHAP, gradient SHAP, and deep SHAP. Then, the main applications of the additive-feature-attribution methods are introduced, dividing them into three main groups: turbulence modeling, fluid-mechanics fundamentals, and applied problems in fluid dynamics and heat transfer. This review shows thatexplainability techniques, and in particular additive-feature-attribution methods, are crucial for implementing interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models in the fluid-mechanics field.

papers.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we automate the discovery of circuits in neural networks for mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability workflow and introduces the ACDC algorithm to automate circuit discovery by using activation patching to find important connections in the computational graph.
papers.conclusion: ACDC is a step towards automating circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability, showing promise on several tasks but with limitations that need to be addressed in future work.
papers.key_findings:
ACDC successfully rediscovers known circuits, such as the Greater-Than circuit in GPT-2 Small and the IOI circuit.
ACDC selects a sparse set of edges (e.g., 68 out of 32,000 in GPT-2 Small for IOI) that match manually found circuits.
ACDC performs competitively with gradient-based methods like Subnetwork Probing and Head Importance Score for Pruning.
ACDC is not robust in all settings, e.g., it fails on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC can miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
papers.limitation:
ACDC can fail in some settings, such as on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC may miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
The ground-truth circuits from previous work are not 100% reliable, limiting the evaluation.
future_direction: Automating the functional interpretation of model components.
Improving circuit discovery methods to handle more complex behaviors and models.
papers.abstract: Through considerable effort and intuition, several recent works have reverse-engineered nontrivial behaviors of transformer models. This paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability process they followed. First, researchers choose a metric and dataset that elicit the desired model behavior. Then, they apply activation patching to find which abstract neural network units are involved in the behavior. By varying the dataset, metric, and units under investigation, researchers can understand the functionality of each component. We automate one of the process' steps: to identify the circuit that implements the specified behavior in the model's computational graph. We propose several algorithms and reproduce previous interpretability results to validate them. For example, the ACDC algorithm rediscovered 5/5 of the component types in a circuit in GPT-2 Small that computes the Greater-Than operation. ACDC selected 68 of the 32,000 edges in GPT-2 Small, all of which were manually found by previous work. Our code is available at https://github.com/ArthurConmy/Automatic-Circuit-Discovery.

papers.title: Noether's Learning Dynamics: Role of Symmetry Breaking in Neural\n Networks
papers.research_question: What is the role of symmetry breaking in the learning dynamics of neural networks? Specifically, how does kinetic symmetry breaking affect efficiency and stability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a theoretical framework based on Lagrangian mechanics to study learning dynamics, revealing that kinetic symmetry breaking induces an implicit adaptive optimization mechanism akin to RMSProp in networks with normalization layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, through the lens of Lagrangian mechanics, we have established a theoretical foundation to discover geometric design principles for the learning dynamics of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Kinetic symmetry breaking (KSB) is a key mechanism in learning dynamics where the kinetic energy (learning rule) breaks the symmetry of the potential (loss function).
Noether’s Learning Dynamics (NLD) generalizes Noether’s theorem to account for KSB and describes the motion of the Noether charge.
In networks with normalization layers, KSB induces an implicit adaptive optimization mechanism that scales gradients similarly to RMSProp.
The implicit adaptive optimization requires finite learning rates and is amplified by momentum and weight decay.
Empirical validation shows that unconstrained filter norm (allowing implicit adaptation) leads to better performance with large learning rates and momentum.
future_direction: Directly simulate gradient flow with implicit acceleration to keep the benefits of finite learning rates.
Explore the role of symmetry breaking in other components of deep learning, such as attention mechanisms or recurrent networks.
papers.abstract:
In nature, symmetry governs regularities, while symmetry breaking brings
texture. In artificial neural networks, symmetry has been a central design
principle to efficiently capture regularities in the world, but the role of
symmetry breaking is not well understood. Here, we develop a theoretical
framework to study the "geometry of learning dynamics" in neural networks, and
reveal a key mechanism of explicit symmetry breaking behind the efficiency and
stability of modern neural networks. To build this understanding, we model the
discrete learning dynamics of gradient descent using a continuous-time
Lagrangian formulation, in which the learning rule corresponds to the kinetic
energy and the loss function corresponds to the potential energy. Then, we
identify "kinetic symmetry breaking" (KSB), the condition when the kinetic
energy explicitly breaks the symmetry of the potential function. We generalize
Noether's theorem known in physics to take into account KSB and derive the
resulting motion of the Noether charge: "Noether's Learning Dynamics" (NLD).
Finally, we apply NLD to neural networks with normalization layers and reveal
how KSB introduces a mechanism of "implicit adaptive optimization",
establishing an analogy between learning dynamics induced by normalization
layers and RMSProp. Overall, through the lens of Lagrangian mechanics, we have
established a theoretical foundation to discover geometric design principles
for the learning dynamics of neural networks.

papers.title: Interpretability for Time Series Transformers using A Concept Bottleneck Framework
papers.research_question: How can we make time series transformers interpretable by steering them to learn predefined, interpretable concepts while maintaining forecasting performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models and Centered Kernel Alignment to steer time series transformers to learn predefined interpretable concepts (e.g., a linear surrogate model and time features) in a designated bottleneck layer, improving interpretability without significantly harming forecasting performance.
papers.conclusion: The concept bottleneck framework successfully improves the interpretability of time series transformers by encouraging specific components to align with human-understandable concepts, with minimal impact on forecasting accuracy, and enables faithful local interventions.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework maintains model performance (MSE, MAE) on benchmark datasets while making the bottleneck layer's representations highly similar to the predefined concepts, as measured by CKA.
Component visualizations and activation patching interventions confirm that the bottleneck components learn and causally influence the model's predictions based on the intended concepts.
The framework is successfully applied to three different transformer architectures (Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer, FEDformer) on synthetic and real-world time series data.
Including a 'free' component in the bottleneck (not constrained by concepts) can help maintain performance and capture additional, non-predefined patterns in the data.
The intervention experiment demonstrates that the model's performance on time-shifted data can be restored by patching the activations of the time-concept component, confirming the causal role of the bottleneck.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes that relevant, interpretable concepts are known a priori and provided to the model.
The framework introduces additional computational cost during training due to the CKA loss calculation.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other types of sequential data beyond time series.
Exploring more complex or domain-specific interpretable concepts.
Investigating the use of the framework for model debugging and out-of-distribution robustness.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability focuses on reverse engineering the internal mechanisms learned by neural networks. We extend our focus and propose to mechanistically forward engineer using our framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models. In the context of long-term time series forecasting, we modify the training objective to encourage a model to develop representations which are similar to predefined, interpretable concepts using Centered Kernel Alignment. This steers the bottleneck components to learn the predefined concepts, while allowing other components to learn other, undefined concepts. We apply the framework to the Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer and FEDformer, and present an in-depth analysis on synthetic data and on a variety of benchmark datasets. We find that the model performance remains mostly unaffected, while the model shows much improved interpretability. Additionally, we verify the interpretation of the bottleneck components with an intervention experiment using activation patching.

papers.title: Unification of Symmetries Inside Neural Networks: Transformer, Feedforward and Neural ODE
papers.research_question: How can gauge symmetries from physics be applied to understand parametric redundancies in neural networks, and can the inner workings of neural networks be interpreted through spacetime diffeomorphisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper unifies symmetries in neural networks by interpreting parametric redundancies as gauge symmetries, showing that gauge symmetries in neural ODEs are spacetime diffeomorphisms, and that rescaling symmetries in feedforward networks and transformers correspond to these diffeomorphisms.
papers.conclusion: Gauge symmetries provide a unifying perspective for analyzing various machine learning architectures, bridging machine learning and physics.
papers.key_findings:
Parametric redundancies in neural networks can be interpreted as gauge symmetries in physics.
Gauge symmetries in neural ODEs are mathematically characterized by spacetime diffeomorphisms.
The rescaling symmetry of feedforward neural networks is lifted to spacetime diffeomorphisms in neural ODEs.
Transformers can be viewed as integrated nonlinear neural ODEs, and their gauge symmetries correspond to diffeomorphisms.
Regularizations in neural networks can be understood as gauge fixing conditions.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of neural networks, including transformers, remains one of the most challenging puzzles in machine learning. This study introduces a novel approach by applying the principles of gauge symmetries, a key concept in physics, to neural network architectures. By regarding model functions as physical observables, we find that parametric redundancies of various machine learning models can be interpreted as gauge symmetries. We mathematically formulate the parametric redundancies in neural ODEs, and find that their gauge symmetries are given by spacetime diffeomorphisms, which play a fundamental role in Einstein's theory of gravity. Viewing neural ODEs as a continuum version of feedforward neural networks, we show that the parametric redundancies in feedforward neural networks are indeed lifted to diffeomorphisms in neural ODEs. We further extend our analysis to transformer models, finding natural correspondences with neural ODEs and their gauge symmetries. The concept of gauge symmetries sheds light on the complex behavior of deep learning models through physics and provides us with a unifying perspective for analyzing various machine learning architectures.

papers.title: Using Degeneracy in the Loss Landscape for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does degeneracy in neural network parameterizations obfuscate internal structure for mechanistic interpretability, and how can we remove these degeneracies to obtain more interpretable representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the concept of degeneracy in neural network parameterizations as an obstacle to interpretability, characterizes three sources of degeneracy, and proposes the Interaction Basis, a technique to obtain a representation invariant to these degeneracies, which may lead to sparser and more interpretable representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that degeneracy in neural network parameterizations hinders interpretability, identifies sources of degeneracy, and proposes the Interaction Basis to remove degeneracies, potentially yielding sparser and more interpretable representations.
papers.key_findings:
Neural network parameters can be degenerate due to linear dependence between activations in a layer, linear dependence between gradients passed back to a layer, and ReLUs which fire on the same subset of datapoints.
Modular networks are likely to be more degenerate, and a metric for identifying modules is developed based on this argument.
The Interaction Basis is a tractable technique to obtain a representation invariant to degeneracies from linear dependence of activations or Jacobians.
Representations invariant to degeneracies are likely to have sparser interactions.
The effective parameter count, derived from the local learning coefficient, measures the number of computationally relevant parameters in the network.
papers.limitation: The derivation of the Interaction Basis relies on two simplifying assumptions of independence about the Hessian, which are strong assumptions.
future_direction: Investigate alternative techniques for finding a basis without the simplifying assumptions about the Hessian.
Determine how to choose an appropriate behavioral loss cutoff epsilon for finite data singular learning theory.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to reverse engineer the algorithms implemented by neural networks by studying their weights and activations. An obstacle to reverse engineering neural networks is that many of the parameters inside a network are not involved in the computation being implemented by the network. These degenerate parameters may obfuscate internal structure. Singular learning theory teaches us that neural network parameterizations are biased towards being more degenerate, and parameterizations with more degeneracy are likely to generalize further. We identify 3 ways that network parameters can be degenerate: linear dependence between activations in a layer; linear dependence between gradients passed back to a layer; ReLUs which fire on the same subset of datapoints. We also present a heuristic argument that modular networks are likely to be more degenerate, and we develop a metric for identifying modules in a network that is based on this argument. We propose that if we can represent a neural network in a way that is invariant to reparameterizations that exploit the degeneracies, then this representation is likely to be more interpretable, and we provide some evidence that such a representation is likely to have sparser interactions. We introduce the Interaction Basis, a tractable technique to obtain a representation that is invariant to degeneracies from linear dependence of activations or Jacobians.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability as Statistical Estimation: A Variance Analysis
papers.research_question: What is the stability of mechanistic interpretability methods, specifically circuit discovery, and how does variance in causal mediation analysis and its approximations affect the reliability of discovered circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that circuit discovery methods are highly unstable due to intrinsic variance in causal mediation analysis scores and amplification by approximation methods, advocating for more rigorous statistical practices in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Circuit discovery is not a stable process and requires statistical rigor, including reporting stability metrics and sensitivity analyses, to become a reliable scientific tool.
papers.key_findings:
Exact causal mediation analysis (CMA) scores exhibit high intrinsic variance across inputs, meaning the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable.
Approximation methods like Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) amplify this variance, leading to low signal-to-noise ratios.
Circuit discovery pipelines are sensitive to data resampling, hyperparameters, and counterfactual definitions, resulting in structurally inconsistent circuits.
Larger models (e.g., Llama-3.2-1B) show higher variability in circuit discovery compared to smaller models (e.g., gpt2-small).
The instability of circuits is not mitigated by instruction tuning (comparing Llama-3.2-1B and its instruct variant).
papers.limitation:
Focus on the EAP family of methods, leaving out newer methods that may have different properties.
Exact CMA analysis was only done on gpt2-small for the IOI task due to computational constraints.
Limited to three classic MI tasks, which may not generalize to fuzzier reasoning tasks.
Stability metrics treat all edges equally, whereas weighted metrics might reveal a stable functional core.
future_direction: Probabilistic circuit discovery: characterizing a distribution over possible circuits.
Decomposing variance into estimator variance and intrinsic variance.
Stability-aware optimization: developing objectives that explicitly optimize for stability.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aims to reverse-engineer model behaviors by identifying functional sub-networks. Yet, the scientific validity of these findings depends on their stability. In this work, we argue that circuit discovery is not a standalone task but a statistical estimation problem built upon causal mediation analysis (CMA). We uncover a fundamental instability at this base layer: exact, single-input CMA scores exhibit high intrinsic variance, implying that the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable rather than a fixed property. We then demonstrate that circuit discovery pipelines inherit this variance and further amplify it. Fast approximation methods, such as Edge Attribution Patching and its successors, introduce additional estimation noise, while aggregating these noisy scores over datasets leads to fragile structural estimates. Consequently, small perturbations in input data or hyperparameters yield vastly different circuits. We systematically decompose these sources of variance and advocate for more rigorous MI practices, prioritizing statistical robustness and routine reporting of stability metrics.

papers.title: On the Learning Mechanisms in Physical Reasoning
papers.research_question: Is dynamics prediction indispensable for physical reasoning? When performing physical reasoning, is it better for machines to learn from intuition by simply analyzing the static physical structure, or to learn from dynamics by predicting future states?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Learning from Intuition (LfI) can be as effective as Learning from Dynamics (LfD) for physical reasoning, and that LfD often degenerates to LfI due to inaccuracies in dynamics prediction, though accurate dynamics (ground truth) provide an upper bound.
papers.conclusion: LfI is a simpler and effective paradigm for physical reasoning, performing competitively with LfD, but the LfD route remains promising if dynamics prediction can be made significantly more accurate.
papers.key_findings:
Simple LfI models (e.g., ViT) achieve state-of-the-art performance on PHYRE-B, even outperforming LfD models in cross-template generalization.
Ground-truth dynamics significantly boost performance, indicating that dynamics can help if accurately predicted.
Approximate dynamics from predictors (e.g., PredRNN) do not improve over LfI and often cause the LfD pipeline to degenerate into LfI.
LfI models are design-efficient, require no extra object information, and generalize well to unseen scenarios.
The performance of LfI models can be further improved with better perceptual modules tailored for physical reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted only on the PHYRE benchmark, lacking a rich suite of physical reasoning tasks.
LfI models are used without extra design for physical reasoning tasks, potentially leaving room for improvement.
The paper does not determine how accurate dynamics prediction needs to be to be beneficial.
future_direction: Develop a suite of physical reasoning tasks for further investigation.
Incorporate better perceptual modules and spatial analyzing modules into LfI models for physical reasoning.
Measure how accurate dynamics prediction needs to be to benefit downstream reasoning.
Explore how dynamics prediction can benefit other reasoning processes like counterfactual and hypothetical reasoning.
papers.abstract: Is dynamics prediction indispensable for physical reasoning? If so, what kind of roles do the dynamics prediction modules play during the physical reasoning process? Most studies focus on designing dynamics prediction networks and treating physical reasoning as a downstream task without investigating the questions above, taking for granted that the designed dynamics prediction would undoubtedly help the reasoning process. In this work, we take a closer look at this assumption, exploring this fundamental hypothesis by comparing two learning mechanisms: Learning from Dynamics (LfD) and Learning from Intuition (LfI). In the first experiment, we directly examine and compare these two mechanisms. Results show a surprising finding: Simple LfI is better than or on par with state-of-the-art LfD. This observation leads to the second experiment with Ground-truth Dynamics, the ideal case of LfD wherein dynamics are obtained directly from a simulator. Results show that dynamics, if directly given instead of approximated, would achieve much higher performance than LfI alone on physical reasoning; this essentially serves as the performance upper bound. Yet practically, LfD mechanism can only predict Approximate Dynamics using dynamics learning modules that mimic the physical laws, making the following downstream physical reasoning modules degenerate into the LfI paradigm; see the third experiment. We note that this issue is hard to mitigate, as dynamics prediction errors inevitably accumulate in the long horizon. Finally, in the fourth experiment, we note that LfI, the extremely simpler strategy when done right, is more effective in learning to solve physical reasoning problems. Taken together, the results on the challenging benchmark of PHYRE show that LfI is, if not better, as good as LfD for dynamics prediction. However, the potential improvement from LfD, though challenging, remains lucrative.

papers.title: Interpretation of Prediction Models Using the Input Gradient
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the behavior of any predictive model? The paper proposes using the partial derivatives of the model with respect to the input to determine which variables affect the prediction and how.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using the gradient of the model with respect to input features as a general method to interpret which input variables affect the prediction and how.
papers.conclusion: The gradient vector with respect to input is a useful quantity for interpreting model behavior, providing insights into feature importance and revealing global structure such as linearity.
papers.key_findings:
The gradient norm with respect to word embeddings in a CNN model can identify the most influential words or expressions for sentiment classification.
For a Bag-of-Words neural network, the average gradient over the test set provides a global ranking of word importance, revealing words like 'excellent' and 'worst' as most influential.
The average gradient vector can approximate the prediction function with 99.6% accuracy, indicating the decision boundary is nearly linear.
The gradient-based interpretation method is general and can be applied to any predictive model, including non-differentiable cases via numerical approximation.
The method is computationally efficient as gradients can be obtained via backpropagation.
papers.abstract: State of the art machine learning algorithms are highly optimized to provide the optimal prediction possible, naturally resulting in complex models. While these models often outperform simpler more interpretable models by order of magnitudes, in terms of understanding the way the model functions, we are often facing a "black box". In this paper we suggest a simple method to interpret the behavior of any predictive model, both for regression and classification. Given a particular model, the information required to interpret it can be obtained by studying the partial derivatives of the model with respect to the input. We exemplify this insight by interpreting convolutional and multi-layer neural networks in the field of natural language processing.

papers.title: Explainable deep learning for rainfall prediction: A CNN-XGBoost hybrid approach in the northern region of Bangladesh
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the application of deep learning models for rainfall prediction in the northern region of Bangladesh, focusing on the comparative performance of six models and the interpretability of a proposed hybrid model.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a hybrid CNN-XGBoost model for rainfall prediction that consistently outperforms other models (CNN, LSTM, XGB, Ensemble, Transformer-XGB) across two distinct datasets and provides interpretability of its decisions using SHAP.
papers.conclusion: The CNN-XGB hybrid model provides accurate and consistent rainfall predictions for the northern region of Bangladesh, outperforming other models, and the use of SHAP enhances model transparency and trust for practical applications like urban planning and disaster management.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN-XGB hybrid model achieved the lowest RMSE (0.65 mm/day) and MAE (0.28 mm/day) and highest R2 (0.99) on the satellite dataset for Rajshahi district.
On the ground dataset, the CNN-XGB model also performed best for Rajshahi district with RMSE of 16.28 mm/month, MAE of 7.85 mm/month, and R2 of 0.98.
The satellite dataset with 16 meteorological variables led to better model performance than the ground dataset with only rainfall data.
SHAP analysis identified that engineered features (e.g., trends, rolling statistics, transformations of precipitation) and climatic variables were the most influential predictors.
The hybrid model effectively captures both spatial and temporal patterns in rainfall data, demonstrating robustness across different districts and data sources.
papers.limitation:
The ground dataset's monthly resolution restricts the model's ability to capture short-term rainfall variability.
Crucial environmental and urban factors such as soil moisture, land use, and topography were excluded due to data unavailability, which may affect localized accuracy.
future_direction: Explore domain adaptation to improve generalization across diverse regions.
Integrate multi-source data (e.g., radar observations, vegetation indices, satellite-derived soil moisture) to enhance robustness under varying climatic conditions.
Couple the proposed model with numerical weather prediction (NWP) models to refine forecasts by blending data-driven and physics-based approaches.
papers.abstract: Abstract Accurate precipitation forecasting is crucial for evaluating various hydrological processes. This research explores the application of deep learning models for rainfall prediction in the northern region of Bangladesh, focusing on the comparative performance of six models: CNN (Convolutional Neural Network), LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory), XGB (Extreme Gradient Boosting), Ensemble Model, Transformer-XGB, and CNN-XGB. Two distinct datasets were utilized to assess the effectiveness of these models. Among them, the CNN-XGB hybrid model consistently demonstrated superior performance across all evaluation metrics, establishing it as the most reliable predictor in this study. Rajshahi district’s satellite dataset showed an RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) of 0.65 mm/day, MAE (Mean Absolute Error) of 0.28 mm/day, and R 2 of 0.99. In the ground dataset, Rajshahi district beat other models with an RMSE of 16.28 mm/month, MAE of 7.85 mm/month, and R 2 of 0.98. These findings demonstrate the model’s efficacy across several data sources. To enhance the interpretability of the proposed CNN-XGB model, we deployed the SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations) explainer, providing insights into the model’s decision-making process. This research highlights the potential of hybrid models in enhancing rainfall prediction accuracy while providing transparency through explainable AI techniques. Beyond hydrology, the predicted rainfall patterns provide essential inputs for urban planners to optimize land-use zoning in flood-prone areas, and guide resilient infrastructure development. Code Available: https://github.com/Shafi3397/Rainfall-Prediction-using-CNN-XGBoost

papers.title: Compact Proofs of Model Performance via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to derive compact formal guarantees on model performance? Does more compact proof require and provide more mechanistic understanding, and does more faithful understanding lead to tighter bounds?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can be used to generate compact formal proofs of model performance, and shows that more compact proofs require more mechanistic understanding and that more faithful understanding leads to tighter bounds.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability can be used to generate compact proofs of model performance, but compounding structureless errors pose a challenge that future work must address.
papers.key_findings:
Shorter proofs seem to require and provide more mechanistic understanding.
More faithful mechanistic understanding leads to tighter performance bounds.
Compounding structureless errors is a key challenge for using mechanistic interpretability to generate compact proofs on model performance.
papers.limitation:
Compounding structureless errors pose a challenge for generating compact proofs.
The approach is demonstrated only on a simple toy setting (Max-of-K).
future_direction: Addressing the challenge of compounding structureless errors in generating compact proofs.
Extending the approach to more complex tasks and models.
papers.abstract: We propose using mechanistic interpretability -- techniques for reverse engineering model weights into human-interpretable algorithms -- to derive and compactly prove formal guarantees on model performance. We prototype this approach by formally proving accuracy lower bounds for a small transformer trained on Max-of-K, validating proof transferability across 151 random seeds and four values of K. We create 102 different computer-assisted proof strategies and assess their length and tightness of bound on each of our models. Using quantitative metrics, we find that shorter proofs seem to require and provide more mechanistic understanding. Moreover, we find that more faithful mechanistic understanding leads to tighter performance bounds. We confirm these connections by qualitatively examining a subset of our proofs. Finally, we identify compounding structureless errors as a key challenge for using mechanistic interpretability to generate compact proofs on model performance.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form abruptly during a phase change in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in in-context learning ability.
Altering the transformer architecture to shift the formation of induction heads also shifts the improvement in in-context learning.
Ablating induction heads in small models greatly reduces in-context learning.
Induction heads exhibit general in-context learning behaviors beyond literal copying, such as translation.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models suggests how they could be repurposed for general in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Evidence for large models is correlational and could be confounded by other factors.
future_direction: Establish the claim more firmly with additional evidence
Study the phase change in more detail
papers.abstract: "Induction heads" are attention heads that implement a simple algorithm to complete token sequences like [A][B] ... [A] -> [B]. In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: Analysis of a convolutional neural network for predicting unsteady volume wake flow fields
papers.research_question: How does a convolutional neural network system learn and predict three-dimensional unsteady wake flow dynamics in different flow regimes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a multi-scale CNN system for predicting 3D unsteady wake flow and investigates its mechanisms, showing that convolution layers integrate and transport wavenumber information to extract flow structures, and that redundant feature maps can be identified and removed to reduce model size without loss of performance.
papers.conclusion: The CNN system predicts wake flow by integrating and transporting wavenumber information through convolution layers, extracting representations of flow dynamics. Redundant feature maps can be removed based on structural similarity, significantly reducing model size without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN system predicts flow in different regimes by transporting wavenumber information through convolution layers.
Feature maps extract similar flow structures (e.g., braid shear layers and shedding vortices) across different Reynolds numbers.
Convolution layers integrate information from all input flow variables and histories, with more recent histories having larger contributions.
Redundant feature maps can be identified using structural similarity (SSIM) and removed, reducing the number of weights by 85% without affecting prediction performance.
papers.abstract: A predictive convolutional neural network is developed to predict the future of three-dimensional unsteady wake flow from past information of flow velocity and pressure. The developed network is found to be capable of predicting vortex dynamics at distinctive flow regimes with flow structures at different scales. Mechanisms of the network on predicting vortex dynamics at two distinctive flow regimes, the mode-B shedding regime and the turbulent wake regime, are investigated. Information in feature maps of the network is visualized and quantitatively assessed to investigate the encoded flow structures. A Fourier analysis is conducted to investigate the mechanisms of the network on learning fluid motions with distinctive flow scales. The transformation of information from the input to prediction layers of the network is tracked to examine how the network transforms the input information for prediction. Structural similarities among feature maps in the network are evaluated to reduce the number of feature maps containing redundant flow structures, which allows reduction of the size of the network without affecting prediction performance.

papers.title: Relative Geometry of Neural Forecasters: Linking Accuracy and Alignment in Learned Latent Geometry
papers.research_question: How do neural forecasters internally represent dynamical systems, and does the alignment of their latent geometries across model families correlate with forecasting accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces anchor-based relative embeddings to compare latent spaces of neural forecasters, revealing family-level alignment patterns and showing that alignment generally correlates with forecasting accuracy but high accuracy can coexist with low alignment (especially in transformers and ESNs).
papers.conclusion: Relative geometry provides a reproducible foundation for comparing how model families internalize dynamical structure, and alignment offers insights beyond task loss.
papers.key_findings:
Anchor-based relative embeddings remove rotational and scaling ambiguities, enabling direct comparison of latent spaces across model families.
MLPs align with other MLPs, RNNs with RNNs, while transformers and ESNs achieve strong forecasts despite weaker alignment.
Alignment generally correlates with forecasting accuracy, but high accuracy can coexist with low alignment (especially in transformers and ESNs).
The alignment signal stabilizes with increasing number of anchors (K>=16).
Noise and input length affect representational stability differently across forecasters.
papers.limitation: Alignment with the 'true system' refers only to alignment with the relative representation of observed trajectories, not to recovery of governing equations or physical state variables.
future_direction: Developing bridging mappings between model families
Alignment-driven training interventions
papers.abstract: Neural networks can accurately forecast complex dynamical systems, yet how they internally represent underlying latent geometry remains poorly understood. We study neural forecasters through the lens of representational alignment, introducing anchor-based, geometry-agnostic relative embeddings that remove rotational and scaling ambiguities in latent spaces. Applying this framework across seven canonical dynamical systems - ranging from periodic to chaotic - we reveal reproducible family-level structure: multilayer perceptrons align with other MLPs, recurrent networks with RNNs, while transformers and echo-state networks achieve strong forecasts despite weaker alignment. Alignment generally correlates with forecasting accuracy, yet high accuracy can coexist with low alignment. Relative geometry thus provides a simple, reproducible foundation for comparing how model families internalize and represent dynamical structure.

papers.title: Invertible Neural Networks for Understanding Semantics of Invariances of CNN Representations
papers.research_question: How can we understand the semantic concepts and invariances learned by deep neural networks (specifically CNNs) by recovering the invariances and translating the representations into an interpretable form without modifying the original model?
papers.core_contribution: An invertible neural network (INN) approach that recovers the invariances a deep model has learned and bijectively translates the model representation and its invariances into a semantically accessible encoding without compromising the original model's performance.
papers.conclusion: The invertible approach provides a powerful, post-hoc diagnostic pipeline for explaining deep representations by recovering invariances and enabling semantic interpretation without retraining the model.
papers.key_findings:
The method visualizes representations and their invariances without artifacts, outperforming existing network inversion methods.
Analysis of FaceNet shows that invariances (e.g., to pose) increase with layer depth, while some features (e.g., glasses) remain identity-relevant across layers.
The approach can quantify how much of a semantic concept (e.g., texture vs. shape) is captured by a model's representation, revealing biases like texture bias in ImageNet-trained CNNs.
Semantic modifications in the interpretable space correctly alter the original representation and can be visualized, enabling diagnostic probing of model sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Abstract To tackle increasingly complex tasks, it has become an essential ability of neural networks to learn abstract representations. These task-specific representations and, particularly, the invariances they capture turn neural networks into black-box models that lack interpretability. To open such a black box, it is, therefore, crucial to uncover the different semantic concepts a model has learned as well as those that it has learned to be invariant to. We present an approach based on invertible neural networks (INNs) that (i) recovers the task-specific, learned invariances by disentangling the remaining factor of variation in the data and that (ii) invertibly transforms these recovered invariances combined with the model representation into an equally expressive one with accessible semantic concepts. As a consequence, neural network representations become understandable by providing the means to (i) expose their semantic meaning, (ii) semantically modify a representation, and (iii) visualize individual learned semantic concepts and invariances. Our invertible approach significantly extends the abilities to understand black-box models by enabling post hoc interpretations of state-of-the-art networks without compromising their performance. Our implementation is available at https://compvis.github.io/invariances/ .

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Neural Networks Trained to Solve Differential Equations Learn General Representations
papers.research_question: How can we measure the generality of neural network layers across a continuously-parametrized set of tasks? What is the generality structure of layers in neural networks trained to solve differential equations?
papers.core_contribution: We develop an efficient method using SVCCA to measure layer generality across continuously-parametrized tasks, and apply it to show that in neural networks trained to solve differential equations, the first layer is general and deeper layers are successively more specific.
papers.conclusion: We presented a method for measuring layer generality using SVCCA, found that first layers of DENNs are general and deeper layers are more specific, validated with transfer learning, and visualized the general components as generalized coordinates.
papers.key_findings:
The first hidden layer is general, and deeper layers become progressively more specific.
The SVCCA-based method agrees with transfer learning experiments but is much faster, especially for continuously-parametrized problems.
The general components of the first layer can be visualized as generalized coordinates that capture regions of interest in the input domain.
Network width affects layer generality: intrinsic dimensionality saturates with width, reproducibility increases with width, and specificity varies with width and layer depth.
Very wide networks may have training dynamics that affect convergence and generality measurements.
papers.limitation:
SVCCA is numerically unstable when correlation values are very close to each other, making component sorting ill-conditioned.
Very wide networks may have broad minima in the loss landscape, causing training to terminate before optimal convergence, potentially affecting generality measurements.
future_direction: Explore the behavior of layer generality at very large network widths.
Develop component analyses that search for closely-coupled components to improve numerical stability.
Investigate different training protocols for very wide DENNs to ensure proper convergence.
papers.abstract: We introduce a technique based on the singular vector canonical correlation analysis (SVCCA) for measuring the generality of neural network layers across a continuously-parametrized set of tasks. We illustrate this method by studying generality in neural networks trained to solve parametrized boundary value problems based on the Poisson partial differential equation. We find that the first hidden layer is general, and that deeper layers are successively more specific. Next, we validate our method against an existing technique that measures layer generality using transfer learning experiments. We find excellent agreement between the two methods, and note that our method is much faster, particularly for continuously-parametrized problems. Finally, we visualize the general representations of the first layers, and interpret them as generalized coordinates over the input domain.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
