papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical understanding of modality collapse as arising from cross-modal polysemantic interference due to rank bottlenecks, and proposes Explicit Basis Reallocation (EBR) to prevent collapse by disentangling and denoising multimodal representations.
papers.conclusion: Modality collapse in multimodal fusion can be understood and effectively prevented through basis reallocation, which disentangles cross-modal feature entanglements and denoises representations, leading to robust multimodal learning.
papers.key_findings:
Modality collapse is caused by cross-modal polysemantic interference where noisy features from one modality entangle with predictive features from another via shared neurons in the fusion head.
This interference is a consequence of low-rank simplicity bias in neural networks, which creates rank bottlenecks in gradient updates.
Cross-modal knowledge distillation implicitly mitigates collapse by freeing up rank bottlenecks, allowing independent denoising of modalities.
Explicit Basis Reallocation (EBR) explicitly disentangles and denoises modalities by reallocating basis vectors, preventing collapse and enabling robust handling of missing modalities.
EBR achieves state-of-the-art performance on multimodal benchmarks with missing modalities.
papers.limitation: Theoretical results rely on the identifiability condition of modality-specific causal factors.
papers.abstract: We aim to develop a fundamental understanding of modality collapse, a recently observed empirical phenomenon wherein models trained for multimodal fusion tend to rely only on a subset of the modalities, ignoring the rest. We show that modality collapse happens when noisy features from one modality are entangled, via a shared set of neurons in the fusion head, with predictive features from another, effectively masking out positive contributions from the predictive features of the former modality and leading to its collapse. We further prove that cross-modal knowledge distillation implicitly disentangles such representations by freeing up rank bottlenecks in the student encoder, denoising the fusion-head outputs without negatively impacting the predictive features from either modality. Based on the above findings, we propose an algorithm that prevents modality collapse through explicit basis reallocation, with applications in dealing with missing modalities. Extensive experiments on multiple multimodal benchmarks validate our theoretical claims. Project page: https://abhrac.github.io/mmcollapse/.

papers.title: What Has a Foundation Model Found? Using Inductive Bias to Probe for World Models
papers.research_question: Does a foundation model's inductive bias align with a postulated world model, indicating that it has learned deeper structure from sequence prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an inductive bias probe to evaluate whether foundation models have learned a postulated world model, and finds that they often fail to do so, instead developing task-specific heuristics.
papers.conclusion: The inductive bias probe reveals that foundation models often fail to learn the underlying world models, instead relying on task-specific heuristics, which limits their generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation models trained on orbital trajectories fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks.
Models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.
In lattice and Othello, models have an inductive bias toward legal next-tokens rather than the world model.
Models that perform better on inductive bias probes have better transfer performance on new tasks that rely on the underlying world model.
LLMs also fail to predict force magnitudes accurately in physics tasks.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning proprietary LLMs is infeasible and running the full inductive bias probe is expensive.
papers.abstract: Foundation models are premised on the idea that sequence prediction can uncover deeper domain understanding, much like how Kepler's predictions of planetary motion later led to the discovery of Newtonian mechanics. However, evaluating whether these models truly capture deeper structure remains a challenge. We develop a technique for evaluating foundation models that examines how they adapt to synthetic datasets generated from some postulated world model. Our technique measures whether the foundation model's inductive bias aligns with the world model, and so we refer to it as an inductive bias probe. Across multiple domains, we find that foundation models can excel at their training tasks yet fail to develop inductive biases towards the underlying world model when adapted to new tasks. We particularly find that foundation models trained on orbital trajectories consistently fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks. Further analysis reveals that these models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: How Much of a Model Do We Need? Redundancy and Slimmability in Remote Sensing Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do remote sensing foundation models enter an overparameterized regime at smaller scales than computer vision models, and do they rely on redundant representations?
papers.core_contribution: Remote sensing foundation models exhibit high post-hoc slimmability, retaining over 71% relative accuracy at 1% compute due to redundant representations, contrasting sharply with computer vision models.
papers.conclusion: RS FMs enter an overparameterized regime at smaller scales than CV models, with redundant representations enabling high slimmability, making post-hoc slimming a practical tool for resource-constrained deployment.
papers.key_findings:
RS FMs maintain over 71% relative accuracy at 1% computational budget across all models and tasks, a sevenfold improvement over CV models.
Learned slimmable training improves MoCo-based models but not MAE-based models, with MoCo showing advantages at low scales.
Feature correlation analysis reveals distinct scaling strategies: DOFA shows organized to independent features, Prithvi shows U-shaped patterns, and TerraMind shows monotonic decrease.
Explained variance ratio indicates that RS FMs distribute task-relevant information with high redundancy, leading to robust slimmability.
Intermediate-scale deployment often achieves superior accuracy through implicit regularization, offering up to 12x speedups.
future_direction: Develop slimmable training techniques for MAE's reconstruction objective.
Investigate modality-specific compression tolerances.
Explore non-uniform slimming strategies.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models (FMs) in remote sensing (RS) are developed based on the paradigms established in computer vision (CV) and have shown promise for various Earth observation applications. However, the direct transfer of scaling assumptions from CV to RS has not been adequately examined. We hypothesize that RS FMs enter an overparameterized regime at substantially smaller scales than their CV counterparts, where increasing parameter count primarily induces redundant representations rather than qualitatively new abstractions. To test this hypothesis, we use post-hoc slimming, where we uniformly reduce the width of pretrained encoder, as a tool to measure representational redundancy across six state-of-the-art RS FMs on four downstream classification tasks. Our findings reveal a significant contrast with those in the CV domain: while a post-hoc slimmed masked autoencoder (MAE) trained on ImageNet retains less than 10% accuracy at 1% FLOPs, RS FMs maintain over 71% relative accuracy at the same budget. This sevenfold difference provides strong empirical support for our hypothesis. We further demonstrate that learned slimmable training can improve both Momentum Contrast (MoCo)- and MAE- based models. In addition, through the explained variance ratio and the feature correlation analysis, we provide mechanistic explanations showing that RS FMs distribute task-relevant information with high redundancy. Our findings establish post-hoc slimmability as both a practical deployment strategy for resource-constrained environments and a diagnostic tool that challenges the prevailing scaling paradigm in RS. Upon acceptance, we will publish all code.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs Philosophy
papers.research_question: How can philosophy contribute to mechanistic interpretability? The paper investigates three open problems in MI and how philosophy can help.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that mechanistic interpretability needs philosophy to clarify its concepts, refine its methods, and assess the epistemic and ethical stakes of interpreting AI systems.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that philosophy is deeply relevant to mechanistic interpretability and invites deeper interdisciplinary collaboration that is technically informed and philosophically grounded.
papers.key_findings:
Philosophy can help in decomposing networks into interpretable parts by providing conceptual tools from mechanistic explanation and challenging the assumption of a single true decomposition.
Philosophy can clarify the concept of 'features' in AI systems by distinguishing between vehicles and content of representations, refining experimental approaches, and suggesting new lines of investigation.
Philosophy can help in detecting deceptive behavior by clarifying concepts like lying and deception, guiding the search for AI beliefs, and drawing ethical and normative boundaries.
future_direction: Deeper interdisciplinary collaboration between philosophy and mechanistic interpretability.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to explain how neural networks work by uncovering their underlying causal mechanisms. As the field grows in influence, it is increasingly important to examine not just models themselves, but the assumptions, concepts and explanatory strategies implicit in MI research. We argue that mechanistic interpretability needs philosophy: not as an afterthought, but as an ongoing partner in clarifying its concepts, refining its methods, and assessing the epistemic and ethical stakes of interpreting AI systems. Taking three open problems from the MI literature as examples, this position paper illustrates the value philosophy can add to MI research, and outlines a path toward deeper interdisciplinary dialogue.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
Polytopes partially define when feature-directions are on- and off-distribution, with dense boundaries near the origin but class changes also occur in low-density regions.
Clustering activations or spline codes yields monosemantic clusters in both image classifiers and language models.
The polytope lens provides a more complete description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but it is not yet clear how to use it for decomposable descriptions.
papers.limitation: The polytope lens sacrifices globally valid feature directions for locally valid ones, making descriptions more complex and less decomposable.
future_direction: Develop the polytope lens into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
Build more robust and scalable methods based on the polytope lens.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain what a neural network has learned at a nuts-and-bolts level. What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations? Previous mechanistic descriptions have used individual neurons or their linear combinations to understand the representations a network has learned. But there are clues that neurons and their linear combinations are not the correct fundamental units of description: directions cannot describe how neural networks use nonlinearities to structure their representations. Moreover, many instances of individual neurons and their combinations are polysemantic (i.e. they have multiple unrelated meanings). Polysemanticity makes interpreting the network in terms of neurons or directions challenging since we can no longer assign a specific feature to a neural unit. In order to find a basic unit of description that does not suffer from these problems, we zoom in beyond just directions to study the way that piecewise linear activation functions (such as ReLU) partition the activation space into numerous discrete polytopes. We call this perspective the polytope lens. The polytope lens makes concrete predictions about the behavior of neural networks, which we evaluate through experiments on both convolutional image classifiers and language models. Specifically, we show that polytopes can be used to identify monosemantic regions of activation space (while directions are not in general monosemantic) and that the density of polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries. We also outline a vision for what mechanistic interpretability might look like through the polytope lens.

papers.title: On the Symmetries of Deep Learning Models and their Internal Representations
papers.research_question: How do the symmetries of a network architecture (via intertwiner groups) relate to the symmetries in the network's internal representations of data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces intertwiner groups to connect architectural symmetries with symmetries in internal representations, and shows that for ReLU networks, the activation basis is special for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intertwiner groups connect architectural symmetries to representation symmetries, and provide a justification for focusing on activation basis in ReLU networks for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Intertwiner groups describe weight space symmetries and propagate to symmetries in internal representations.
Stitching with GReLU transformations incurs a small accuracy penalty, indicating that much of the variation between networks can be accounted for by GReLU.
GReLU-Procrustes and GReLU-CKA are effective dissimilarity measures invariant to GReLU transformations.
For ReLU networks, interpretability is higher in the activation basis than in arbitrary linear combinations, but this is not the case for networks without ReLU.
papers.limitation:
The theory does not fully account for residual connections, as noted in remark 3.6.
Stitching with GReLU does not achieve full accuracy, indicating that internal representations are not perfectly aligned by permutations and scalings.
papers.abstract: Symmetry is a fundamental tool in the exploration of a broad range of complex systems. In machine learning symmetry has been explored in both models and data. In this paper we seek to connect the symmetries arising from the architecture of a family of models with the symmetries of that family's internal representation of data. We do this by calculating a set of fundamental symmetry groups, which we call the intertwiner groups of the model. We connect intertwiner groups to a model's internal representations of data through a range of experiments that probe similarities between hidden states across models with the same architecture. Our work suggests that the symmetries of a network are propagated into the symmetries in that network's representation of data, providing us with a better understanding of how architecture affects the learning and prediction process. Finally, we speculate that for ReLU networks, the intertwiner groups may provide a justification for the common practice of concentrating model interpretability exploration on the activation basis in hidden layers rather than arbitrary linear combinations thereof.

papers.title: Challenges in Mechanistically Interpreting Model Representations
papers.research_question: What are the challenges in mechanistically interpreting model representations, and how do current mechanistic interpretability tools fall short in understanding complex behaviors like dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the importance of studying feature and behavior representations in models, performs an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in Mistral-7B, and shows that current mechanistic interpretability tools are insufficient for understanding such representations, advocating for new frameworks.
papers.conclusion: Studying representations for features and behaviors is crucial for understanding models, but current mechanistic interpretability tooling is inadequate for answering key questions about representations, necessitating new frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations for dishonesty can be found and used to steer model behavior, but they are not simply boosting generically dishonest tokens.
Continual injections of the dishonesty direction are required for open-ended dishonest generation, not just at the first token.
Direct logit attribution shows that directional injections affect many components, with MLPs having a more direct effect than attention heads.
Activation patching reveals that many components are involved in the dishonesty behavior, making sparse circuit analysis difficult and less helpful.
Current mechanistic interpretability tooling (e.g., patching) is insufficient for understanding how representations are formed and how they affect long-term generation.
papers.limitation: Patching methods (activation and path patching) do not rigorously prove that circuits found are indeed reserved to that task, and patching only one component at a time might not isolate components if multiple perform the same job.
future_direction: Study how different components interact with representations and alter them.
Explore the training dynamics of a model and study the emergence of representations as a model trains.
Develop new frameworks to think about and study representations.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to understand AI models by reverse-engineering the exact algorithms neural networks learn. Most works in MI so far have studied behaviors and capabilities that are trivial and token-aligned. However, most capabilities important for safety and trust are not that trivial, which advocates for the study of hidden representations inside these networks as the unit of analysis. We formalize representations for features and behaviors, highlight their importance and evaluation, and perform an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1'. We justify that studying representations is an important and under-studied field, and highlight several challenges that arise while attempting to do so through currently established methods in MI, showing their insufficiency and advocating work on new frameworks for the same.

papers.title: Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context
papers.research_question: How do transformers perform in-context learning of dynamical systems, and what mechanisms enable them to forecast unseen physical systems without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on dynamical systems learn to perform time-delay embedding and approximate transfer operators in-context, enabling out-of-distribution generalization to unseen systems.
papers.conclusion: Transformers extract a system-independent forecasting strategy by performing time-delay embedding and approximating transfer operators in-context, explaining their ability to generalize to unseen dynamical systems.
papers.key_findings:
An early tradeoff between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance manifests as a secondary double descent phenomenon during training.
Transformers adaptively perform time-delay embedding during inference to estimate the intrinsic dimensionality of the input system's attractor.
Transformers learn to approximate the Perron-Frobenius (transfer) operator of the fully-observed system in-context, capturing its dominant timescales and metastable states.
Out-of-distribution generalization error scales linearly with the KL divergence between the training and testing system attractors.
The effective order of the Markov chain approximating the transformer's dynamics scales linearly with the intrinsic dimension of the test system's attractor, consistent with Takens' theorem.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models for scientific machine learning adapt to physical settings unseen during training, such as zero-shot transfer between turbulent scales. This phenomenon, in-context learning, challenges conventional understanding of learning and adaptation in physical systems. Here, we study in-context learning of dynamical systems in a minimal setting: we train a small two-layer, single-head transformer to forecast one dynamical system, and then evaluate its ability to forecast a different dynamical system without retraining. We discover an early tradeoff in training between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance, which manifests as a secondary double descent phenomenon. We discover that attention-based models apply a transfer-operator forecasting strategy in-context. They (1) lift low-dimensional time series using delay embedding, to detect the system's higher-dimensional dynamical manifold, and (2) identify and forecast long-lived invariant sets that characterize the global flow on this manifold. Our results clarify the mechanism enabling large pretrained models to forecast unseen physical systems at test without retraining, and they illustrate the unique ability of attention-based models to leverage global attractor information in service of short-term forecasts.

papers.title: A PDE-based Explanation of Extreme Numerical Sensitivities and Edge of Stability in Training Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do extreme numerical sensitivities arise in training neural networks, and how are they linked to the Edge of Stability phenomenon?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers restrained numerical instabilities in deep network training and provides a PDE-based theoretical framework explaining how they arise from exceeding stable learning rates, linking them to the Edge of Stability phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: Numerical stability is a critical but previously overlooked factor in deep network training, and the PDE-based framework provides new insights into the Edge of Stability, suggesting the need for adaptive learning rate schemes.
papers.key_findings:
Floating-point arithmetic errors on the order of the smallest bit can be significantly amplified during training, leading to test accuracy variance comparable to that from SGD stochasticity.
Restrained instabilities occur when the learning rate exceeds the stability limit predicted by PDE analysis, causing localized oscillations without full divergence.
The Edge of Stability (EoS) is explained as a manifestation of these restrained instabilities in the training dynamics of CNNs.
The stability conditions depend on learning rate, weight decay, and network complexity, with larger networks more prone to such instabilities.
Both SGD and Adam optimizers exhibit restrained instabilities, indicating the phenomenon is fundamental to current training practices.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis focuses on deterministic gradient descent and a simplified CNN model, not fully accounting for stochasticity in SGD.
The analysis is primarily for convolutional neural networks; extension to other architectures (e.g., transformers) is not covered.
future_direction: Developing adaptive learning rate schemes that ensure stability while maintaining training speed.
Extending the analysis to stochastic gradient descent and other network architectures.
Investigating the role of regularization and network complexity in stability more thoroughly.
papers.abstract: We discover restrained numerical instabilities in current training practices of deep networks with stochastic gradient descent (SGD), and its variants. We show numerical error (on the order of the smallest floating point bit and thus the most extreme or limiting numerical perturbations induced from floating point arithmetic in training deep nets can be amplified significantly and result in significant test accuracy variance (sensitivities), comparable to the test accuracy variance due to stochasticity in SGD. We show how this is likely traced to instabilities of the optimization dynamics that are restrained, i.e., localized over iterations and regions of the weight tensor space. We do this by presenting a theoretical framework using numerical analysis of partial differential equations (PDE), and analyzing the gradient descent PDE of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). We show that it is stable only under certain conditions on the learning rate and weight decay. We show that rather than blowing up when the conditions are violated, the instability can be restrained. We show this is a consequence of the non-linear PDE associated with the gradient descent of the CNN, whose local linearization changes when over-driving the step size of the discretization, resulting in a stabilizing effect. We link restrained instabilities to the recently discovered Edge of Stability (EoS) phenomena, in which the stable step size predicted by classical theory is exceeded while continuing to optimize the loss and still converging. Because restrained instabilities occur at the EoS, our theory provides new insights and predictions about the EoS, in particular, the role of regularization and the dependence on the network complexity.

papers.title: The Cognitive Revolution in Interpretability: From Explaining Behavior to Interpreting Representations and Algorithms
papers.research_question: How can we understand, interpret, and explain the behavior of complex intelligent AI systems like large language models, and how can mechanistic interpretability be grounded in cognitive science?
papers.core_contribution: The paper grounds mechanistic interpretability in cognitive science, proposing a taxonomy that categorizes interpretation methods into semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that a cognitive revolution in deep learning interpretability is underway, shifting from explaining behavior to interpreting representations and algorithms, and calls for a unified framework that integrates semantic and algorithmic interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Current interpretability methods are ripe for a transition echoing the 'cognitive revolution' in psychology, shifting from pure behaviorism to studying internal representations and processing.
A taxonomy mirroring computational neuroscience distinguishes semantic interpretation (studying latent representations) and algorithmic interpretation (studying operations and algorithms).
Semantic interpretation methods include optimization and search, structural probing, causal probing, and dictionary learning, each with distinct assumptions and challenges.
Algorithmic interpretation focuses on circuit discovery, using interventions like knockouts and patching to understand the role of sub-networks in model behavior.
The paper discusses parallels and distinctions between approaches, analyzes strengths and weaknesses, and outlines challenges and the possibility of a unified framework.
future_direction: Unifying semantic and algorithmic interpretation under a common framework.
Addressing challenges in scalability, evaluation, and the Rashomon effect in causal analysis.
Developing automated and scalable methods for feature interpretation and evaluation in dictionary learning.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have long been understood as "black boxes": though we know their computation graphs and learned parameters, the knowledge encoded by these weights and functions they perform are not inherently interpretable. As such, from the early days of deep learning, there have been efforts to explain these models' behavior and understand them internally; and recently, mechanistic interpretability (MI) has emerged as a distinct research area studying the features and implicit algorithms learned by foundation models such as large language models. In this work, we aim to ground MI in the context of cognitive science, which has long struggled with analogous questions in studying and explaining the behavior of "black box" intelligent systems like the human brain. We leverage several important ideas and developments in the history of cognitive science to disentangle divergent objectives in MI and indicate a clear path forward. First, we argue that current methods are ripe to facilitate a transition in deep learning interpretation echoing the "cognitive revolution" in 20th-century psychology that shifted the study of human psychology from pure behaviorism toward mental representations and processing. Second, we propose a taxonomy mirroring key parallels in computational neuroscience to describe two broad categories of MI research, semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned and used) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations) to elucidate their divergent goals and objects of study. Finally, we elaborate the parallels and distinctions between various approaches in both categories, analyze the respective strengths and weaknesses of representative works, clarify underlying assumptions, outline key challenges, and discuss the possibility of unifying these modes of interpretation under a common framework.

papers.title: Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the key open problems in mechanistic interpretability methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges that need to be addressed to achieve the field's goals?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes and outlines key open problems in mechanistic interpretability, covering methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges to guide future research.
papers.conclusion: The review outlines critical open problems in mechanistic interpretability that must be addressed to achieve scientific and engineering goals, emphasizing the need for methodological improvements and socio-technical integration.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability methods, such as sparse dictionary learning, suffer from practical and conceptual limitations like high reconstruction errors and unclear theoretical foundations.
Applying interpretability to AI safety requires robust methods for monitoring internal states and controlling behavior, but current techniques are insufficient.
Socio-technical challenges include integrating interpretability into AI governance and addressing philosophical questions about the field's goals.
future_direction: Developing better decomposition methods like sparse dictionary learning with lower reconstruction errors.
Creating validation frameworks for interpretability hypotheses.
Applying interpretability to AI safety monitoring and control.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the computational mechanisms underlying neural networks' capabilities in order to accomplish concrete scientific and engineering goals. Progress in this field thus promises to provide greater assurance over AI system behavior and shed light on exciting scientific questions about the nature of intelligence. Despite recent progress toward these goals, there are many open problems in the field that require solutions before many scientific and practical benefits can be realized: Our methods require both conceptual and practical improvements to reveal deeper insights; we must figure out how best to apply our methods in pursuit of specific goals; and the field must grapple with socio-technical challenges that influence and are influenced by our work. This forward-facing review discusses the current frontier of mechanistic interpretability and the open problems that the field may benefit from prioritizing.

papers.title: PAHQ: Accelerating Automated Circuit Discovery through Mixed-Precision Inference Optimization
papers.research_question: How can automated circuit discovery be accelerated while maintaining faithfulness, addressing its computational inefficiency and high memory requirements?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PAHQ, a training-free mixed-precision quantization method that accelerates automated circuit discovery by maintaining high precision for critical attention heads and reducing precision elsewhere, achieving significant speedup and memory reduction with minimal faithfulness loss.
papers.conclusion: PAHQ provides an efficient acceleration approach for mechanistic interpretability research without sacrificing analytical quality, making circuit discovery more computationally feasible.
papers.key_findings:
PAHQ-accelerated ACDC reduces runtime by up to 80% and memory consumption by up to 30% compared to unaccelerated ACDC while maintaining faithfulness.
PAHQ outperforms RTN quantization and Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) in terms of AUC-ROC on circuit discovery tasks like IOI, Docstring, and Greater Than.
The method is training-free and readily integrates with existing edge-based circuit discovery techniques by modifying the attention computation mechanism.
PAHQ's selective precision allocation and three-stream parallel scheduler effectively mask data transfer latency, enabling near-optimal throughput.
The method scales effectively to larger transformer models (GPT-2-medium, large, XL) while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.limitation:
PAHQ is designed for algorithms that evaluate edges sequentially (like ACDC) and may not be as effective for methods that evaluate multiple edges simultaneously (like EAP).
PAHQ makes circuit discovery more feasible for moderately larger models but does not solve the scalability challenge for foundation models with hundreds of billions of parameters.
The method is empirically validated but lacks theoretical analysis on how high-precision signals propagate through lower-precision layers.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery, which involves identifying sparse and task-relevant subnetworks in pre-trained language models, is a cornerstone of mechanistic interpretability. Automated Circuit Discovery (ACDC) has emerged as a pivotal methodology in circuit discovery, but its application to large language models is severely limited by computational inefficiency and prohibitively high memory requirements. Although several accelerated approaches have been proposed, they primarily rely on linear approximations to ACDC, which significantly compromises analytical faithfulness. Our proposed method for accelerating automated circuit discovery, Per Attention Head Quantization (PAHQ), takes a fundamentally different approach by optimizing the efficiency of each individual patching operation. PAHQ leverages a fundamental alignment between activation patching and mixed-precision quantization (MPQ): interpretability analysis through patching essentially performs targeted ablation studies. Therefore, we can maintain high precision exclusively for investigated components while safely reducing precision elsewhere in the network. PAHQ-accelerated ACDC reduces runtime by up to 80\% and memory consumption by up to 30\% compared to unaccelerated ACDC while maintaining faithfulness. Importantly, our method readily integrates with existing edge-based circuit discovery techniques by modifying the attention computation mechanism. This training-free approach provides a practical and novel pathway for accelerating mechanistic interpretability methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/626619403/PAHQ.

papers.title: Using explainability to design physics-aware CNNs for solving subsurface inverse problems
papers.research_question: How can explainability techniques be used to design physics-aware convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for solving subsurface inverse problems?
papers.core_contribution: A framework for using explainability techniques (Score-CAM and Deep SHAP) to iteratively select CNN hyperparameters (e.g., kernel size, network depth) to develop physics-aware models for subsurface imaging that maintain high predictive accuracy while improving descriptive accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that explainability methods (Score-CAM and Deep SHAP) can be used to iteratively tune CNN hyperparameters, leading to physics-aware models with high descriptive accuracy without compromising predictive accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Initial deep CNNs (Transpose Convolution and Dense networks) had good predictive accuracy but low descriptive accuracy, as they focused on non-physical, low-power regions in the input dispersion images.
Changing the kernel size from 3x3 to 3x1 in deep networks did not significantly change predictive accuracy but showed slightly better descriptive accuracy.
Reducing network depth (shallow networks) improved descriptive accuracy, with the shallow 3x1 kernel network focusing primarily on the physically meaningful high-power modal trend in the dispersion images.
The shallow 3x1 kernel CNN is recommended as it achieves high descriptive accuracy (making logical, physics-aware predictions) without a considerable loss in predictive accuracy.
papers.limitation: The shallow network recommended is sensitive to noisy inputs and may require additional denoising layers for field applications.
future_direction: Adding denoising layers to the shallow network for robustness to noisy field data.
Extending the framework to tune more hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: We present a novel method of using explainability techniques to design physics-aware neural networks. We demonstrate our approach by developing a convolutional neural network (CNN) for solving an inverse problem for shallow subsurface imaging. Although CNNs have gained popularity in recent years across many fields, the development of CNNs remains an art, as there are no clear guidelines regarding the selection of hyperparameters that will yield the best network. While optimization algorithms may be used to select hyperparameters automatically, these methods focus on developing networks with high predictive accuracy while disregarding model explainability (descriptive accuracy). However, the field of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) addresses the absence of model explainability by providing tools that allow developers to evaluate the internal logic of neural networks. In this study, we use the explainability methods Score-CAM and Deep SHAP to select hyperparameters, such as kernel sizes and network depth, to develop a physics-aware CNN for shallow subsurface imaging. We begin with a relatively deep Encoder-Decoder network, which uses surface wave dispersion images as inputs and generates 2D shear wave velocity subsurface images as outputs. Through model explanations, we ultimately find that a shallow CNN using two convolutional layers with an atypical kernel size of 3x1 yields comparable predictive accuracy but with increased descriptive accuracy. We also show that explainability methods can be used to evaluate the network's complexity and decision-making. We believe this method can be used to develop neural networks with high predictive accuracy while also providing inherent explainability.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety -- A Review
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes mechanistic interpretability research, establishing foundational concepts, surveying methodologies, and examining its relevance to AI safety, while advocating for future directions.
papers.limitation:
Scalability challenges and risks of human reliance.
Cherry-picking and streetlight interpretability.
future_direction: Clarifying concepts and integrating with existing literature.
Setting standards through metrics, benchmarks, and algorithmic testbeds.
Scaling up techniques to handle complex models and behaviors.
Expanding scope to vision, multimodal, and reinforcement learning models.
papers.abstract: Understanding AI systems' inner workings is critical for ensuring value alignment and safety. This review explores mechanistic interpretability: reverse engineering the computational mechanisms and representations learned by neural networks into human-understandable algorithms and concepts to provide a granular, causal understanding. We establish foundational concepts such as features encoding knowledge within neural activations and hypotheses about their representation and computation. We survey methodologies for causally dissecting model behaviors and assess the relevance of mechanistic interpretability to AI safety. We examine benefits in understanding, control, alignment, and risks such as capability gains and dual-use concerns. We investigate challenges surrounding scalability, automation, and comprehensive interpretation. We advocate for clarifying concepts, setting standards, and scaling techniques to handle complex models and behaviors and expand to domains such as vision and reinforcement learning. Mechanistic interpretability could help prevent catastrophic outcomes as AI systems become more powerful and inscrutable.

papers.title: LLMs learn governing principles of dynamical systems, revealing an in-context neural scaling law
papers.research_question: Can LLMs learn the governing principles of dynamical systems from in-context data, and does the accuracy of learned rules scale with context length?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can learn the probabilistic transition rules of various dynamical systems from in-context data without fine-tuning, and the accuracy of the learned rules follows a power-law scaling with context length, revealing an in-context neural scaling law.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained LLMs can accurately recover the probabilistic transition rules underlying deterministic, chaotic, and stochastic time series when provided with sufficient context, and this learning follows an in-context scaling law.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs (LLaMA-13b, LLaMA-70b) can accurately predict the next state in time series from stochastic, chaotic, continuous, and discrete dynamical systems without any fine-tuning or prompt engineering.
The discrepancy between the learned transition rules and ground truth decreases as a power law with the length of the observed time series, indicating an in-context neural scaling law.
The introduced Hierarchy-PDF algorithm efficiently extracts probability density functions for multi-digit numbers from LLM predictions.
For deterministic systems, the squared deviations from the mean (SDM) loss is more stable than the Bhattacharyya distance for capturing learning dynamics.
LLMs can learn both the mean and variance of next-state distributions for stochastic systems, as demonstrated on the noisy logistic map and geometric Brownian motion.
papers.limitation:
Although unlikely, the possibility of data leakage (memorization) cannot be completely ruled out and requires rigorous testing in future work.
The study does not evaluate newer models like LLaMA-3 due to time and computational constraints, limiting the comprehensiveness of the findings.
future_direction: Investigating how LLMs encode spatio-temporal features in stochastic dynamical time series and how they represent the learned transition rules.
Examining how LLMs perform subtasks necessary for learning stochastic dynamical systems, such as collecting Markovian transition statistics from discrete data and performing density estimation.
Assessing to what extent training on natural language enhances a transformer's mathematical ability to in-context learn dynamical systems, and vice-versa.
papers.abstract: Pretrained large language models (LLMs) are surprisingly effective at performing zero-shot tasks, including time-series forecasting. However, understanding the mechanisms behind such capabilities remains highly challenging due to the complexity of the models. We study LLMs' ability to extrapolate the behavior of dynamical systems whose evolution is governed by principles of physical interest. Our results show that LLaMA 2, a language model trained primarily on texts, achieves accurate predictions of dynamical system time series without fine-tuning or prompt engineering. Moreover, the accuracy of the learned physical rules increases with the length of the input context window, revealing an in-context version of neural scaling law. Along the way, we present a flexible and efficient algorithm for extracting probability density functions of multi-digit numbers directly from LLMs.

papers.title: Differentiable Autoencoding Neural Operator for Interpretable and Integrable Latent Space Modeling
papers.research_question: How to achieve interpretable latent space modeling in scientific machine learning by integrating differentiable PDE solvers for physics-consistent dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DIANO, a deterministic autoencoding neural operator framework that constructs interpretable latent spaces for dimensionality and geometric reduction, with integrated differentiable PDE solvers for physics-consistent temporal evolution.
papers.conclusion: DIANO demonstrates capability for interpretable and integrable latent space modeling, enabling dimensional and geometrical reduction with physics-based dynamics for complex spatio-temporal flows.
papers.key_findings:
DIANO produces interpretable latent vorticity structures with fewer Fourier modes, balancing reconstruction accuracy and interpretability.
DIANO enables temporal evolution of latent states using integrated PDE solvers, accurately predicting future flow fields.
The framework supports geometrical reduction from 2D to 1D, solving reduced PDEs in latent space and reconstructing to original geometry.
DIANO outperforms baseline models like CNO, CNN-AE, and NN-AE in terms of latent space interpretability and reconstruction error.
Solving lower-fidelity PDEs in latent space allows trade-offs between solver complexity, efficiency, and accuracy.
papers.abstract: Scientific machine learning has enabled the extraction of physical insights from high-dimensional spatiotemporal flow data using linear and nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques. Despite these advances, achieving interpretability within the latent space remains a challenge. To address this, we propose the DIfferentiable Autoencoding Neural Operator (DIANO), a deterministic autoencoding neural operator framework that constructs physically interpretable latent spaces for both dimensional and geometric reduction, with the provision to enforce differential governing equations directly within the latent space. Built upon neural operators, DIANO compresses high-dimensional input functions into a low-dimensional latent space via spatial coarsening through an encoding neural operator and subsequently reconstructs the original inputs using a decoding neural operator through spatial refinement. We assess DIANO's latent space interpretability and performance in dimensionality reduction against baseline models, including the Convolutional Neural Operator and standard autoencoders. Furthermore, a fully differentiable partial differential equation (PDE) solver is developed and integrated within the latent space, enabling the temporal advancement of both high- and low-fidelity PDEs, thereby embedding physical priors into the latent dynamics. We further investigate various PDE formulations, including the 2D unsteady advection-diffusion and the 3D Pressure-Poisson equation, to examine their influence on shaping the latent flow representations. Benchmark problems considered include flow past a 2D cylinder, flow through a 2D symmetric stenosed artery, and a 3D patient-specific coronary artery. These case studies demonstrate DIANO's capability to solve PDEs within a latent space that facilitates both dimensional and geometrical reduction while allowing latent interpretability.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: Exploration and adaptation of large language models for specialized domains
papers.research_question: Can large language models overcome challenges in specialized domains, and how can they be effectively adapted to domain-specific requirements?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation provides insights into the inner workings of LLMs and proposes adaptation methods that demonstrate LLMs can be effectively used in specialized domains, particularly clinical NLP.
papers.conclusion: The work provides new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models and multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.
papers.key_findings:
Layers of Transformer-based LLMs encode different dimensions of input text, with contextual representations and general language knowledge being beneficial for complex tasks.
Pre-trained language models outperform traditional approaches on clinical tasks.
Integration of domain-specific resources (like ICD hierarchy) improves model generalization.
Behavioral testing framework can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts.
Prototypical networks can provide interpretable diagnosis predictions.
papers.limitation: There is no ground truth in clinical data
future_direction: Integration of multimodal and multilingual data
Efficient methods for large language models
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed the field of natural language processing (NLP). Their improved performance on various NLP benchmarks makes them a promising tool—also for the application in specialized domains. Such domains are characterized by highly trained professionals with particular domain expertise. Since these experts are rare, improving the efficiency of their work with automated systems is especially desirable. However, domain-specific text resources hold various challenges for NLP systems. These challenges include distinct language, noisy and scarce data, and a high level of variation. Further, specialized domains present an increased need for transparent systems since they are often applied in high stakes settings. In this dissertation, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can overcome some of these challenges and propose methods to effectively adapt them to domain-specific requirements. We first investigate the inner workings and abilities of LLMs and show how they can fill the gaps that are present in previous NLP algorithms for specialized domains. To this end, we explore the sources of errors produced by earlier systems to identify which of them can be addressed by using LLMs. Following this, we take a closer look at how information is processed within Transformer-based LLMs to better understand their capabilities. We find that their layers encode different dimensions of the input text. Here, the contextual vector representation, and the general language knowledge learned during pre-training are especially beneficial for solving complex and multi-step tasks common in specialized domains. Following this exploration, we propose solutions for further adapting LLMs to the requirements of domain-specific tasks. We focus on the clinical domain, which incorporates many typical challenges found in specialized domains. We show how to improve generalization by integrating different domain-specific resources into our models. We further analyze the behavior of the produced models and propose a behavioral testing framework that can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts. Finally, we present an approach for incorporating the benefits of LLMs while fulfilling requirements such as interpretability and modularity. The presented solutions show improvements in performance on benchmark datasets and in manually conducted analyses with medical professionals. Our work provides both new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models as well as multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: Translation Equivariant Transformer Neural Processes
papers.research_question: How to incorporate translation equivariance into transformer neural processes to improve their performance on spatio-temporal data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces translation equivariant transformer neural processes (TE-TNPs) by developing translation equivariant attention mechanisms, improving performance on spatio-temporal tasks.
papers.conclusion: TE-TNPs and TE-PT-TNPs are effective and versatile models that incorporate translation equivariance, performing on par or better than state-of-the-art NPs, though with increased computational cost.
papers.key_findings:
TE-TNPs outperform non-translation-equivariant TNPs and other NP baselines on synthetic 1-D regression, especially when test data is shifted.
TE-PT-TNPs achieve state-of-the-art performance on image completion tasks with MNIST and CIFAR10.
TE-PT-TNPs significantly outperform other models on Kolmogorov flow and environmental data modelling.
Translation equivariance helps models generalize to inputs outside the training range.
Dynamically updating input locations improves performance for complex input distributions.
papers.limitation:
Increased computational cost due to passing input locations through attention mechanisms at each layer.
Initialization of pseudo-locations in TE-PT-TNPs can lead to poor performance in pathological cases.
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of neural processes (NPs) in modelling posterior prediction maps -- the mapping from data to posterior predictive distributions -- has significantly improved since their inception. This improvement can be attributed to two principal factors: (1) advancements in the architecture of permutation invariant set functions, which are intrinsic to all NPs; and (2) leveraging symmetries present in the true posterior predictive map, which are problem dependent. Transformers are a notable development in permutation invariant set functions, and their utility within NPs has been demonstrated through the family of models we refer to as TNPs. Despite significant interest in TNPs, little attention has been given to incorporating symmetries. Notably, the posterior prediction maps for data that are stationary -- a common assumption in spatio-temporal modelling -- exhibit translation equivariance. In this paper, we introduce of a new family of translation equivariant TNPs that incorporate translation equivariance. Through an extensive range of experiments on synthetic and real-world spatio-temporal data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of TE-TNPs relative to their non-translation-equivariant counterparts and other NP baselines.

papers.title: Representation Mechanics: Invariant-Governed Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can neural networks with set-valued operations and learned selection achieve generalization by learning and preserving invariants, as evidenced by early phase transitions (the Platonic Spike)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Representation Mechanics, showing that neural networks with set-valued operations and learned selection can achieve generalization by learning invariants, as evidenced by the Platonic Spike (early phase transition where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that invariant-preserving inductive bias is sufficient for rule learning and that constructing reliable AI requires respecting the mechanics of representation (treating embeddings as physical objects with inertia, boundaries, and elasticity).
papers.key_findings:
Set-valued weights with learned selection lead to early phase transitions (Platonic Spike) where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy.
Classical activations (e.g., GELU, ELU, ReLU) interfere with basin preservation and cause overfitting or boundary erosion.
Basin preservation via path freezing can prevent catastrophic forgetting by maintaining separatrix integrity.
The Surgical Clutch mechanism allows for invariant maintenance under continual learning by dynamically routing gradients.
The architecture achieves high accuracy on synthetic logic and language tasks without relying on n-gram statistics.
papers.limitation: The current work uses explicit rule contexts, which may not be available in all domains, and the architecture has not yet been tested at scale.
future_direction: Testing the architecture at scale
Exploring amplification strategies (more branches, hierarchical scoring, contrastive loss)
Extending to domains without explicit rule contexts
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> We present Representation Mechanics, a theoretical and empirical framework characterizing learning in invariant-governed domains. We demonstrate that neural networks with set-valued operations (discrete potentials {-W, 0, +W}) and learned selection exhibit sharp phase transitions to generalization without pretraining. The Platonic Spike (Early Phase Transition)—where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy in early epochs—signals the discovery of structural invariants before instance memorization. We validate these findings on controlled synthetic tasks (spiral classification, closed-world logic, declarative language) to isolate geometric mechanics from natural language statistical confounds. We contrast this Form-First paradigm with diffusion-dominated learning and define the conditions (Basin Preservation and Friction Set tracking) required to maintain these invariants under continual learning pressure. Our results suggest that restricting representational freedom via discrete potentials is not a limitation but a necessary inductive bias for rule-consistent generalization.

papers.title: A Differential Manifold Perspective and Universality Analysis of Continuous Attractors in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we establish a unified mathematical framework to analyze continuous attractors in artificial neural networks from a differential manifold perspective?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a unified framework based on differential manifolds and Jacobian matrix analysis to study continuous attractors, demonstrating universal singular value stratification in classification networks and linking attractor dimensionality to eigenvalue/singular value structure.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a novel, unified approach to investigating continuous attractors via eigenvalue/singular value analysis of the Jacobian, validates the prevalence of stratification in classification networks, and lays a foundation for a general theory of attractors in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed differential manifold framework is compatible with prior conclusions about continuous attractors.
Continuous attractor phenomena are linked to eigenvalues of the local Jacobian matrix, with stratification indicating approximate attractor behavior.
Singular value stratification is universal across common classification models (MLP, CNN, ResNet) and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, Fruit).
The framework can determine the dimensionality of continuous attractors via the rank of the Jacobian.
Approximate continuous attractor behavior, indicated by eigenvalue/singular value stratification, emerges during neural network training and correlates with generalization.
papers.limitation:
Lacks a rigorous mathematical derivation extending eigenvalue stratification to singular value stratification.
The existence of continuous attractors in tasks beyond classification remains an open question.
future_direction: Develop a general theory of continuous attractors in neural networks.
Apply the methodology to deep neural networks to study optimization landscapes, generalization mechanisms, and training stability.
papers.abstract: Continuous attractors are critical for information processing in both biological and artificial neural systems, with implications for spatial navigation, memory, and deep learning optimization. However, existing research lacks a unified framework to analyze their properties across diverse dynamical systems, limiting cross-architectural generalizability. This study establishes a novel framework from the perspective of differential manifolds to investigate continuous attractors in artificial neural networks. It verifies compatibility with prior conclusions, elucidates links between continuous attractor phenomena and eigenvalues of the local Jacobian matrix, and demonstrates the universality of singular value stratification in common classification models and datasets. These findings suggest continuous attractors may be ubiquitous in general neural networks, highlighting the need for a general theory, with the proposed framework offering a promising foundation given the close mathematical connection between eigenvalues and singular values.

papers.title: Statistical Physics of Deep Neural Networks: Generalization Capability, Beyond the Infinite Width, and Feature Learning
papers.research_question: This thesis investigates three interconnected questions: (1) Can we derive an improved asymptotic bound on the generalization performance of DNNs? (2) How do DNNs behave in a thermodynamic limit where the number of training examples scales with the number of neurons per layer? (3) Do DNNs truly learn dataset features or merely memorize them?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis contributes three main results: (1) an improved asymptotic bound on generalization error that depends only on the last layer size, (2) a statistical mechanics framework for DNNs in a proportional regime beyond the infinite width limit, linking them to Student's t-processes, and (3) a task-explicit analysis showing conditions under which DNNs learn dataset features rather than memorizing.
papers.conclusion: The thesis demonstrates that statistical physics methods can provide significant insights into the generalization, behavior in proportional regimes, and feature learning of DNNs, contributing to more interpretable AI.
papers.key_findings:
An asymptotic generalization bound that depends only on the last layer size, improving classical statistical learning theory bounds.
A closed formula for the generalization error of a finite-width one-hidden layer network in the proportional regime.
An approximate expression for the partition function of deep neural networks in the proportional regime.
A link between deep neural networks in the proportional regime and Student's t-processes.
Evidence that DNNs can learn dataset features rather than memorizing, as shown by analyzing the volume of the solution space and Gaussianity breaking.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at many tasks, often rivaling or surpassing human performance. Yet their internal processes remain elusive, frequently described as "black boxes." While performance can be refined experimentally, achieving a fundamental grasp of their inner workings is still a challenge. Statistical Mechanics has long tackled computational problems, and this thesis applies physics-based insights to understand DNNs via three complementary approaches. First, by averaging over data, we derive an asymptotic bound on generalization that depends solely on the size of the last layer, rather than on the total number of parameters -- revealing how deep architectures process information differently across layers. Second, adopting a data-dependent viewpoint, we explore a finite-width thermodynamic limit beyond the infinite-width regime. This leads to: (i) a closed-form expression for the generalization error in a finite-width one-hidden-layer network (regression task); (ii) an approximate partition function for deeper architectures; and (iii) a link between deep networks in this thermodynamic limit and Student's t-processes. Finally, from a task-explicit perspective, we present a preliminary analysis of how DNNs interact with a controlled dataset, investigating whether they truly internalize its structure -- collapsing to the teacher -- or merely memorize it. By understanding when a network must learn data structure rather than just memorize, it sheds light on fostering meaningful internal representations. In essence, this thesis leverages the synergy between Statistical Physics and Machine Learning to illuminate the inner behavior of DNNs.

papers.title: Gradient Routing: Masking Gradients to Localize Computation in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can gradient routing, a training method that applies data-dependent masks to gradients, be used to localize capabilities to specific subregions of neural networks for interpretability, unlearning, and oversight?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces gradient routing, a training method that uses data-dependent gradient masks to localize capabilities to specific subregions of neural networks, enabling interpretable representations, robust unlearning, and scalable oversight.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that gradient routing is a promising localization technique for real-world applications with scarce quality data, and may address limitations of black-box training in high-stakes machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient routing can partition learned representations in an interpretable way, as demonstrated by splitting MNIST digit encodings into non-overlapping halves.
Gradient routing enables robust unlearning via ablation of a pre-specified network subregion, outperforming data filtering when labels are limited.
Gradient routing allows scalable oversight in reinforcement learning by localizing modules responsible for different behaviors, even with limited labeled data.
Gradient routing exhibits an absorption effect, where localization applied to narrow data (e.g., specific tokens) generalizes to broader capabilities (e.g., semantic concepts).
Gradient routing can localize concepts to individual dimensions of the residual stream, enabling model steering with a single scalar value.
papers.limitation:
Clean separation of representations in the MNIST autoencoder depends on specific problem setup and heavy L1 regularization.
The learning dynamics of gradient routing, including potential 'internal tug of war' effects, remain an open question.
The reinforcement learning environment used is simple and may not reflect the complexity of real-world problems.
future_direction: Further investigation into the learning dynamics of gradient routing.
Application of gradient routing to more complex environments and larger models.
Empirical and conceptual work needed for scalable oversight in real-world settings.
