papers.abstract: Neural networks are trained primarily based on their inputs and outputs, without regard for their internal mechanisms. These neglected mechanisms determine properties that are critical for safety, like (i) transparency; (ii) the absence of sensitive information or harmful capabilities; and (iii) reliable generalization of goals beyond the training distribution. To address this shortcoming, we introduce gradient routing, a training method that isolates capabilities to specific subregions of a neural network. Gradient routing applies data-dependent, weighted masks to gradients during backpropagation. These masks are supplied by the user in order to configure which parameters are updated by which data points. We show that gradient routing can be used to (1) learn representations which are partitioned in an interpretable way; (2) enable robust unlearning via ablation of a pre-specified network subregion; and (3) achieve scalable oversight of a reinforcement learner by localizing modules responsible for different behaviors. Throughout, we find that gradient routing localizes capabilities even when applied to a limited, ad-hoc subset of the data. We conclude that the approach holds promise for challenging, real-world applications where quality data are scarce.

papers.title: Encoding and Understanding Astrophysical Information in Large Language Model-Generated Summaries
papers.research_question: To what extent does prompt engineering affect the correlation between text embeddings and physical quantities, and how is physics information encoded in text summaries?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can encode physical information from astrophysical text, with structured prompting improving alignment between embeddings and physical quantities, and sparse autoencoders reveal the semantic concepts driving this encoding.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can capture, learn, and represent physics concepts in textual data, and prompt engineering enhances the correlation between text embeddings and physical quantities. Sparse autoencoders provide insight into the semantic concepts underlying this encoding.
papers.key_findings:
Structured prompts significantly improve the clustering purity of LLM embeddings with respect to physical quantities, with improvements up to 57.5% for variability index.
Sparse autoencoders extract interpretable features from text embeddings that correlate with specific astrophysical properties, such as non-thermal characteristics linked to power-law gamma values.
LLMs infer physical parameters from text descriptions even when numerical values are not explicitly stated, demonstrating an understanding of astrophysical concepts.
Concepts like 'eclipsing binaries' and 'galaxy cluster thermal dynamics' are encoded in the embeddings and associated with physical measurements.
The method allows for visual and quantitative analysis of how physics is encoded in language through t-SNE clustering and SAE feature activation.
future_direction: Expanding the dataset to include more sources
Optimizing prompting with different models
Creating an interface for astronomer validation of possibly anomalous objects
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated the ability to generalize well at many levels across domains, modalities, and even shown in-context learning capabilities. This enables research questions regarding how they can be used to encode physical information that is usually only available from scientific measurements, and loosely encoded in textual descriptions. Using astrophysics as a test bed, we investigate if LLM embeddings can codify physical summary statistics that are obtained from scientific measurements through two main questions: 1) Does prompting play a role on how those quantities are codified by the LLM? and 2) What aspects of language are most important in encoding the physics represented by the measurement? We investigate this using sparse autoencoders that extract interpretable features from the text.

papers.title: Getting a CLUE: A Method for Explaining Uncertainty Estimates
papers.research_question: How can we interpret uncertainty estimates from probabilistic models by finding counterfactual explanations that indicate how to change an input to make the model more confident?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Counterfactual Latent Uncertainty Explanations (CLUE), a method to generate counterfactual explanations for uncertainty estimates by searching in the latent space of a deep generative model, and proposes a framework for evaluating such explanations.
papers.conclusion: CLUE is an effective method for generating counterfactual explanations of uncertainty, outperforming baselines and helping practitioners understand sources of uncertainty.
papers.key_findings:
CLUE outperforms baseline methods in explaining uncertainty across multiple datasets.
CLUE generates counterfactuals that are on the data manifold and plausible.
The proposed computational evaluation framework allows for quantitative assessment of counterfactual explanations.
User studies demonstrate that CLUE helps practitioners predict on which new inputs a BNN will be uncertain.
papers.limitation:
CLUE relies on the quality of the auxiliary deep generative model; if the DGM fails to capture the data manifold, CLUE may generate unrealistic counterfactuals.
CLUE is designed for differentiable probabilistic models, which may limit its applicability.
future_direction: Extending CLUE to other types of uncertainty estimates.
Exploring the use of CLUE in active learning and Bayesian optimization.
Investigating other distance metrics for the counterfactual search.
papers.abstract: Both uncertainty estimation and interpretability are important factors for trustworthy machine learning systems. However, there is little work at the intersection of these two areas. We address this gap by proposing a novel method for interpreting uncertainty estimates from differentiable probabilistic models, like Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). Our method, Counterfactual Latent Uncertainty Explanations (CLUE), indicates how to change an input, while keeping it on the data manifold, such that a BNN becomes more confident about the input's prediction. We validate CLUE through 1) a novel framework for evaluating counterfactual explanations of uncertainty, 2) a series of ablation experiments, and 3) a user study. Our experiments show that CLUE outperforms baselines and enables practitioners to better understand which input patterns are responsible for predictive uncertainty.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: Explaining the Machine Learning Solution of the Ising Model
papers.research_question: How can we explain the results from machine learning models applied to the Ising model? Specifically, how do PCA and a simple neural network identify phases and the critical temperature?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that PCA identifies the order parameter and temperature as the control variable, and that a single-layer neural network informed by symmetry can accurately predict the critical temperature, with the explanation revealing that the network learns to use the magnetization direction.
papers.conclusion: The explanation of the strategies used by simpler ML models indicates the directions that can be taken to fully explain more sophisticated ones, opening the ML black-boxes and paving the way to extract physical laws from model parameters.
papers.key_findings:
PCA not only identifies the magnetization as the order parameter but also shows that the greatest variance is in the direction of the temperature gradient.
A single-layer neural network (SLNN) with no hidden layers, informed by spin inversion symmetry, can accurately estimate the critical temperature of the Ising model.
The SLNN works by aligning its weight vector with the magnetization direction and scaling the argument to separate phases.
A one-hidden-layer NN with two units can solve the general case without sign restriction, and the output layer combines the hidden units' outputs to correct labeling.
The explanation allows predicting the minimal NN architecture needed for more complex phase transitions.
papers.limitation:
The method may require more hidden units or non-linear techniques for more complex phase diagrams.
It has not yet been possible to extract physical laws from the inferred parameters.
future_direction: Applying the method to other physics systems with more general phase transitions, both classical and quantum.
Extracting physical laws from the parameters of the models.
papers.abstract: As powerful as machine learning (ML) techniques are in solving problems involving data with large dimensionality, explaining the results from the fitted parameters remains a challenging task of utmost importance, especially in physics applications. This work shows how this can be accomplished for the ferromagnetic Ising model, the main target of several ML studies in statistical physics. Here it is demonstrated that the successful unsupervised identification of the phases and order parameter by principal component analysis, a common method in those studies, detects that the magnetization per spin has its greatest variation with the temperature, the actual control parameter of the phase transition. Then, by using a neural network (NN) without hidden layers (the simplest possible) and informed by the symmetry of the Hamiltonian, an explanation is provided for the strategy used in finding the supervised learning solution for the critical temperature of the model's continuous phase transition. This allows the prediction of the minimal extension of the NN to solve the problem when the symmetry is not known, which becomes also explainable. These results pave the way to a physics-informed explainable generalized framework, enabling the extraction of physical laws and principles from the parameters of the models.

papers.title: Efficient Representations are Controllable Representations
papers.research_question: What is the most brute-force way to install interpretable, controllable features into a model’s activations? Can a model's efficiency pressure be exploited to induce interpretable, controllable representations?
papers.core_contribution: By finetuning an LLM with a simple auxiliary loss to write binary feature classifications into a small set of residual stream dimensions, the model reorganizes to depend on these flags, making them genuine internal features that can be used to steer generation at inference time. This works due to the model's efficiency pressure under capacity constraints.
papers.conclusion: The residual stream is writable, and a model's own efficiency pressure can be exploited to induce interpretable and controllable representations. This inverts the usual controllability problem by providing signals that the model will naturally consolidate around.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns to write correct feature flags to the designated 'fenced' dimensions after training.
The model learns to depend on these flags during generation, as shown by overwriting experiments that causally steer generation.
The model erodes its own alternative representations of the fenced features, consolidating feature information into the fenced dimensions.
The efficiency pressure (representational cost) leads the model to consolidate around the reliably supplied feature signals.
The method incurs a negligible perplexity cost when fencing a small number of dimensions, but the cost grows as more dimensions are fenced.
papers.limitation:
Early layers (k < 5) struggle to produce clean flags, consistent with the view that early layers have not yet derived the relevant features.
At the current level of training, the model has begun to erode previous representations but some residual information persists in the remaining dimensions.
papers.abstract: What is the most brute-force way to install interpretable, controllable features into a model's activations? Controlling how LLMs internally represent concepts typically requires sophisticated methods to first identify, then intervene on the model's existing feature geometry. We bypass all of this. We finetune an LLM with a simple auxiliary loss, training 16 of its 3072 residual stream dimensions to be inert interpretability flags that simply indicate what concepts are required for generation. The model reorganizes around them anyway, learning to rely on these flags during actual generation tasks. As a result, these inert flags become genuine internal features: interpretable control switches that allow us to steer generation at inference time. Why does this work? When a feature is reliably supplied at a fixed location, gradient descent gradually eliminates redundant encodings elsewhere, and the model erodes its own alternative representations. A model's efficiency pressure is a lever - exploitable to induce interpretable, controllable representations.

papers.title: Does TabPFN Understand Causal Structures?
papers.research_question: Does TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model, encode causal knowledge in its internal representations beyond statistical correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and introduces an adapter framework that can extract this information for causal discovery, outperforming traditional statistical methods.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and the proposed adapter framework can extract this information for causal discovery, establishing a new direction for interpretable and adaptable tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Causal information is concentrated in the middle layers (4-6) of TabPFN's encoder.
The proposed framework extracts causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and outperforms statistical baselines (GIES, IGSP, DCDI) on ROC AUC, performing closely to the specialized neural causal discovery model A VICI.
The decoder architecture is crucial for performance; using a learnable decoder significantly improves results compared to using no decoder.
Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, particularly for dense graph structures like Erdős-Rényi and Stochastic Block Model graphs.
Using embeddings from the pre-trained TabPFN encoder (optimal weights) yields better causal discovery performance than using randomly initialized or degraded encoder weights.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, and the approach is sensitive to the type of graph structure.
future_direction: Leveraging pre-trained tabular models for extracting causal structures and improving their interpretability.
Understanding how tabular foundation models reason about different datasets.
Repurposing tabular foundation models for different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Causal discovery is fundamental for multiple scientific domains, yet extracting causal information from real world data remains a significant challenge. Given the recent success on real data, we investigate whether TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model pre-trained on synthetic datasets generated from structural causal models, encodes causal information in its internal representations. We develop an adapter framework using a learnable decoder and causal tokens that extract causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and decode them into adjacency matrices for causal discovery. Our evaluations demonstrate that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, outperforming several traditional causal discovery algorithms, with such causal information being concentrated in mid-range layers. These findings establish a new direction for interpretable and adaptable foundation models and demonstrate the potential for leveraging pre-trained tabular models for causal discovery.

papers.title: Neural Networks as Physics-Consistent Surrogates: An \textit{Explainable AI} Validation Framework for Learning Constitutive Relations
papers.research_question: How can neural networks for constitutive modeling of solid materials be validated and interpreted to confirm they learn physically meaningful principles rather than merely curve-fitting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops and applies a Physics-Explainable AI (XAI) framework to validate that neural network surrogates for constitutive modeling learn underlying physical mechanisms (stiffness, history-dependence, temporal damping) rather than just curve-fitting.
papers.conclusion: The Physics-XAI framework successfully validates that neural constitutive models learn physically interpretable representations of stiffness, path dependence, and fractional-order memory, transforming them from black boxes into transparent, mechanically grounded glass boxes.
papers.key_findings:
For hyperelasticity, gradient-based attributions (Grad Input and Integrated Gradients) match the analytical tangent modulus, proving the network learned material stiffness.
For elastoplasticity, SHAP and PCA show the RNN internalizes path-dependent memory, with plastic strain identified as the dominant feature governing stress prediction.
For viscoelasticity, latent-space and wavelet analyses of GRU layers reveal a temporal hierarchy encoding instantaneous elastic response, intermediate relaxation, and long-term fractional memory.
The Physics-Aware Distillation (PAD) procedure extracts interpretable material constants (e.g., Mooney-Rivlin coefficients) from the trained neural networks.
Quantitative metrics (MSE, MAE, R2, attribution correlations) confirm high fidelity and physical consistency across all three material models.
papers.limitation: The work focuses on uniaxial settings and noise-free synthetic data.
future_direction: Extend to multiaxial loading, anisotropic materials, and experimental datasets.
Integrate XAI with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs).
Incorporate uncertainty quantification and robustness analysis for verification and validation.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a Physics-\textit{Explainable AI} (XAI) framework to validate and interpret neural networks for the constitutive modeling of solid materials. The study bridges the gap between data-driven models and continuum mechanics by applying a suite of explainability methods to neural networks trained on three distinct material behaviors: hyperelasticity (\textit{Mooney-Rivlin}), elastoplasticity (\textit{Chaboche}), and viscoelasticity (\textit{Fractional Zener}). First, high-fidelity surrogate models, including dense feed-forward networks, LSTMs, and GRUs, are trained on synthetically generated data to accurately capture complex material responses. The core of the work then employs XAI techniques to "open the black box" and confirm that the networks learn physically meaningful principles. For hyperelasticity, gradient-based attributions (\textit{Grad Input} (GI)) successfully match the analytical tangent modulus, proving the network learned material stiffness. For elastoplasticity, \textit{SHapley Additive exPlanations} (SHAP) and \textit{Principal Component Analysis} (PCA) demonstrate the \textit{Recurrent Neural Network} (RNN) internalizes path-dependent memory, with SHAP identifying \textit{plastic strain} as the dominant feature governing the stress prediction. For viscoelasticity, latent-space and wavelet analyses of the \textit{Gated Recurrent Unit. } GRU layers reveal a clear temporal hierarchy, with different layers encoding instantaneous elastic response, intermediate relaxation, and long-term fractional memory. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that the XAI framework can verify that the neural networks are not merely curve-fitting but are, in fact, learning the underlying physical mechanisms of stiffness, history-dependence, and temporal damping.

papers.title: Do Llamas understand the periodic table?
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) represent the periodic table of elements, and what is the geometric structure of their hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally develop structured geometric representations (a 3D spiral) of the periodic table in their hidden states, with knowledge encoded as continuous manifolds in middle layers that sharpen into categorical distinctions in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs represent symbolic scientific knowledge as coherent, geometry-aware manifolds that reflect the natural order of the physical world, which can inform interpretability and trust in LLMs for scientific applications.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure in LLM hidden states aligns with the conceptual organization of the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous, overlapping attribute subspaces, while deeper layers sharpen decision boundaries and integrate linguistic context.
Linguistic structure increasingly shapes factual representations in later layers.
Strong linear associations between related attributes in middle layers enable indirect recall.
Regression probing shows continuous numerical features are effectively represented in intermediate layers, while classification probing shows later layers are better for fine-grained categorical decisions.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to chemical elements in the periodic table; future studies could expand to other chemical structures and properties.
The hypothesis-driven validation of geometric structures may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Expand to other chemical structures and properties.
Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge.
papers.abstract: We observe a 3D spiral structure in the hidden states of LLMs that aligns with the conceptual structure of the periodic table.

papers.title: Data-Driven Insights into Jet Turbulence: Explainable AI Approaches
papers.research_question: Which regions of a turbulent jet flow field are most relevant for prediction by a neural network, and how do different XAI methods compare in identifying these regions?
papers.core_contribution: Applying XAI methods to a turbulent jet prediction model reveals that regions of moderate vorticity, rather than high vorticity, are most important for prediction, and these regions correspond to areas of high dissipation. Gradient-based methods (Grad-CAM and Gradient-SHAP) provide a less biased view compared to SHAP.
papers.conclusion: XAI methods applied to a jet turbulence prediction model show that regions of moderate vorticity are key for prediction and are linked to high dissipation. Gradient-based methods avoid segmentation bias and highlight uniformly distributed, nearly circular structures associated with vortex rings and turbulent mixing.
papers.key_findings:
The most relevant flow structures for prediction are not those with high vorticity but those with moderate vorticity (ω*_z between 0.25 and 0.5).
Structures with high normalized Shapley values coincide with those contributing most to turbulent kinetic energy dissipation.
Grad-CAM and Gradient-SHAP identify regions with uniform spatial distribution, suggesting correlation with momentum transport by smaller-scale vortices.
The identified structures by Grad-CAM and Gradient-SHAP are often nearly circular (shape factor close to 1), indicating vortex rings are dominant in energy transfer and mixing.
Compared to SHAP, Grad-CAM and Gradient-SHAP do not require pre-segmentation and thus avoid bias, providing a more direct identification of physically significant regions.
papers.limitation: SHAP requires pre-defined segmentation of the flow field into regions, which may introduce bias in identifying relevant features.
papers.abstract: In this study, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods are applied to analyze flow fields obtained through PIV measurements of an axisymmetric turbulent jet. A convolutional neural network (U-Net) was trained to predict velocity fields at subsequent time steps. Three XAI methods: SHapley Additive explanations (SHAP), Gradient-SHAP, and Grad-CAM were employed to identify the flow field regions relevant for prediction. SHAP requires predefined segmentation of the flow field into relevant regions, while Gradient-SHAP and Grad-CAM avoid this bias by generating gradient-based heatmaps. The results show that the most relevant structures do not necessarily coincide with regions of maximum vorticity but rather with those exhibiting moderate vorticity, highlighting the critical role of these regions in energy transfer and jet dynamics. Additionally, structures with high turbulent dissipation values are identified as the most significant. Gradient-SHAP and Grad-CAM methods reveal a uniform spatial distribution of relevant regions, emphasizing the contribution of nearly circular structures to turbulent mixing. This study advances the understanding of turbulent dynamics through XAI tools, providing an innovative approach to correlate machine learning models with physical phenomena.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: A simple probabilistic neural network for machine understanding
papers.research_question: What are the properties of learning machines with a fixed internal representation, derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, in unsupervised learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM), a probabilistic neural network with a fixed internal representation derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, and shows that it has desirable properties like continuity, controllable compression, and ability to support functions beyond generalization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that learning machines with a fixed internal representation, such as the HFM, operate in a qualitatively different regime from traditional models like RBMs, with data-specific information stored in weights and potential for higher cognitive functions.
papers.key_findings:
The HFM is uniquely identified by the principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance when hidden units are binary.
The HFM exhibits a phase transition at a critical coupling parameter g, with a divergence in specific heat.
Training the HFM with an EM algorithm allows features to be learned sequentially, with low-order features remaining stable as new features are added.
The internal representation of the HFM is robust to changes in the coupling parameter and dataset size, and low-order features capture most of the relevant information.
The learning modality of HFM is qualitatively different from RBMs: in HFM, data-specific information is stored in the weights, while in RBMs it is transferred to the internal representation.
future_direction: Investigating whether a universal data-independent internal representation emerges spontaneously in deep layers of learning architectures.
Relating the findings to thermodynamic costs of learning.
Exploring the hypothesis that internal representations evolve with depth in hierarchical learning systems.
papers.abstract: We discuss probabilistic neural networks with a fixed internal representation as models for machine understanding. Here understanding is intended as mapping data to an already existing representation which encodes an {\em a priori} organisation of the feature space. We derive the internal representation by requiring that it satisfies the principles of maximal relevance and of maximal ignorance about how different features are combined. We show that, when hidden units are binary variables, these two principles identify a unique model -- the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM) -- which is fully solvable and provides a natural interpretation in terms of features. We argue that learning machines with this architecture enjoy a number of interesting properties, like the continuity of the representation with respect to changes in parameters and data, the possibility to control the level of compression and the ability to support functions that go beyond generalisation. We explore the behaviour of the model with extensive numerical experiments and argue that models where the internal representation is fixed reproduce a learning modality which is qualitatively different from that of traditional models such as Restricted Boltzmann Machines.

papers.title: Validating Mechanistic Interpretations: An Axiomatic Approach
papers.research_question: How can we formally characterize and validate mechanistic interpretations of neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a set of axioms that formally characterize a mechanistic interpretation as a description that approximately captures the semantics of a neural network in a compositional manner, and demonstrates their applicability for validation.
papers.conclusion: The axiomatic approach provides a rigorous foundation for validating mechanistic interpretations of neural networks, and its utility is demonstrated through case studies on modular addition and 2-SAT models.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed axioms provide a formal framework for validating mechanistic interpretations, requiring both component-wise and compositional evaluation.
In the 2-SAT case study, the model's first block parses the input formula into clauses, while the second block evaluates satisfiability via enumeration of variable assignments.
The axioms can reveal errors in interpretations that component-wise evaluation alone might miss, highlighting the importance of compositional validation.
The approach is successfully applied to validate an existing interpretation of a modular addition model and a new interpretation of a 2-SAT model.
The axioms are inspired by abstract interpretation and require the definition of abstraction and concretization functions to map between concrete and abstract representations.
papers.limitation:
The axioms are necessary but may not be sufficient in all cases for characterizing a mechanistic interpretation.
The axioms require the model's output to be discrete and necessitate the design of abstraction and concretization functions, which can be challenging.
future_direction: Extending the approach to analyze models trained for other problems.
Exploring the more informal axioms (Axioms 5 and 6) related to the compilability of the mechanistic interpretation.
Applying the framework to circuit-style interpretations, such as the Indirect Object Identification circuit.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse engineer the computation performed by a neural network in terms of its internal components. Although there is a growing body of research on mechanistic interpretation of neural networks, the notion of a mechanistic interpretation itself is often ad-hoc. Inspired by the notion of abstract interpretation from the program analysis literature that aims to develop approximate semantics for programs, we give a set of axioms that formally characterize a mechanistic interpretation as a description that approximately captures the semantics of the neural network under analysis in a compositional manner. We demonstrate the applicability of these axioms for validating mechanistic interpretations on an existing, well-known interpretability study as well as on a new case study involving a Transformer-based model trained to solve the well-known 2-SAT problem.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: From Kepler to Newton: Inductive Biases Guide Learned World Models in Transformers
papers.research_question: Why do transformers fail to learn the Newtonian world model for planetary motion, and how can we fix this problem?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that three minimal inductive biases—spatial smoothness, spatial stability, and temporal locality—enable generic Transformers to learn Newtonian world models for planetary motion, transitioning from curve-fitting (Keplerian) to mechanistic (Newtonian) understanding.
papers.conclusion: Simple inductive biases (spatial smoothness, stability, and temporal locality) are necessary and sufficient for transformers to learn world models, and true scientific understanding requires discovering governing mechanisms rather than just curve-fitting.
papers.key_findings:
Tokenization disrupts spatial smoothness and prevents the emergence of a high-quality spatial map in the embedding space.
Using continuous coordinates with noisy context learning (spatial stability) mitigates error accumulation and improves prediction accuracy over tokenized classification.
Short context lengths (temporal locality) induce Newtonian world models (force-based), while long context lengths induce Keplerian world models (geometry-based).
There is a phase transition between Keplerian and Newtonian world models as context length varies.
Regression models with continuous inputs outperform classification models with tokenization when hyperparameters are optimized.
papers.limitation:
The study simplified the setup of Vafa et al. by using one time-scale instead of two.
Linear probing only reveals implicit knowledge and requires knowing what to look for a priori; a fully autonomous 'AI Physicist' would need additional mechanisms for symbolic extraction.
papers.abstract: Can general-purpose AI architectures go beyond prediction to discover the physical laws governing the universe? True intelligence relies on "world models" -- causal abstractions that allow an agent to not only predict future states but understand the underlying governing dynamics. While previous "AI Physicist" approaches have successfully recovered such laws, they typically rely on strong, domain-specific priors that effectively "bake in" the physics. Conversely, Vafa et al. recently showed that generic Transformers fail to acquire these world models, achieving high predictive accuracy without capturing the underlying physical laws. We bridge this gap by systematically introducing three minimal inductive biases. We show that ensuring spatial smoothness (by formulating prediction as continuous regression) and stability (by training with noisy contexts to mitigate error accumulation) enables generic Transformers to surpass prior failures and learn a coherent Keplerian world model, successfully fitting ellipses to planetary trajectories. However, true physical insight requires a third bias: temporal locality. By restricting the attention window to the immediate past -- imposing the simple assumption that future states depend only on the local state rather than a complex history -- we force the model to abandon curve-fitting and discover Newtonian force representations. Our results demonstrate that simple architectural choices determine whether an AI becomes a curve-fitter or a physicist, marking a critical step toward automated scientific discovery.

papers.title: GPCR-BERT: Interpreting Sequential Design of G Protein Coupled Receptors Using Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the correlation between variations in conserved motifs of GPCRs and other amino acids? Can we predict missing residues and identify key contributing amino acids?
papers.core_contribution: Developed GPCR-BERT, a fine-tuned protein language model, to interpret sequential design of GPCRs, achieving high accuracy in predicting masked residues and identifying residue correlations through attention analysis.
papers.conclusion: GPCR-BERT effectively predicts residues and distinguishes GPCR classes, providing insights into functional relationships and potential applications in mutation studies and drug development.
papers.key_findings:
GPCR-BERT achieved high accuracy (up to 100%) in predicting masked residues in conserved motifs.
The model successfully clustered GPCRs of the same class in embedding space, indicating it captures class-specific features.
Attention analysis revealed correlations between masked residues and other amino acids, some of which align with experimental mutagenesis data.
The model's predictions for CWxP motif were less accurate, likely due to smaller dataset size.
GPCR-BERT outperformed BERT and SVM on the prediction tasks, demonstrating the advantage of protein-specific pre-training.
papers.limitation: The conserved motifs are not 100% conserved (e.g., CWxP motif is only 71% conserved), so the model might not apply to GPCRs with varied versions of the motifs.
papers.abstract: With the rise of Transformers and Large Language Models (LLMs) in Chemistry and Biology, new avenues for the design and understanding of therapeutics have opened up to the scientific community. Protein sequences can be modeled as language and can take advantage of recent advances in LLMs, specifically with the abundance of our access to the protein sequence datasets. In this paper, we developed the GPCR-BERT model for understanding the sequential design of G Protein-Coupled Receptors (GPCRs). GPCRs are the target of over one-third of FDA-approved pharmaceuticals. However, there is a lack of comprehensive understanding regarding the relationship between amino acid sequence, ligand selectivity, and conformational motifs (such as NPxxY, CWxP, E/DRY). By utilizing the pre-trained protein model (Prot-Bert) and fine-tuning with prediction tasks of variations in the motifs, we were able to shed light on several relationships between residues in the binding pocket and some of the conserved motifs. To achieve this, we took advantage of attention weights, and hidden states of the model that are interpreted to extract the extent of contributions of amino acids in dictating the type of masked ones. The fine-tuned models demonstrated high accuracy in predicting hidden residues within the motifs. In addition, the analysis of embedding was performed over 3D structures to elucidate the higher-order interactions within the conformations of the receptors.

papers.title: Unveiling the Mystery of Weight in Large Foundation Models: Gaussian Distribution Never Fades
papers.research_question: What are the distributional properties of weights in large foundation models, and how can these properties be leveraged to simplify model adaptation and editing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that weights in large foundation models follow a Gaussian distribution and that transformation weights can be derived from Gaussian noise, leading to a method that improves adaptation and editing by adjusting the standard deviation of the noise and updating outliers.
papers.conclusion: The Gaussian distribution of weights is a fundamental property that can be leveraged to simplify adaptation and editing, and optimal weights are sparse with a Gaussian-like distribution.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained weights of LFMs predominantly follow a Gaussian distribution.
Transformation weights (∆W) can be derived from Gaussian noise and primarily increase the standard deviation of pre-trained weights.
The standard deviation of transformation weights grows with layer depth.
Optimal weights should exhibit zero-mean, symmetry, and sparsity, with sparse values following a truncated Gaussian distribution and a few outliers.
Adaptation and editing can be improved by adjusting Gaussian signals and outliers.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a pioneering exploration of the mechanisms underlying large foundation models' (LFMs) weights, aiming to simplify AI research. Through extensive observation and analysis on prevailing LFMs, we find that regardless of initialization strategies, their weights predominantly follow a Gaussian distribution, with occasional sharp, inverted T-shaped, or linear patterns. We further discover that the weights share the i.i.d. properties of Gaussian noise, and explore their direct relationship. We find that transformation weights can be derived from Gaussian noise, and they primarily serve to increase the standard deviation of pre-trained weights, with their standard deviation growing with layer depth. In other words, transformation weights broaden the acceptable deviation from the optimal weights, facilitating adaptation to downstream tasks. Building upon the above conclusions, we thoroughly discussed the nature of optimal weights, ultimately concluding that they should exhibit zero-mean, symmetry, and sparsity, with the sparse values being a truncated Gaussian distribution and a few outliers. Our experiments in LFM adaptation and editing demonstrate the effectiveness of these insights. We hope these findings can provide a foundational understanding to pave the way for future advancements in the LFM community.

papers.title: Phase transition encoded in neural network
papers.research_question: How do temperature-supervised neural networks capture information of phase transition and what physical quantities do they learn?
papers.core_contribution: Temperature-supervised neural networks encode phase transition information in their weights, learning either magnetization or internal energy as features depending on network architecture and prediction accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks trained to predict temperature encode phase transition information in their weights, and the extracted physical quantity (magnetization or energy) depends on the network architecture and training accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
The fully-connected neural network learns magnetization from input spin configurations, and its weights show a drastic change at the critical temperature, enabling phase transition detection.
The convolutional neural network learns internal energy, achieves higher temperature prediction accuracy, and its weights are proportional to free energy, encoding phase transition information more implicitly.
The phase transition information is captured in the neural network weights even without explicit supervision of phase labels.
The accuracy of temperature prediction is theoretically bounded by the overlap of energy probability distributions at different temperatures.
Convolutional networks perform better because they capture spatial correlations, leading to learning internal energy rather than magnetization.
papers.limitation:
The method may not correctly detect phase transitions driven by different physical mechanisms such as Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transitions or topological phase transitions.
The fully-connected network only distinguishes between ordered and disordered phases and cannot predict fine-grained temperatures within each phase.
The accuracy of temperature prediction is limited by the overlap of energy distributions at different temperatures in finite systems.
papers.abstract: Abstract We discuss an aspect of neural networks for the purpose of phase transition detection. To this end, we first train the neural network by feeding Ising/Potts configurations with labels of temperature so that it can predict the temperature of the input. We do not explicitly supervise whether the configurations are in the ordered/disordered phase. Nevertheless, we can identify the critical temperature from the parameters (weights and biases) of the trained neural network. We attempt to understand how temperature-supervised neural networks capture information on the phase transition by paying attention to what quantities they learn. Our detailed analyses reveal that they learn different physical quantities depending on how well they are trained. The main observation in this study is how the weights in the trained neural network can have information on the phase transition in addition to temperature.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Imbedding Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we explicate the depth variable in neural networks to reduce optimal control problems to forward-facing initial value problems?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Invariant Imbedding Networks (InImNets), which explicate depth as a variable and reduce optimal control problems to forward-facing initial value problems, enabling efficient training and inspection of network depth properties.
papers.conclusion: InImNets provide a new way to understand depth in neural networks, reduce optimal control problems to initial value problems, and show competitive performance on benchmark tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The invariant imbedding method transforms the two-point boundary value problem into a system of forward-facing initial value problems.
InImNets achieve competitive performance on rotating MNIST and bouncing balls tasks compared to state-of-the-art methods.
InImNets are computationally more efficient than some existing methods (e.g., Vialard et al. 2020).
InImNets allow extrapolation of outputs beyond the trained depth, providing insight into depth-dependent behavior.
The approximation of input gradients (Equation 21) works well in practice, mitigating memory costs.
papers.limitation: Computation of nested Jacobians is expensive and increases exponentially with depth, posing a challenge for training deep networks.
future_direction: Study the variability of depth in optimal systems using Theorem 3.
Investigate stability issues related to Lyapunov exponents in InImNets.
papers.abstract: Continuous-depth neural networks, such as Neural ODEs, have refashioned the understanding of residual neural networks in terms of non-linear vector-valued optimal control problems. The common solution is to use the adjoint sensitivity method to replicate a forward-backward pass optimisation problem. We propose a new approach which explicates the network's `depth' as a fundamental variable, thus reducing the problem to a system of forward-facing initial value problems. This new method is based on the principle of `Invariant Imbedding' for which we prove a general solution, applicable to all non-linear, vector-valued optimal control problems with both running and terminal loss. Our new architectures provide a tangible tool for inspecting the theoretical--and to a great extent unexplained--properties of network depth. They also constitute a resource of discrete implementations of Neural ODEs comparable to classes of imbedded residual neural networks. Through a series of experiments, we show the competitive performance of the proposed architectures for supervised learning and time series prediction.

papers.title: Concept Bottleneck Language Models For protein design
papers.research_question: How can we design a protein language model that is controllable, interpretable, and debuggable without sacrificing performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Bottleneck Language Models, a novel architecture that incorporates human-understandable concepts via a concept bottleneck layer, enabling precise control, interpretability, and debugging while maintaining performance comparable to traditional language models.
papers.conclusion: CB-pLM provides a framework for controllable, interpretable, and debuggable language models without sacrificing performance, making it particularly valuable for high-stakes domains like protein design.
papers.key_findings:
CB-pLM achieves 3x better control in terms of change in concept magnitude and 16% improvement in control accuracy compared to baselines.
CB-pLM maintains pre-training perplexity and downstream task performance comparable to traditional masked protein language models.
CB-pLM enables multi-concept interventions with high accuracy (94% control accuracy).
CB-pLM allows interpretability and debugging by inspecting the linear decoder weights, revealing concept-token relationships.
CB-pLM can generalize to unseen concept combinations, as demonstrated on ColorMNIST.
future_direction: Extending CB-LM to other domains and architectures
Adding new concepts to a trained CB-LM via fine-tuning
Generalization to new concept combinations
papers.abstract: We introduce Concept Bottleneck Protein Language Models (CB-pLM), a generative masked language model with a layer where each neuron corresponds to an interpretable concept. Our architecture offers three key benefits: i) Control: We can intervene on concept values to precisely control the properties of generated proteins, achieving a 3 times larger change in desired concept values compared to baselines. ii) Interpretability: A linear mapping between concept values and predicted tokens allows transparent analysis of the model's decision-making process. iii) Debugging: This transparency facilitates easy debugging of trained models. Our models achieve pre-training perplexity and downstream task performance comparable to traditional masked protein language models, demonstrating that interpretability does not compromise performance. While adaptable to any language model, we focus on masked protein language models due to their importance in drug discovery and the ability to validate our model's capabilities through real-world experiments and expert knowledge. We scale our CB-pLM from 24 million to 3 billion parameters, making them the largest Concept Bottleneck Models trained and the first capable of generative language modeling.

papers.title: Multiscale Graph Neural Network Autoencoders for Interpretable Scientific Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we develop an autoencoder-based model that achieves both latent space interpretability and compatibility with unstructured meshes for complex fluid flow applications?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a novel graph neural network autoencoder that uses adaptive Top-K pooling to create interpretable latent graphs (visualized as masked fields) and multiscale message passing layers to efficiently reconstruct flow fields from unstructured mesh data.
papers.conclusion: The developed GNN autoencoder provides an interpretable and mesh-compatible framework for scientific machine learning, effectively identifying coherent flow structures and reconstructing flow fields, with promising potential for reduced-order modeling.
papers.key_findings:
The inclusion of multiscale message passing (MMP) layers, especially with coarsening in both encoder and decoder, significantly improves flow field reconstruction accuracy from the latent graph.
The latent graphs produced by the Top-K pooling layer (visualized as masked fields) identify time-evolving coherent structures in the flow, such as recirculation zones, providing direct physical interpretability.
Increasing the level of graph reduction (compression) leads to higher reconstruction errors, but the masked fields show how the model adapts its focus, e.g., shifting attention to inflow/outflow boundaries at high compression.
Reconstruction errors (RMSE) are more sensitive to Reynolds number for the streamwise velocity component compared to the vertical velocity component.
The architecture successfully handles unstructured meshes and complex geometries inherent to computational fluid dynamics simulations.
papers.limitation:
The effects of increased message passing and coarsening operations within the MMP layer warrant further investigation to potentially alleviate increased reconstruction error in higher-compression models.
Geometry extrapolation capability (performance on unseen geometric configurations) was not explored in this work.
future_direction: Investigating the effects of increased message passing and coarsening operations within the MMP layer.
Assessment of latent graph properties and model performance on different geometric configurations to solidify general applicability.
Using the concept of masked field evolution for interpretable data-based surrogate modeling of complex fluid flow phenomena.
papers.abstract: The goal of this work is to address two limitations in autoencoder-based models: latent space interpretability and compatibility with unstructured meshes. This is accomplished here with the development of a novel graph neural network (GNN) autoencoding architecture with demonstrations on complex fluid flow applications. To address the first goal of interpretability, the GNN autoencoder achieves reduction in the number nodes in the encoding stage through an adaptive graph reduction procedure. This reduction procedure essentially amounts to flowfield-conditioned node sampling and sensor identification, and produces interpretable latent graph representations tailored to the flowfield reconstruction task in the form of so-called masked fields. These masked fields allow the user to (a) visualize where in physical space a given latent graph is active, and (b) interpret the time-evolution of the latent graph connectivity in accordance with the time-evolution of unsteady flow features (e.g. recirculation zones, shear layers) in the domain. To address the goal of unstructured mesh compatibility, the autoencoding architecture utilizes a series of multi-scale message passing (MMP) layers, each of which models information exchange among node neighborhoods at various lengthscales. The MMP layer, which augments standard single-scale message passing with learnable coarsening operations, allows the decoder to more efficiently reconstruct the flowfield from the identified regions in the masked fields. Analysis of latent graphs produced by the autoencoder for various model settings are conducted using using unstructured snapshot data sourced from large-eddy simulations in a backward-facing step (BFS) flow configuration with an OpenFOAM-based flow solver at high Reynolds numbers.

papers.title: The Computational Complexity of Circuit Discovery for Inner Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the computational complexity of circuit discovery queries for inner interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a complexity analysis of circuit discovery queries, showing that many are intractable (NP-hard, Σp2-hard, etc.), but also identifies tractable relaxations such as quasi-minimal circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that circuit discovery for inner interpretability is computationally challenging, but identifies tractable relaxations and provides a framework for understanding the complexity of interpretability queries.
papers.key_findings:
Many circuit discovery queries (e.g., sufficient circuit, circuit ablation) are NP-hard or Σp2-hard.
Some queries remain fixed-parameter intractable (W[1]-hard) even when parameterizing by model depth or other features.
Some queries are inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes.
There is a formal separation between local and global query complexity, which helps explain interpretability illusions.
Quasi-minimal circuit queries are tractable (PTIME) and retain useful affordances for description and control.
future_direction: Empirical and formal characterization of learned weights to inform average-case analyses.
Exploring more parameters for fixed-parameter tractability in circuit discovery queries.
Designing queries that rely on mid-level abstractions to bridge circuits and human-intelligible algorithms.
papers.abstract: Many proposed applications of neural networks in machine learning, cognitive/brain science, and society hinge on the feasibility of inner interpretability via circuit discovery. This calls for empirical and theoretical explorations of viable algorithmic options. Despite advances in the design and testing of heuristics, there are concerns about their scalability and faithfulness at a time when we lack understanding of the complexity properties of the problems they are deployed to solve. To address this, we study circuit discovery with classical and parameterized computational complexity theory: (1) we describe a conceptual scaffolding to reason about circuit finding queries in terms of affordances for description, explanation, prediction and control; (2) we formalize a comprehensive set of queries for mechanistic explanation, and propose a formal framework for their analysis; (3) we use it to settle the complexity of many query variants and relaxations of practical interest on multi-layer perceptrons. Our findings reveal a challenging complexity landscape. Many queries are intractable, remain fixed-parameter intractable relative to model/circuit features, and inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes. To navigate this landscape, we prove there exist transformations to tackle some of these hard problems with better-understood heuristics, and prove the tractability or fixed-parameter tractability of more modest queries which retain useful affordances. This framework allows us to understand the scope and limits of interpretability queries, explore viable options, and compare their resource demands on existing and future architectures.

papers.title: The Representation and Recall of Interwoven Structured Knowledge in LLMs: A Geometric and Layered Analysis
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode interwoven scientific knowledge, and do they reflect geometric structures like the periodic table?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode scientific knowledge in geometric structures, such as a 3D spiral aligning with the periodic table, representing knowledge as interwoven manifolds rather than isolated facts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations that reflect the structured geometry of scientific knowledge, representing symbolic knowledge as geometry-aware, interwoven manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure is observed in hidden states that aligns with the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous attributes enabling indirect recall, while deeper layers sharpen categorical distinctions.
Linguistic context increasingly shapes representations in later layers.
Middle layers have strong linear associations between related attributes, which weaken in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Prompts are focused on chemical elements and may not extend to domains with more abstract features.
Hypothesis-driven validation may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge, such as materials property prediction.
Informing the design of downstream embedding-based tasks.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs) represent and recall multi-associated attributes across transformer layers. We show that intermediate layers encode factual knowledge by superimposing related attributes in overlapping spaces, along with effective recall even when attributes are not explicitly prompted. In contrast, later layers refine linguistic patterns and progressively separate attribute representations, optimizing task-specific outputs while appropriately narrowing attribute recall. We identify diverse encoding patterns including, for the first time, the observation of 3D spiral structures when exploring information related to the periodic table of elements. Our findings reveal a dynamic transition in attribute representations across layers, contributing to mechanistic interpretability and providing insights for understanding how LLMs handle complex, interrelated knowledge.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Learning biologically relevant features in a pathology foundation model using sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from the embeddings of a pathology foundation model, and how do these features evolve across model layers and generalize across domains?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from a pathology foundation model's embeddings, revealing that these features evolve across layers (from low-level color to high-level cell-type concepts) and are robust to domain shifts like scanner and stain type.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders enable the extraction of interpretable, monosemantic, and biologically-grounded features from a pathology foundation model, demonstrating the model's internal representations evolve to capture robust biological concepts, which motivates further work on explainable features for medical applications.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE dimensions show strong correlations with counts of specific cell types (e.g., plasma cells, lymphocytes), demonstrating monosemantic representation of biological concepts.
These biologically-grounded SAE features are unique to the pathology-pretrained model (PLUTO) and are not found in a self-supervised model (DINO) pretrained on natural images.
SAE features evolve across the model's depth: early layers correlate with low-level color features, while later layers correlate with high-level cell-type features, indicating the model gains invariance to spurious factors.
The monosemantic SAE representations (e.g., for plasma cells) are robust and generalizable to out-of-domain pathology datasets (CPTAC).
Cell-type specific SAE dimensions identified in later layers show reduced sensitivity to scanner and stain variations, indicating the model learns robust biological representations.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was restricted to a vanilla sparse autoencoder; newer variations like gated SAE and k-sparse SAE were not applied.
The findings are based on a single pathology foundation model (PLUTO); translation to other pathology foundation models is left for future study.
Interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features were not performed.
future_direction: Application of newer sparse autoencoder variations (e.g., gated SAE, k-sparse SAE) in pathology.
Analysis of how the findings translate to other pathology foundation models.
Performing interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features.
papers.abstract: Pathology plays an important role in disease diagnosis, treatment decision-making and drug development. Previous works on interpretability for machine learning models on pathology images have revolved around methods such as attention value visualization and deriving human-interpretable features from model heatmaps. Mechanistic interpretability is an emerging area of model interpretability that focuses on reverse-engineering neural networks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising direction in terms of extracting monosemantic features from polysemantic model activations. In this work, we trained a Sparse Autoencoder on the embeddings of a pathology pretrained foundation model. We found that Sparse Autoencoder features represent interpretable and monosemantic biological concepts. In particular, individual SAE dimensions showed strong correlations with cell type counts such as plasma cells and lymphocytes. These biological representations were unique to the pathology pretrained model and were not found in a self-supervised model pretrained on natural images. We demonstrated that such biologically-grounded monosemantic representations evolved across the model's depth, and the pathology foundation model eventually gained robustness to non-biological factors such as scanner type. The emergence of biologically relevant SAE features was generalizable to an out-of-domain dataset. Our work paves the way for further exploration around interpretable feature dimensions and their utility for medical and clinical applications.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
